citations.quote: For every field $F$, every ideal of $F[x]$ is generated by one polynomial; equivalently, $F[x]$ is a principal ideal domain.

For a field $F$,
$$ F[x]_{(x)}=\left\{\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\in F(x):g(0)\ne0\right\}. $$
This is the ring of rational functions defined at $0$. Its maximal ideal is generated by $x$, and its residue field is canonically $F$.

Let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal of a commutative ring $R$. Then $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is a nonzero local ring. Its unique maximal ideal is
$$ \mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}=\{r/s:r\in\mathfrak p,\ s\notin\mathfrak p\}, $$
and its units are exactly the fractions $r/s$ with $r\notin\mathfrak p$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $\mathfrak p\subset R$ be a prime ideal. Since $1\notin\mathfrak p$ and the product of two elements outside $\mathfrak p$ remains outside $\mathfrak p$, the complement $R\setminus\mathfrak p$ is multiplicative. The **localisation of $R$ at $\mathfrak p$** is
$$ R_{\mathfrak p}=(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}R. $$
Its elements are fractions $r/s$ with $s\notin\mathfrak p$.

Let $R$ be a nonfield domain. The following are equivalent.

1. $R$ is a discrete valuation ring.
2. $R$ is a Noetherian valuation ring.
3. $R$ is a one-dimensional Noetherian local integrally closed domain.
4. $R$ is a local principal ideal domain with nonzero maximal ideal.
Every discrete valuation ring is a principal ideal domain.

Let $K$ be a field and let $v$ be a discrete valuation on $K$
([[def-discrete-valuation]]). Its **valuation ring** is
$$ V_v:=\{x\in K:v(x)\ge 0\}. $$
This is a valuation ring in the sense of [[def-valuation-ring]].

A **discrete valuation ring** (DVR) is a subring $V\subseteq K$ of the form
$V=V_v$ for some discrete valuation $v$ on $K$. Because $v$ is surjective,
there is an element of value $1$, so $V$ has a nonunit and is therefore not a
field.

For every field $F$, the polynomial ring $F[t]$ is an integral domain, and
$$ F(t):=\operatorname{Frac}(F[t])=\left\{\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}:f,g\in F[t],\ g\ne0\right\} $$
is a field containing an embedded copy of $F[t]$. It is called the **rational function field** over $F$. In particular, $\mathbb R(t)=\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb R[t])$.

Let $\mathbb Z[t]$ be the polynomial ring over the integers
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]],
[[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]) and let
$$S=\{t^k:k\ge0\}.$$
The set $S$ is multiplicative, and the **Laurent polynomial ring** is the
principal localisation
$$\Lambda_1:=\mathbb Z[t]_S=S^{-1}\mathbb Z[t]$$
([[def-principal-localisation]], [[def-multiplicative-subset-and-localisation]]).
It is a commutative ring with unit $1=t^0$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]). Write
again $t$ for the image of the indeterminate under the localisation map; then
$t$ is a unit with inverse $t^{-1}$
([[prop-units-in-a-localisation]]). Every element of $\Lambda_1$ has a
representative
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k,\qquad a_k\in\mathbb Z,$$
with only finitely many nonzero coefficients, obtained by writing a fraction
$p/t^N$ as a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of the powers
$t^{k-N}$; the finite coefficient sequence is unique: after multiplying two such sums
by a common sufficiently large power of $t$, equality becomes equality of
ordinary polynomials. The localisation map $\mathbb Z[t]\to\Lambda_1$ is
injective because $\mathbb Z[t]$ is a domain; hence their coefficients agree
([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-domain-is-a-domain]]). Equivalently, two such
sums are equal exactly when their coefficient sequences agree
([[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]).

**Universal property.** Let $A$ be a ring with unit and let
$\varphi\colon\mathbb Z[t]\to A$ be a unital ring homomorphism with
$\varphi(t)$ a unit of $A$. Then there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\widetilde\varphi\colon\Lambda_1\to A$ with
$\widetilde\varphi(t)=\varphi(t)$. Equivalently, for every unital ring $A$ and
every unit $u\in A$ there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\Lambda_1\to A$ with $t\mapsto u$ ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]],
[[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

The cited localisation theorem treats commutative target rings. For the
possibly noncommutative target used here, define
$\sum_k a_kt^k\mapsto\sum_k(a_k1_A)u^k$. Unique Laurent coefficients make
this well defined. Integer multiples of $1_A$ are central, and
$u^ku^l=u^{k+l}$ for all integers $k,l$, so finite distributivity proves
additivity, multiplicativity and preservation of $1$. Every unital
homomorphism must send $a_k$ to $a_k1_A$ and $t^k$ to $u^k$, proving
uniqueness. Taking $u=\varphi(t)$ gives the asserted extension of $\varphi$.

**Augmentation.** There is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$$\varepsilon\colon\Lambda_1\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,\qquad \varepsilon\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k\Bigr)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k,$$
the **sum-of-coefficients map** ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]]); it
is well defined because the coefficients are summable and their total sum is
unchanged along the relation of
[[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]. Its kernel is the
principal ideal $(t-1)$: indeed $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$, and if
$\varepsilon(x)=0$ then, writing $x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k$ with finite
support and using that $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k=0$, one has
$$x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k(t^k-1)=(t-1)\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k\,(1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}),$$
where $1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}$ denotes the empty sum $0$ for $k=0$ and, for
$k=-j<0$, the negative sum
$-(t^{-1}+t^{-2}+\cdots+t^{-j})$, so that
$t^{-j}-1=-(t-1)(t^{-1}+\cdots+t^{-j})$; hence $x\in(t-1)$, and the reverse
inclusion is $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$.

**Caveats.** This item realises $\Lambda_1$ by localisation and does **not**
identify it with an integral group ring: the additive group underlying
$\Lambda_1$ is $\bigoplus_{k\in\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z\,t^k$ and its multiplication
is the polynomial one ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-domain-is-a-domain]] is not
needed for the ring laws but records that $\mathbb Z[t]$ is a domain). The
deck-module structures on homology introduced later on this page are defined
separately, by the universal property above.

derivations.claim: Evaluation at $0$ has kernel $(q)$ and induces $\mathbb Q[q]/(q)\cong\mathbb Q$, so $(q)$ is a maximal ideal of $\mathbb Q[q]$ and $q\neq0$ ([[def-local-ring]]); in particular $(q)$ is a nonzero prime ideal of the PID $\mathbb Q[q]$.

The field of fractions of $A_0$ is $\mathbb Q(q)$: every polynomial $f\in\mathbb Q[q]$ lies in $A_0$ as $f/1$, so $\operatorname{Frac}(A_0)$ contains $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb Q[q])=\mathbb Q(q)$ by [L3]; conversely $A_0\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$ and $\mathbb Q(q)$ is a field, so $\operatorname{Frac}(A_0)\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$.

By [F2] applied to $\mathfrak p=(q)$, the localisation $A_0$ is a local ring with maximal ideal $(q)A_0=qA_0$, residue field $\mathbb Q$ under evaluation $f/g\mapsto f(0)/g(0)$: this map is surjective on constants and its kernel consists precisely of fractions with $f(0)=0$, namely $qA_0$, and units exactly the fractions $f/g$ with $f
otin(q)$, that is, $f(0)
eq0$ and $g(0)
eq0$.

By step 1.1, $(q)$ is a nonzero prime ideal of the principal ideal domain $\mathbb Q[q]$, and by step 2.1 the ring $A_0$ is a local domain with maximal ideal $qA_0\neq0$. Every ideal $J$ of $A_0$ is generated by its contraction: if $f/g\in J$ with $g(0)\neq0$ then $f=g\cdot(f/g)\in J\cap\mathbb Q[q]$ and $f/g=f\cdot(1/g)\in(J\cap\mathbb Q[q])A_0$, while $J\cap\mathbb Q[q]\subseteq J$ gives the reverse inclusion, so $J=(J\cap\mathbb Q[q])A_0$. The contraction $J\cap\mathbb Q[q]$ is an ideal of the principal ideal domain $\mathbb Q[q]$, hence principal, so $J$ is principal and $A_0$ is a local principal ideal domain with nonzero maximal ideal. By [L1] it is a discrete valuation ring; its maximal ideal is generated by $q/1$, so $q/1$ is a uniformiser, and by [L2] there is a discrete valuation $v$ of $\mathbb Q(q)$ with $A_0=\{h:v(h)\ge0\}$.

Normalisation. Every nonzero $x=f/g\in\mathbb Q(q)$ can be written uniquely as $q^nu$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$ and $u\in A_0^\times$: factor the maximal powers of $q$ from the nonzero polynomials $f,g$ and subtract their exponents. For the discrete valuation $v$ of step 3.1, units have value zero because both $u$ and $u^{-1}$ lie in $A_0$, so $v(x)=nv(q)$. Surjectivity of $v$ onto $\mathbb Z$ therefore forces $v(q)=1$. Set $\operatorname{ord}_q=v$; this is the vanishing order just computed, with value group $\mathbb Z$ and valuation ring $A_0$.

Uniqueness and units: if $w$ is any discrete valuation with $V_w=A_0$ and $w(q)=1$, then $w=\operatorname{ord}_q$. Indeed, for $x\in\mathbb Q(q)^\times$ one has $w(x)=0$ exactly when $x\in A_0$ and $x^{-1}\in A_0$, that is, exactly when $x\in A_0^\times$; for nonzero $x$ the element $x/q^{\operatorname{ord}_q(x)}$ lies in $A_0^\times$, so $w(x)=w(q^{\operatorname{ord}_q(x)})+0=\operatorname{ord}_q(x)$, using $w(q)=1$, additivity and $w(1)=0$. Thus $\operatorname{ord}_q$ is the unique such valuation and $A_0=\{h:\operatorname{ord}_q(h)\ge0\}$, with units $\{h\neq0:\operatorname{ord}_q(h)=0\}$.

The crystal limit: let $L=\bigoplus_{j\in J}A_0e_j$ be a free $A_0$-module with the displayed basis. The residue classes $e_j+qL$ form a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $L/qL$ because $A_0/qA_0\cong\mathbb Q$ by step 2.1, and the elements $1\otimes e_j$ form a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $\mathbb Q\otimes_{A_0}L$; the displayed map sends the second basis to the first, so it is an isomorphism. For $\lambda\in\mathbb Q(q)^\times$, multiplication by $\lambda$ is a bijection $L\to\lambda L$ carrying $qL$ onto $q\lambda L=\lambda qL$, hence induces an $A_0$-module isomorphism $L/qL\to\lambda L/q\lambda L$. No choice principle is used: the basis of $L$ is given, and all further objects are residue projections of explicitly presented fractional ideals of $\mathbb Q[q]$.

boundaries.evidence: The Definition quantifies over all free $A_0$-modules and all fractions $f/g$ with $g(0)\ne0$; the multiplicative set $\mathbb Q[q]\setminus(q)$ contains $1$, so the localisation is not the zero ring, and step 7.1 is applied to every free module $L$, including $L=0$, where both sides of the crystal-limit map are $0$.

The boundary "zero" is the maximal ideal rather than the number $0$: step 1.1 computes the kernel of evaluation at $0$ as $(q)$ and step 2.1 identifies $qA_0$ as the unique maximal ideal, so $0\in qA_0$ and the residue field is $\mathbb Q$; no argument divides by an element of $A_0$ that vanishes at $0$, since units are exactly the fractions with $f(0),g(0)\ne0$ in step 2.1.

The unit $1$ has order $0$ and is a unit of $A_0$; step 5.1 characterises $A_0^\times$ exactly as the elements of normalised valuation $0$, which is the case $k=0$ of the element $x/q^{\operatorname{ord}_q(x)}$ appearing there.

Step 4.1 factors every nonzero rational function as $q^nu$ with $u$ a unit. Thus all valuation values are multiples of $v(q)$; surjectivity forces $v(q)=1$, rather than dividing an arbitrary value group by $v(q)$.

The comparison elements of step 6.1 are the two boundary elements $q^{-1}$ and $(1+q)^{-1}$: $q^{-1}\in A\setminus A_0$ and $(1+q)^{-1}\in A_0\setminus A$ show that neither of the two subrings contains the other, and the valuation range of $\operatorname{ord}_q$ on $\mathbb Q(q)^\times$ is all of $\mathbb Z$ by step 4.1, so there is no endpoint in the value group.

No choice is used: step 7.1 exhibits the isomorphism $\mathbb Q\otimes_{A_0}L\to L/qL$ and the $\lambda$-scaling isomorphism by explicit formulas on the elements of an arbitrary given free basis, and steps 4.1-5.1 fix the normalisation $\operatorname{ord}_q(q)=1$ uniquely; nothing selects from a family of nonempty sets.

The biconditional "x\in A_0^\times$ if and only if $\operatorname{ord}_q(x)=0$" is proved in step 5.1: forward, if $x$ is a unit then $x,x^{-1}\in A_0$, so $\operatorname{ord}_q(x)\ge0$ and $\operatorname{ord}_q(x^{-1})\ge0$ give equality to $0$.

Converse reading of the same statement in step 5.1: if $\operatorname{ord}_q(x)=0$ then $x/q^{0}=x$ and its inverse both have nonnegative order, hence both lie in $A_0$ and $x\in A_0^\times$; the step records both directions together with the uniqueness of the normalised valuation.

citations.quote:
Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group
with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), with root lattice $Q$,
simple roots $\alpha_i\in P$ and integer pairing
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$, and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with generators $E_i,F_i,K_h$
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). The lattice $P$ plays
the role of the integral weights of the classical theory
([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]); the pairing need not
be perfect, and no identification $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$ is
assumed anywhere.

A **$P$-graded type-one quantum weight module** is a left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$
together with a direct sum decomposition

$$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$$

(an internal direct sum of $\mathbb Q(q)$-subspaces, only finitely many nonzero
on each vector) such that, for all $\mu\in P$, $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $i\in I$,

$$K_h\ \text{acts on}\ M_\mu\ \text{by the scalar}\ q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle},\qquad E_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu+\alpha_i},\qquad F_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu-\alpha_i}.$$

The subspaces $M_\mu$ are the **chosen label-weight spaces**: the grading is
part of the structure and is not reconstructed from the action, because the
pairing may have a kernel. **Morphisms** of $P$-graded type-one weight modules
are the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps $f\colon M\to N$ with
$f(M_\mu)\subseteq N_\mu$ for every $\mu$; the weight submodules and quotients
considered on this page are those with the induced grading (Verification, step 2.2).

The module is **integrable** if $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every
vector: for every $v\in M$ and every $i$ there are integers $N_e(v,i),N_f(v,i)\ge1$
with $E_i^{N_e(v,i)}v=0$ and $F_i^{N_f(v,i)}v=0$. The exponents may depend on
the vector and on $i$, and both directions are required independently;
integrability is not a uniform nilpotence condition.

The following are additional hypotheses, never part of the definition:
finiteness of the dimension of every $M_\mu$; boundedness of the set of $\mu$
with $M_\mu\ne0$ above (or below); finite generation of $M$. The zero module is
a $P$-graded type-one weight module with the empty grading ($M_\mu=0$ for all
$\mu$), and it is integrable.

Two remarks are recorded here and proved below. First, when the pairing
separates $P$, the spaces $M_\mu$ are exactly the simultaneous eigenspaces of
the $K_h$, and the present definition recovers the usual type-one weight
modules (Verification, steps 2.1 and 4.1). Second, when the pairing does not
separate, distinct labels $\mu\ne\mu'$ may carry the same toral character, and
a simultaneous toral eigenspace must not be equated with a single label space;
the definition therefore takes the label grading as data. The regularization of
finite-cone support and all highest-weight comparisons on this page are proved
later, not assumed here by writing $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$.
No choice principle enters this definition.

A **generalized Cartan matrix** (GCM) is an integer matrix $A=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$, where $I=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $n\ge1$, such that $a_{ii}=2$, $a_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and $a_{ij}=0\iff a_{ji}=0$. It is **indecomposable** if there is no partition $I=J\sqcup K$ into nonempty sets with all entries between $J$ and $K$ zero.

A **symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group** consists of a finite nonempty index set $I=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, a symmetrizable generalized Cartan matrix $A=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$ ([[def-generalized-cartan-matrix]], [[def-symmetrizable-generalized-cartan-matrix]]) and a chosen diagonal symmetrizer $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$ with $d_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$ and $d_i a_{ij}=d_j a_{ji}$ for all $i,j$; free abelian groups $P^\vee$ and $P$ ([[def-free-abelian-group]]) with an integer-valued bilinear pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times P^\vee\to\mathbb Z$; simple coroots $h_i\in P^\vee$ that are linearly independent in $P^\vee\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$; and simple roots $\alpha_i\in P$ that freely generate the root lattice $Q=\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\alpha_i\subseteq P$ ([[def-kac-moody-root-lattice-height-and-positive-cone]]) and satisfy $\langle\alpha_j,h_i\rangle=a_{ij}$ for all $i,j$ ([[def-realization-of-a-generalized-cartan-matrix]], [[prop-minimal-realizations-exist-and-are-unique-up-to-isomorphism]]).

The index set is finite and $A$ need not be nonsingular. We do not require the simple coroots to span $P^\vee\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$, and the pairing is not required to be perfect; choosing $P$ and $P^\vee$ is part of the datum, not something determined by the matrix alone.

We fix an indeterminate $q$ over $\mathbb Q$, work over $\mathbb Q(q)$, and set $q_i=q^{d_i}$. For $h\in P^\vee$, $\langle\alpha_i,h\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ is the exponent in $q^{\langle\alpha_i,h\rangle}$. We use the row convention $\langle\alpha_j,h_i\rangle=a_{ij}$ throughout. No fundamental weights with prescribed values on all $h_i$ are part of this definition.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. For $m\in\mathbb N$, define the **$q_i$-integer**

$$[m]_i:=\frac{q_i^m-q_i^{-m}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}},\qquad [0]_i:=0,$$

and the **$q_i$-factorial**

$$[m]_i!:=\prod_{k=1}^m[k]_i,\qquad [0]_i!:=1.$$

For $0\le r\le m$, define the **Gaussian binomial** $\binom{m}{r}_i:=[m]_i!/([r]_i![m-r]_i!)$, and set it to $0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$. In the published one-parameter convention, write $\binom{m}{r}_t:=\binom{m}{r,m-r}_t$ for the two-part $q$-multinomial coefficient of [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]].

For an element $x$ of a unital $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and $m\ge0$, define its **divided power at $q_i$** by $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$, so $x^{(0)}=1$ and $x^{(1)}=x$.

The symmetric convention and the published asymmetric convention are related, for $m\ge0$ and $0\le r\le m$, by

$$[m]_i=q_i^{-(m-1)}[m]_{q_i^2},\qquad \binom{m}{r}_i=q_i^{-r(m-r)}\binom{m}{r}_{q_i^2}.$$

In particular $[m]_i$ is invariant under $q_i\mapsto q_i^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the symmetrizer only through $q_i=q^{d_i}$.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$, an index $i\in I$, and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. Let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra and let $A_i$ be the subalgebra generated by $E_i,F_i,K_i^{\pm1}$ ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]); write $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$ for the divided powers of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]].

(i) The assignment $e\mapsto E_i$, $f\mapsto F_i$, $k\mapsto K_i$, $k^{-1}\mapsto K_i^{-1}$ defines an algebra isomorphism from the standard rank-one algebra $\mathbb A$ over $\mathbb Q(q)$, presented by $e,f,k^{\pm1}$ with $kek^{-1}=q_i^2e$, $kfk^{-1}=q_i^{-2}f$ and $[e,f]=(k-k^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ onto $A_i$; the images of the monomials $F_i^aK_i^mE_i^b$ ($a,b\ge0$, $m\in\mathbb Z$) are linearly independent in $U_q(\mathfrak g)$, being images of the PBW monomials of the triangular decomposition ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]).

(ii) For all $a,b\ge0$, $K_iE_i^{(a)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{2a}E_i^{(a)}$ and $K_iF_i^{(b)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{-2b}F_i^{(b)}$, and for $b\ge1$ the divided powers satisfy the exact commutation formula
$$E_iF_i^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}E_i+\frac{F_i^{(b-1)}}{q_i^{b}-q_i^{-b}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}\bigl(q_i^{-2s}K_i-q_i^{2s}K_i^{-1}\bigr);$$
iterating it computes $E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}$ as a finite sum of monomials $F_i^{(b-t)}K_i^{m}E_i^{(a-t)}$ ($0\le t\le\min(a,b)$) with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$.

(iii) For every $N\ge0$ there is a simple $A_i$-module $L_i(N)$ of dimension $N+1$: it is the quotient of the cyclic module $\widetilde M(N):=A_i/\bigl(A_iE_i+A_i(K_i-q_i^N)\bigr)$ by the submodule generated by $F_i^{(N+1)}w_N$, where $w_N$ is the image of $1$, with basis the images $v_t$ of $F_i^{(t)}w_N$, $0\le t\le N$, on which $K_iv_t=q_i^{N-2t}v_t$, $F_iv_t=[t+1]_iv_{t+1}$ and $E_iv_t=[N-t+1]_iv_{t-1}$ (with $v_{-1}=v_{N+1}=0$); $L_i(N)$ is the unique simple $A_i$-module generated by a vector $v\ne0$ with $E_iv=0$, $K_iv=q_i^Nv$ and $F_i^{N+1}v=0$.

Let $T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$, and factor its minimal polynomial in the UFD $F[x]$ as

$$\mu_T=\prod_{i<r}q_i^{e_i},$$

where the $q_i$ are distinct monic irreducibles and $e_i\ge1$. Then the subspaces $V_i:=\ker q_i(T)^{e_i}$ are $T$-invariant and

$$V=\bigoplus_{i<r}V_i.$$

Moreover, the minimal polynomial of $T|_{V_i}$ is exactly $q_i^{e_i}$. If $V=0$, then $r=0$ and this is the empty direct sum.

A **composition series** of a left $R$-module $M$ is a finite chain $$0=M_0<M_1<\cdots<M_n=M$$ whose factors $M_i/M_{i-1}$ are simple. If such a series exists, the **length** $\ell_R(M)$ is its number $n$ of factors; [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]] proves independence of the chosen series. The zero module has the empty series and length $0$.

derivations.claim: Finite-dimensional reduction. Let $u\in M_\lambda$. Choose $N\ge0$ with $E_i^Nu=0$ and set $W:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q(q)}\{F_i^{(a)}E_i^bu:0\le b<N,\ a\ge0\}$. Then $W$ is finite-dimensional: for each of the finitely many $b<N$ the local nilpotence of $F_i$ gives an integer $A_b$ with $F_i^{A_b}E_i^bu=0$, so the span of the vectors $F_i^{(a)}E_i^bu$, $a\ge0$, is already spanned by the finitely many vectors with $a<A_b$.

The commutation scalar. Let $v$ be a weight vector with $E_iv=0$ and $K_iv=q_i^av$, where $a=\langle\mathrm{wt}(v),h_i\rangle$. For $b\ge1$ the formula of [F4] gives $E_iF_i^{(b)}v=F_i^{(b-1)}\Theta_{i,b}v$, and $\Theta_{i,b}$ acts on $v$ by the scalar $(q_i^{b}-q_i^{-b})^{-1}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}(q_i^{-2s}q_i^{a}-q_i^{2s}q_i^{-a})=[a-b+1]_i$ by the finite geometric-sum identities; hence $E_iF_i^{(b)}v=[a-b+1]_iF_i^{(b-1)}v$.

The Casimir. Put $\varphi(K_i):=(q_iK_i+q_i^{-1}K_i^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})^2$ and $C:=F_iE_i+\varphi(K_i)\in A_i$. Then $C$ is central in $A_i$: from $K_iE_iK_i^{-1}=q_i^2E_i$ and $K_iF_iK_i^{-1}=q_i^{-2}F_i$ one computes $\varphi(q_i^{2}K_i)-\varphi(K_i)=(q_i^{2}K_i-q_i^{-2}K_i^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ and hence $[\varphi(K_i),E_i]=E_i(\varphi(q_i^2K_i)-\varphi(K_i))=(K_i-K_i^{-1})E_i/(q_i-q_i^{-1})=-[F_iE_i,E_i]$, while $\varphi(q_i^{-2}K_i)-\varphi(K_i)=-(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ gives $[\varphi(K_i),F_i]=-F_i(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})=-[F_iE_i,F_i]$; so $[C,E_i]=[C,F_i]=0$, and $C$ commutes with $K_i^{\pm1}$ visibly. Moreover $C$ acts on every weight vector $v$ with $E_iv=0$ and $K_iv=q_i^av$ by the scalar $c_a:=\varphi(q_i^a)=(q_i^{a+1}+q_i^{-a-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})^2$.

The scalars $c_a$ for $a\ge0$ are pairwise distinct: if $c_a=c_b$ with $a,b\ge0$, then $q_i^{a+1}+q_i^{-a-1}=q_i^{b+1}+q_i^{-b-1}$, that is $(q_i^{a+1}-q_i^{b+1})(1-q_i^{-(a+b+2)})=0$; as $q_i$ is transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, $q_i^m=1$ forces $m=0$, so the second factor is nonzero and $q_i^{a+1}=q_i^{b+1}$ gives $a=b$.

$W$ is a finite-dimensional $A_i$-submodule on which $E_i$ and $F_i$ are nilpotent and $K_i$ is diagonalisable with eigenvalues in $q_i^{\mathbb Z}$. Indeed $F_iF_i^{(a)}=[a+1]_iF_i^{(a+1)}$ and $K_iF_i^{(a)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{-2a}F_i^{(a)}$ show that $F_i$ and $K_i$ preserve $W$, and for $a\ge1$ the commutation formula of [F4] gives $E_iF_i^{(a)}E_i^bu=F_i^{(a)}E_i^{b+1}u+F_i^{(a-1)}\Theta_{i,a}E_i^bu$, where $\Theta_{i,a}$ acts on the weight vector $E_i^bu$ by a scalar; for $b+1<N$ both terms lie in $W$, and for $b+1=N$ the first term is $F_i^{(a)}E_i^Nu=0$, so $E_i$ preserves $W$. Nilpotence is inherited from local nilpotence on the finite-dimensional $W$, and diagonalisability with the eigenvalue form from [F1] and [F2].

e0$; decomposing $v_0$ into weight components and using that $E_i$ preserves weights, some nonzero weight component $v$ satisfies $E_iv=0$. With $a:=\langle\mathrm{wt}(v),h_iangle$, step 3.1 gives $a\ge0$, $F_i^{(a)}v
e0$ and $F_i^{(a+1)}v=0$. The span of $v,F_iv,\dots,F_i^{(a)}v$ is a nonzero $A_i$-submodule by the formulas of steps 1.2 and 2.2 together with $[0]_i=0$, so it equals the simple module $S$; these $a+1$ vectors have distinct weights, whence $\dim S=a+1$ and $C$ acts on $S$ by the scalar $c_a$ of step 1.3.

Generalized-eigenspace splitting. Let $W$ be as in steps 1.1-2.2. A finite-dimensional module has a composition series: take a proper submodule of largest possible dimension, whose quotient is simple, and repeat inside that submodule; dimensions strictly decrease. Since $C$ is central, it preserves this finite filtration and acts on each simple factor by some $c_a$ from step 4.1. The product of the corresponding linear operators $(C-c_a)$ annihilates $W$, since each factor lowers the filtration by one. Its minimal polynomial therefore has only these linear factors. Applying [F5], the generalized eigenspaces $W[a]:=\ker(C-c_a)^{m}\cap W$ are $A_i$-submodules with $W=\bigoplus_aW[a]$. Every composition factor of $W[a]$ has highest label $a$: a factor of label $b\ne a$, $b\ge0$, would make $C-c_b$ non-invertible on $W[a]$, whereas $C-c_b$ is invertible on the generalized eigenspace of the distinct scalar $c_a$.

Blocks. Fix $a\ge0$ with $W[a]\ne0$ and let $r:=\dim W[a]/(a+1)$, the number of composition factors of $W[a]$ counted with multiplicity. Each factor has by step 4.1 a weight-space decomposition into one-dimensional spaces of $K_i$-eigenvalues $q_i^{a},q_i^{a-2},\dots,q_i^{-a}$; Weight multiplicities add along this filtration: a lift of an eigenvector in a quotient can be projected to its eigenspace by the finite interpolation polynomial in the diagonal operator $K_i$, so the eigenspace sequence is exact. Hence the weight space of eigenvalue $q_i^{a-2n}$ has dimension $r$ for $0\le n\le a$, and $W[a]$ has no weight of eigenvalue $q_i^{m}$ with $m>a$. In particular $k:=\dim W[a]_{a}=r$, $\dim W[a]=k(a+1)$, and $E_i$ kills the top weight space $W[a]_{a}$ because it would raise the eigenvalue to $q_i^{a+2}$.

e0$: if $F_i^{(n)}w=0$ for some minimal $n\ge1$, then $F_i^{(n-1)}w
e0$ and step 1.2 gives $0=E_iF_i^{(n)}w=[a-n+1]_iF_i^{(n-1)}w$, forcing $n=a+1>a$ by [F3]. Hence each $N_n:=F_i^{(n)}W[a]_{a}$, $0\le n\le a$, has dimension $k$, and the $N_n$ lie in the distinct weight spaces of eigenvalues $q_i^{a-2n}$, so they are independent; their sum is $A_i$-stable because $E_iF_i^{(n)}w=[a-n+1]_iF_i^{(n-1)}w$ and $F_iF_i^{(n)}w=[n+1]_iF_i^{(n+1)}w$ for $w\in W[a]_a$; being a submodule of dimension $k(a+1)=\dim W[a]$, the sum equals $W[a]$.

Existence. Let $u\in M_\lambda$ be homogeneous and let $W$ be the finite-dimensional reduction of steps 1.1-2.2, which contains $u$ and splits as $W=\bigoplus_aW[a]=\bigoplus_a\bigoplus_{n=0}^{a}F_i^{(n)}W[a]_{a}$ by steps 5.1-7.1. All generators of $W$ have labels in $\lambda+\mathbb Z\alpha_i$; within this coset the integer $\langle\cdot,h_i\rangle$ distinguishes labels because $\langle\alpha_i,h_i\rangle=2$. Thus a summand $F_i^{(n)}W[a]_{a}$ lies in label weight $\lambda$ exactly when $a-2n=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle$, and then $W[a]_{a}\subseteq M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ with $E_i$ killing it, so it is contained in $H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$. Collecting, for each $n\ge0$, the top vectors of all blocks with $a=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle+2n$ into $u_n\in H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ gives $u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n$; here $u_n\ne0$ only when $0\le n\le a=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle+2n$, which is exactly the admissibility condition $n\le\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$. For a general $u\in M_\lambda$, apply this to the finitely many nonzero homogeneous components of $u$ and add.

Uniqueness. Suppose $\sum_{n=0}^{N}F_i^{(n)}u_n=0$ with $u_n\in H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ admissible and $u_N\ne0$. By [F4], $E_i^{N}F_i^{(n)}$ is a finite sum of terms $F_i^{(n-t)}K_i^{m}E_i^{N-t}$ with $0\le t\le n$; for $n<N$ every $t\le n$ satisfies $N-t\ge N-n\ge1$, so each term kills $u_n$ (as $E_iu_n=0$), while for $n=N$ only $t=N$ survives and, by iterating step 1.2, $E_i^{N}F_i^{(N)}u_N=\bigl(\prod_{t=1}^{N}[a_N-t+1]_i\bigr)u_N$ with $a_N=\langle\lambda+N\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$. Admissibility gives $a_N\ge N$, so $a_N-t+1\ge1$ for $1\le t\le N$ and the product is nonzero by [F3]. Hence $0=E_i^{N}0=\bigl(\prod_{t=1}^{N}[a_N-t+1]_i\bigr)u_N$ forces $u_N=0$, a contradiction.

Direct sum. By step 3.1(ii) applied to $H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$, the map $F_i^{(n)}$ on $H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ is injective for $n\le\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$ and zero otherwise. Steps 8.1 and 9.1 say that every $u\in M_\lambda$ is a unique sum of vectors from the nonzero spaces $F_i^{(n)}H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$, which is exactly the statement that $M_\lambda$ is their internal direct sum. All selections in the argument were among finitely many vectors or finitely many scalars, so no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: The statement is pointwise in $u$ and quantified over every $\mu$; for $u=0$ the admissible sum of (iii) has every coefficient zero and step 8.1's existence argument applies to an arbitrary homogeneous element including $0$, while $H_\mu=0$ for $a_\mu<0$ is step 3.1's first case.

Vanishing values are the subject of (i) and (ii): $H_\mu=0$ for $a_\mu<0$ and $F_i^{(n)}$ is the zero map for $n>a_\mu$ by step 3.1; in the uniqueness step 9.1 the top nonzero coefficient $u_N\ne0$ is assumed, so the zero decomposition is excluded from the nontrivial branch.

A decomposition with a single coefficient is the vector $F_i^{(n)}u_n$ of one string position; steps 7.1 and 8.1 build the length $\langle\mu,h_i\rangle+1$ string of a highest vector, whose first case $n=0$ is the highest vector itself, and step 3.1 covers the endpoints of that range.

The only module hypothesis is the chosen $P$-grading together with local nilpotence of $E_i,F_i$; step 1.1 constructs the finite-dimensional reduction $W$ for each vector from the bounds $A_b$ supplied by that nilpotence, and no finite-dimensionality, bounded support or uniform nilpotence of $M$ is assumed.

The top position $n=0$ is allowed and need not vanish. Step 3.1 proves injectivity for $0\le n\le a_\mu$ and vanishing beyond $a_\mu$; admissibility specifies only the beyond-bottom coefficients to be zero.

No choice is used: step 1.1 obtains $N$ and the finitely many bounds $A_b$ from the given local nilpotence, steps 5.1-6.1 split a finite-dimensional module by the generalized eigenspaces of the central Casimir $C$, and step 7.1 passes to the canonical blocks $W[a]$.

boundaries.reason: The theorem states existence and uniqueness of the admissible decomposition rather than a biconditional over propositions; its two halves are existence (step 8.1) and uniqueness (step 9.1), so there are no forward and reverse implications to separate.

The uniqueness half is a single statement proved once in step 9.1 by applying the $E_i$-power expansion of [F4] to a putative relation; no claim of the theorem has the shape of two mutually converse implications.

risk_review.notes: Checked every step, rank-one supplier formula, primary decomposition and composition-series statements; Kashiwara p.473 and JKK pp.14–15 state the usual decomposition, whereas this local finite-dimensional argument also handles unbounded arbitrary-dimensional integrable M. W is finite and invariant, Casimir values c_a are distinct for a>=0, composition multiplicities give k(a+1), and F^(n) is injective on the top. Labels are distinguished inside the single root coset even if the pairing has a kernel. Applying E^N proves uniqueness including N=0; negative highest labels and length-zero strings are covered. Corrected factorial coefficient and explicit splitting dependencies are sound; no AC. Current raw hash matches the reader result.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group
with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), with root lattice $Q$,
simple roots $\alpha_i\in P$ and integer pairing
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$, and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with generators $E_i,F_i,K_h$
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). The lattice $P$ plays
the role of the integral weights of the classical theory
([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]); the pairing need not
be perfect, and no identification $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$ is
assumed anywhere.

A **$P$-graded type-one quantum weight module** is a left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$
together with a direct sum decomposition

$$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$$

(an internal direct sum of $\mathbb Q(q)$-subspaces, only finitely many nonzero
on each vector) such that, for all $\mu\in P$, $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $i\in I$,

$$K_h\ \text{acts on}\ M_\mu\ \text{by the scalar}\ q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle},\qquad E_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu+\alpha_i},\qquad F_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu-\alpha_i}.$$

The subspaces $M_\mu$ are the **chosen label-weight spaces**: the grading is
part of the structure and is not reconstructed from the action, because the
pairing may have a kernel. **Morphisms** of $P$-graded type-one weight modules
are the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps $f\colon M\to N$ with
$f(M_\mu)\subseteq N_\mu$ for every $\mu$; the weight submodules and quotients
considered on this page are those with the induced grading (Verification, step 2.2).

The module is **integrable** if $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every
vector: for every $v\in M$ and every $i$ there are integers $N_e(v,i),N_f(v,i)\ge1$
with $E_i^{N_e(v,i)}v=0$ and $F_i^{N_f(v,i)}v=0$. The exponents may depend on
the vector and on $i$, and both directions are required independently;
integrability is not a uniform nilpotence condition.

The following are additional hypotheses, never part of the definition:
finiteness of the dimension of every $M_\mu$; boundedness of the set of $\mu$
with $M_\mu\ne0$ above (or below); finite generation of $M$. The zero module is
a $P$-graded type-one weight module with the empty grading ($M_\mu=0$ for all
$\mu$), and it is integrable.

Two remarks are recorded here and proved below. First, when the pairing
separates $P$, the spaces $M_\mu$ are exactly the simultaneous eigenspaces of
the $K_h$, and the present definition recovers the usual type-one weight
modules (Verification, steps 2.1 and 4.1). Second, when the pairing does not
separate, distinct labels $\mu\ne\mu'$ may carry the same toral character, and
a simultaneous toral eigenspace must not be equated with a single label space;
the definition therefore takes the label grading as data. The regularization of
finite-cone support and all highest-weight comparisons on this page are proved
later, not assumed here by writing $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$.
No choice principle enters this definition.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$, an index $i\in I$, and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. Let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra and let $A_i$ be the subalgebra generated by $E_i,F_i,K_i^{\pm1}$ ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]); write $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$ for the divided powers of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]].

(i) The assignment $e\mapsto E_i$, $f\mapsto F_i$, $k\mapsto K_i$, $k^{-1}\mapsto K_i^{-1}$ defines an algebra isomorphism from the standard rank-one algebra $\mathbb A$ over $\mathbb Q(q)$, presented by $e,f,k^{\pm1}$ with $kek^{-1}=q_i^2e$, $kfk^{-1}=q_i^{-2}f$ and $[e,f]=(k-k^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ onto $A_i$; the images of the monomials $F_i^aK_i^mE_i^b$ ($a,b\ge0$, $m\in\mathbb Z$) are linearly independent in $U_q(\mathfrak g)$, being images of the PBW monomials of the triangular decomposition ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]).

(ii) For all $a,b\ge0$, $K_iE_i^{(a)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{2a}E_i^{(a)}$ and $K_iF_i^{(b)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{-2b}F_i^{(b)}$, and for $b\ge1$ the divided powers satisfy the exact commutation formula
$$E_iF_i^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}E_i+\frac{F_i^{(b-1)}}{q_i^{b}-q_i^{-b}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}\bigl(q_i^{-2s}K_i-q_i^{2s}K_i^{-1}\bigr);$$
iterating it computes $E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}$ as a finite sum of monomials $F_i^{(b-t)}K_i^{m}E_i^{(a-t)}$ ($0\le t\le\min(a,b)$) with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$.

(iii) For every $N\ge0$ there is a simple $A_i$-module $L_i(N)$ of dimension $N+1$: it is the quotient of the cyclic module $\widetilde M(N):=A_i/\bigl(A_iE_i+A_i(K_i-q_i^N)\bigr)$ by the submodule generated by $F_i^{(N+1)}w_N$, where $w_N$ is the image of $1$, with basis the images $v_t$ of $F_i^{(t)}w_N$, $0\le t\le N$, on which $K_iv_t=q_i^{N-2t}v_t$, $F_iv_t=[t+1]_iv_{t+1}$ and $E_iv_t=[N-t+1]_iv_{t-1}$ (with $v_{-1}=v_{N+1}=0$); $L_i(N)$ is the unique simple $A_i$-module generated by a vector $v\ne0$ with $E_iv=0$, $K_iv=q_i^Nv$ and $F_i^{N+1}v=0$.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. For $m\in\mathbb N$, define the **$q_i$-integer**

$$[m]_i:=\frac{q_i^m-q_i^{-m}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}},\qquad [0]_i:=0,$$

and the **$q_i$-factorial**

$$[m]_i!:=\prod_{k=1}^m[k]_i,\qquad [0]_i!:=1.$$

For $0\le r\le m$, define the **Gaussian binomial** $\binom{m}{r}_i:=[m]_i!/([r]_i![m-r]_i!)$, and set it to $0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$. In the published one-parameter convention, write $\binom{m}{r}_t:=\binom{m}{r,m-r}_t$ for the two-part $q$-multinomial coefficient of [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]].

For an element $x$ of a unital $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and $m\ge0$, define its **divided power at $q_i$** by $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$, so $x^{(0)}=1$ and $x^{(1)}=x$.

The symmetric convention and the published asymmetric convention are related, for $m\ge0$ and $0\le r\le m$, by

$$[m]_i=q_i^{-(m-1)}[m]_{q_i^2},\qquad \binom{m}{r}_i=q_i^{-r(m-r)}\binom{m}{r}_{q_i^2}.$$

In particular $[m]_i$ is invariant under $q_i\mapsto q_i^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the symmetrizer only through $q_i=q^{d_i}$.

derivations.claim: Linearity and weights. On a string position $F_i^{(n)}u_n$ with $u_n\in H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ put $\tilde e_i(F_i^{(n)}u_n):=F_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ for $n\ge1$ and $0$ for $n=0$, and $\tilde f_i(F_i^{(n)}u_n):=F_i^{(n+1)}u_n$. By [F2] every $u$ is a unique sum of such positions inside its decomposition, so these prescriptions define linear maps on $M$; the shifted vectors lie in $M_{\lambda+\alpha_i}$ and $M_{\lambda-\alpha_i}$ respectively, since $F_i^{(n-1)}u_n\in M_{\lambda+\alpha_i}$ and $F_i^{(n+1)}u_n\in M_{\lambda-\alpha_i}$ by [F1].

The top projection. Writing $p_{\mathrm{top}}u:=u_0$ gives a well-defined linear idempotent by [F2]. For $u=\sum_nF_i^{(n)}u_n$ one has $\tilde f_i\tilde e_iu=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n)}u_n$ by step 1.1, hence $u-\tilde f_i\tilde e_iu=u_0=p_{\mathrm{top}}u$; equivalently $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{top}}$, and on each position with $n\ge1$ the composition $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i$ is the identity.

The bottom projection. For a nonzero coefficient $u_n$, if $n\ge\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$, then $n$ equals that length by [F1], and $F_i^{(n+1)}u_n=0$ because $F_i^{(n)}$ is zero beyond the string length; thus $\tilde f_iu=\sum_{n<\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle}F_i^{(n+1)}u_n$, which is the admissible decomposition of $\tilde f_iu$ (its $m$-th top coefficient is $u_{m-1}$ for $m\ge1$). Applying step 1.1 to this decomposition, $\tilde e_i\tilde f_iu=\sum_{n<\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle}F_i^{(n)}u_n$, so $u-\tilde e_i\tilde f_iu=\sum_{n=\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle}F_i^{(n)}u_n=p_{\mathrm{bottom}}u$; in particular on each position that is not a bottom the composition $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i$ is the identity.

Kernels. For $u=\sum_nF_i^{(n)}u_n$, step 1.1 gives $\tilde e_iu=0$ exactly when $u_n=0$ for all $n\ge1$, that is $u=u_0\in H_\lambda$. On the other hand [F3] gives $E_iu=\sum_{n\ge1}[a_n-n+1]_iF_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ with $a_n=\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$; here $a_n-n+1\ge1$ for $n\le a_n$ by admissibility and the term vanishes for $n>a_n$, so $E_iu=0$ exactly when $u_n=0$ for all $n\ge1$ as well; hence $\ker\tilde e_i=\ker E_i$. Likewise $\tilde f_iu=\sum_{n<a_n}F_i^{(n+1)}u_n=0$ exactly when $u_n=0$ for all $n<a_n$, and $F_iu=\sum_{n<a_n}[n+1]_iF_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ vanishes exactly then because $[n+1]_i\neq0$; hence $\ker\tilde f_i=\ker F_i$.

Agreement on the kernels. If $u\in\ker E_i$ then $u=u_0$ by [F2], so $\tilde f_iu=F_iu_0=F_iu$; if $u\in\ker F_i$ then every nonzero coefficient $u_n$ sits at a bottom, $n=a_n$, so $E_iu=\sum_{n\ge1}[a_n-n+1]_iF_i^{(n-1)}u_n=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n-1)}u_n=\tilde e_iu$; the $n=a_n=0$ strings contribute zero to both raising operators by [F3].

Naturality. Let $\varphi:M\to N$ be a homomorphism of weight-graded $A_i$-modules, so $\varphi$ commutes with $E_i$, $F_i$ and $K_i$ and preserves each $H_\mu$ and each weight space. Applying $\varphi$ to the admissible decomposition of $u$ gives the admissible decomposition of $\varphi(u)$ by uniqueness [F2], because $\varphi$ commutes with divided powers; hence $\varphi\tilde e_iu=\tilde e_i\varphi(u)$, $\varphi\tilde f_iu=\tilde f_i\varphi(u)$, and the same holds for the projections.

Interior comparison. In $L_i(2)$ take the highest vector $v=v_0$ and $u=F_iv=[1]_iv_1$; by [F3] $F_iu=[2]_iF_i^{(2)}v$, whereas $u$ is the position-$1$ vector of the string of $v$ of length $2$, so $\tilde f_iu=F_i^{(2)}v$. Since $[2]_i=q_i+q_i^{-1}$ and $q_i$ is transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, $[2]_i\neq1$, so $\tilde f_i$ differs from $F_i$ at this interior position.

boundaries.evidence: The operators are defined coefficientwise on the unique decomposition, so for $u=0$ every $u_n=0$ and both operators return $0$; step 2.5's naturality is stated for an arbitrary homomorphism of weight-graded modules, including the zero map.

The zero values at string ends are part of the construction: step 2.1 proves $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\operatorname{id}-p_{\mathrm{top}}$ with $\tilde e_i$ killing the top position, and step 2.2 proves $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}-p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$ with $\tilde f_i$ killing the bottom position $n=\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$.

A vector whose decomposition has a single coefficient $u_n$ is moved one position with coefficient $1$ by step 1.1; a one-vertex string ($n=0=a_\lambda$) is a top vector, so $\tilde e_i u=0$ and $\tilde f_i u=F_iu$ by step 2.4's agreement on the kernel of $E_i$.

No nondegeneracy beyond the chosen $P$-grading is assumed, and the construction is interior to each finite decomposition; step 3.1 records the honest interior comparison in $L_i(2)$, where $F_iu=[2]_i\tilde f_iu$ with $[2]_i=q_i+q_i^{-1}\ne1$, so no normalization by a vanishing scalar is made.

The string endpoints enter in the projection formulas of steps 2.1-2.2: $\tilde e_i$ kills top positions and $\tilde f_i$ kills bottoms, and the identities $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\operatorname{id}-p_{\mathrm{top}}$, $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}-p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$ are exactly the two endpoint corrections.

No choice is used: the definitions sum the given unique decomposition term by term in step 1.1, the projections of steps 2.1-2.2 read off the same decomposition, and naturality in step 2.5 selects nothing.

The set identity $\ker\tilde e_i=\ker E_i$ is proved from its two inclusions in step 2.3: the forward direction $\tilde e_iu=0$ forces all positive string coefficients to vanish, so $u=u_0$ lies in $H_\lambda=\ker E_i$.

The reverse inclusion of step 2.3: for $u\in\ker E_i$ the decomposition has $u=u_0$, hence $\tilde e_iu=0$; step 2.4 adds the agreement statements on the kernels, including $\tilde f_iu=F_iu$ on $\ker E_i$ and $\tilde e_iu=E_iu$ on $\ker F_i$.

Let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]] with its root-lattice grading $U_q(\mathfrak g)=\bigoplus_{\beta\in Q}U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]$. Define

$$U_q^+:=\langle E_i\ :\ i\in I\rangle,\qquad U_q^-:=\langle F_i\ :\ i\in I\rangle,\qquad U_q^0:=\langle K_h\ :\ h\in P^{\vee}\rangle,$$

the $\mathbb Q(q)$-subalgebras generated by the indicated images, and let $Q_+=\bigoplus_i\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$. Then

$$U_q^\pm=\bigoplus_{\beta\in Q_+}U_q^\pm[\pm\beta],\qquad U_q^+[\beta]:=U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]\cap U_q^+,\quad U_q^-[ -\beta]:=U_q(\mathfrak g)[-\beta]\cap U_q^-.$$

The degree-zero component $U_q(\mathfrak g)[0]$ contains $U_q^0$, and for every $x\in U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]$ and $h\in P^{\vee}$,

$$K_hxK_h^{-1}=q^{\beta(h)}x.$$

Thus each $K_h\in U_q^0$ acts by conjugation on the degree-$\beta$ component as the scalar $q^{\beta(h)}$. The elements $K_h$ span $U_q^0$ and satisfy $K_hK_{h'}=K_{h+h'}$ with $K_0=1$; hence $U_q^0$ is a quotient of the group algebra $\mathbb Q(q)[P^{\vee}]$. The subalgebras $U_q^\pm$ are spanned by finite monomials in the $E_i$ and $F_i$, respectively. Define the nonnegative and nonpositive product spans by

$$U_q^{\ge0}:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q(q)}(U_q^0U_q^+),\qquad U_q^{\le0}:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q(q)}(U_q^-U_q^0).$$

This definition asserts no linear independence of these spanning families and no injectivity of the natural maps; those claims belong to [[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]].

Let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra of
[[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], with its generated
subalgebras $U_q^-,U_q^0,U_q^+$ and root gradings
$U_q^-=\bigoplus_{\nu\in Q_+}U_q^-[-\nu]$ of
[[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]
($Q_+=\bigoplus_i\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$, height $\operatorname{ht}$ of
[[def-kac-moody-root-lattice-height-and-positive-cone]]). Fix $i\in I$ and
write $K_i:=K_{d_ih_i}$, so that $K_iF_jK_i^{-1}=q_i^{-a_{ij}}F_j$ and
$q_i-q_i^{-1}\ne0$.

For every $P\in U_q^-$ there exist unique elements $Q,R\in U_q^-$ with

$$E_iP-PE_i=\frac{K_iQ-K_i^{-1}R}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}.$$

Define the **Kashiwara skew derivations** $e_i',e_i'':U_q^-\to U_q^-$ by

$$e_i'(P):=R\qquad\text{and}\qquad e_i''(P):=Q .$$

Thus $e_i'$ is the operator whose value is the coefficient of $K_i^{-1}$ and
$e_i''$ is the operator whose value is the coefficient of $K_i$ in the
commutator with $E_i$. The maps have the following properties, all proved in
the Verification below.

(a) $e_i'$ and $e_i''$ are $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear, vanish on $1$, and
$e_i'(F_j)=e_i''(F_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for all $j\in I$.

(b) (Twisted Leibniz rules) For homogeneous $x,y\in U_q^-$, with the actual
weight $\operatorname{wt}(x)\in Q$ of [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]],
$$e_i'(xy)=e_i'(x)y+q_i^{\langle\operatorname{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}x\,e_i'(y),\qquad e_i''(xy)=e_i''(x)y+q_i^{-\langle\operatorname{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}x\,e_i''(y).$$

(c) (Commutation with the generators) For all $j\in I$ and all $y\in U_q^-$,
$$e_i'(F_jy)=q_i^{-a_{ij}}F_j\,e_i'(y)+\delta_{ij}y,\qquad e_i''(F_jy)=q_i^{a_{ij}}F_j\,e_i''(y)+\delta_{ij}y,$$

equivalently $e_i'F_j=q_i^{-a_{ij}}F_je_i'+\delta_{ij}$ and
$e_i''F_j=q_i^{a_{ij}}F_je_i''+\delta_{ij}$ as operators on $U_q^-$.

(d) (Grading, height and nilpotence) For every $\nu\in Q_+$,

$$e_i'\bigl(U_q^-[-\nu]\bigr),\ e_i''\bigl(U_q^-[-\nu]\bigr)\ \subseteq\ U_q^-[ -(\nu-\alpha_i)],$$

the right-hand side being $0$ when $\nu-\alpha_i\notin Q_+$. In particular both
maps raise the actual weight by $\alpha_i$, lower the positive height by one,
and are locally nilpotent: $(e_i')^{k}(P)=(e_i'')^{k}(P)=0$ for $k$ larger than
the height of the degree of a homogeneous $P$.

(e) (Bar compatibility) Let $\psi$ be the semilinear algebra involution
$q\mapsto q^{-1}$, $E_i\mapsto E_i$, $F_i\mapsto F_i$, $K_h\mapsto K_{-h}$ of
[[lem-quantum-serre-relations-are-stable-under-the-chevalley-involutions]].
Then $e_i''=\psi\,e_i'\,\psi$ on $U_q^-$.

The commutator construction also fixes the orientation: the
$K_i^{-1}$-coefficient is $e_i'$ and the $K_i$-coefficient is $e_i''$. The
twists $q_i^{\pm\langle\operatorname{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}$ in (b) are the twists
of the corresponding coefficient maps of the negative-half coproduct in the
source's dictionary; the explicit commutator computation used here is the
definition of record, and no imaginary-simple-root convention is needed, since
every Cartan datum of this library has $a_{ii}=2$.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. For $m\in\mathbb N$, define the **$q_i$-integer**

$$[m]_i:=\frac{q_i^m-q_i^{-m}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}},\qquad [0]_i:=0,$$

and the **$q_i$-factorial**

$$[m]_i!:=\prod_{k=1}^m[k]_i,\qquad [0]_i!:=1.$$

For $0\le r\le m$, define the **Gaussian binomial** $\binom{m}{r}_i:=[m]_i!/([r]_i![m-r]_i!)$, and set it to $0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$. In the published one-parameter convention, write $\binom{m}{r}_t:=\binom{m}{r,m-r}_t$ for the two-part $q$-multinomial coefficient of [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]].

For an element $x$ of a unital $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and $m\ge0$, define its **divided power at $q_i$** by $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$, so $x^{(0)}=1$ and $x^{(1)}=x$.

The symmetric convention and the published asymmetric convention are related, for $m\ge0$ and $0\le r\le m$, by

$$[m]_i=q_i^{-(m-1)}[m]_{q_i^2},\qquad \binom{m}{r}_i=q_i^{-r(m-r)}\binom{m}{r}_{q_i^2}.$$

In particular $[m]_i$ is invariant under $q_i\mapsto q_i^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the symmetrizer only through $q_i=q^{d_i}$.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum and $i\in I$, and use the conventions of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $C_{m,r}:=\binom{m}{r}_i$, with $C_{m,r}=0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$.

(i) **Pascal recurrences.** For $m\ge1$ and every integer $r$,

$$C_{m,r}=q_i^{-r}C_{m-1,r}+q_i^{m-r}C_{m-1,r-1}=q_i^rC_{m-1,r}+q_i^{r-m}C_{m-1,r-1}.$$

(ii) **Symmetry.** For $0\le r\le m$, $C_{m,r}=C_{m,m-r}$.

(iii) **Gauss product formula.** For every $N\ge0$, in the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q(q)[z]$,

$$\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}(1+q_i^{2j}z)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}q_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}z^r.$$

Consequently, for $N\ge1$,

$$\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-1)^rq_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}=0.$$

(iv) **Integrality.** For $0\le r\le m$,

$$C_{m,r}\in q_i^{-r(m-r)}\mathbb Z[q_i^2]\subseteq\mathbb Z[q_i^{\pm1}].$$

Thus every Gaussian quotient is a Laurent polynomial in $q_i$ with integer coefficients, and the Pascal recurrences hold in that Laurent polynomial ring.

Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half of the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with its
Kashiwara skew derivations $e_i',e_i''$
([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]), let
$A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ and let $U_A^-$ be the divided-power half generated by
the $F_i^{(r)}$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]). Then:

(i) $e_i'$ preserves $U_A^-$: $e_i'(U_A^-)\subseteq U_A^-$.

(ii) Define, for $x\in U_q^-$,
$$P_ix:=\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^nq_i^{-n(n-1)/2}\,F_i^{(n)}(e_i')^n x,$$
the sum being finite on each $x$ because $e_i'$ is locally nilpotent, and the
powers $(e_i')^n$ being ordinary, not divided, powers of the derivation. Then
$P_i$ is a well-defined $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear map with $e_i'P_i=0$ that fixes
$\ker e_i'$ pointwise and annihilates $F_iU_q^-$; hence
$U_q^-=\ker e_i'\oplus F_iU_q^-$ and $P_i$ is the projection onto $\ker e_i'$
along $F_iU_q^-$.

(iii) Every $x\in U_A^-$ has a unique finite expansion
$$x=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}x_n,\qquad e_i'x_n=0,$$
with $x_n=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_i(e_i')^nx\in U_A^-$ for every $n$; the sum is finite
because $(e_i')^nx=0$ for large $n$. Consequently the string operators
$\tilde e_i\bigl(\sum_nF_i^{(n)}x_n\bigr):=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n-1)}x_n$ and
$\tilde f_i\bigl(\sum_nF_i^{(n)}x_n\bigr):=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n+1)}x_n$
preserve $U_A^-$.

No global $A$-basis and no freeness of $U_A^-$ over $A$ is assumed or asserted.

derivations.claim: The $q$-boson relation. By [F2] with $j=i$ and $a_{ii}=2$, $e_i'F_i=q_i^{-2}F_ie_i'+1$; applying the Leibniz rule to $F_i^r$ and summing the geometric series gives $e_i'(F_i^r)=q_i^{-(r-1)}[r]_iF_i^{r-1}$, and dividing by $[r]_i!$ yields $e_i'F_i^{(r)}=q_i^{-(r-1)}F_i^{(r-1)}+q_i^{-2r}F_i^{(r)}e_i'$ for $r\ge1$.

Iterated deletion. If $e_i'u=0$, then induction on $n$ using step 1.1 gives $(e_i')^nF_i^{(m)}u=q_i^{-nm+n(n+1)/2}F_i^{(m-n)}u$ for $0\le n\le m$, while $(e_i')^nF_i^{(m)}u=(e_i')^{n-m}u=0$ for $n>m$.

Termination. By [F2] the derivation $e_i'$ lowers positive height by one, so for homogeneous $x\in U_q^-[-
u]$ one has $(e_i')^nx=0$ whenever $n>\sum_j
u_j=\operatorname{ht}(
u)$; hence on each $x$ only finitely many terms of the sum defining $P_i$ are nonzero, and $P_i$ is a well-defined $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear endomorphism of $U_q^-$.

The projection. For $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ and $M\ge0$, steps 2.1 and [F3] give $P_iF_i^{(M)}u=\sum_{m=0}^{M}(-1)^mq_i^{-m(m-1)/2}q_i^{-mM+m(m+1)/2}\binom{M}{m}_iF_i^{(M)}u=\bigl(\sum_{m=0}^{M}(-1)^mq_i^{-m(M-1)}\binom{M}{m}_i\bigr)F_i^{(M)}u$, which by the Gaussian identity [F4] equals $u$ for $M=0$ and $0$ for $M\ge1$. Hence $P_iF_i=0$, $P_i$ fixes $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$, and $P_i$ kills $f_iU_q^-$; moreover $e_i'P_i=0$ by the cancellation of consecutive terms in $e_i'F_i^{(m)}e_i'^{\,m}$ using step 1.1, so $P_i^2=P_i$ and $P_i$ is the projection onto $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ along $f_iU_q^-$, with $U_q^-=\operatorname{Ker}e_i'\oplus f_iU_q^-$ because $u=P_iu+(u-P_iu)$ lies in the two subspaces.

Existence of the string decomposition. Let $u\in U_q^-$. By [F5], for each $n\ge0$ the element $u_n:=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u$ lies in $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ (as $e_i'P_i=0$ by step 3.1), and the sum $\sum_nf_i^{(n)}u_n$ is finite because $e_i'^{\,n}u=0$ for $n$ large by step 2.2; the operator identity $\sum_nq_i^{n(n-1)/2}f_i^{(n)}P_ie_i'^{\,n}=\mathrm{id}$ supplied by [F5] gives $u=\sum_nf_i^{(n)}u_n$.

Uniqueness and the coefficient formula. Suppose $u=\sum_mf_i^{(m)}v_m$ with $v_m\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ and $v_m=0$ for $m$ large. Applying $e_i'^{\,n}$ and then $P_i$ for fixed $n$: by step 2.1, $e_i'^{\,n}f_i^{(m)}v_m=q_i^{-nm+n(n+1)/2}f_i^{(m-n)}v_m$ for $m\ge n$ and $0$ for $m<n$, and by step 3.1, $P_if_i^{(m-n)}v_m=0$ for $m>n$ while $P_iv_n=v_n$; hence $P_ie_i'^{\,n}u=q_i^{-n(n-1)/2}v_n$, that is $v_n=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u=u_n$. Thus the components of step 4.1 are determined by $u$, giving uniqueness and the displayed coefficient formula.

The Kashiwara operators. Given the unique decomposition $u=\sum_nf_i^{(n)}u_n$ of steps 4.1-5.1, the prescriptions $\tilde e_iu:=\sum_{n\ge1}f_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ and $\tilde f_iu:=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ are well-defined $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear maps by uniqueness; shifting the index shows $\tilde e_i\tilde f_iu=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n)}u_n=u$, so $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}_{U_q^-}$.

Kernel, injectivity and value at $1$. For $u=\sum_nf_i^{(n)}u_n$ one has $\tilde e_iu=0$ exactly when $u_n=0$ for every $n\ge1$, that is $u=u_0\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$; hence $\ker\tilde e_i=\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$. If $\tilde f_iu=0$, then $\sum_nf_i^{(n+1)}u_n=0$ is a decomposition with all top coefficients $u_n$ in $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$, so uniqueness in step 5.1 forces $u_n=0$ for all $n$, that is $u=0$; hence $\tilde f_i$ is injective. Finally $1\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ has decomposition $1=f_i^{(0)}\cdot1$, so $\tilde f_i(1)=f_i^{(1)}=F_i$.

Root grading. Let $u\in U_q^-[-
u]$ be homogeneous. Since $f_i^{(n)}$ raises the degree by $-n\alpha_i$, the components $u_n$ of steps 4.1-5.1 may be taken homogeneous of degree $-
u+n\alpha_i$ (decompose $u$ and each $u_n$ into finitely many homogeneous pieces and compare degrees), so $f_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ has degree $-
u+\alpha_i$ and $f_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ has degree $-
u-\alpha_i$; hence $	ilde e_i(U_q^-[-
u])\subseteq U_q^-[-
u+\alpha_i]$ and $	ilde f_i(U_q^-[-
u])\subseteq U_q^-[-
u-\alpha_i]$.

Integrality and choice. By [F5] the projector $P_i$ and every coefficient $u_n=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u$ preserve the divided-power lattice $U_A^-$, and the shifts of step 6.1 preserve it as well; no freeness of $U_A^-$ is asserted. All constructions used unique decompositions, finite sums and the explicit operator $P_i$; no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: The degree-zero component is $U_q^-[0]=\mathbb Q(q)\mathbf 1$ by [F1], and the expansion of (ii) is finite on each element; step 8.1 notes explicitly that no freeness of the divided-power lattice is asserted, so the empty index case is the unit itself.

The zero vector has every coefficient zero by uniqueness. A zero top coefficient alone does not imply a zero vector: $F_i$ has $u_0=0,u_1=1$. Step 3.1 kills $F_iU_q^-$ and step 5.1 recovers every coefficient separately.

Since $f_i^{(1)}=F_i$ by [F3], the first position of each string is the generator itself; step 6.1's shifts give $\tilde f_i(\mathbf 1)=F_i$ at the unit, the smallest case, and step 7.1 records $\tilde e_i(\mathbf 1)=0$ because $\mathbf 1\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$.

The negative half is not finite-dimensional and its strings are infinite; step 2.2 bounds the nonzero coefficients on each element by the height $\operatorname{ht}(\nu)$, and step 4.1's sum is finite for that reason, while step 8.1 explicitly avoids asserting freeness or finite generation of the divided lattice.

The top of each string is its $n=0$ coefficient in $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$, and there is no bottom: step 7.1 proves $\ker\tilde e_i=\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ and $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}$, so no position is annihilated by $\tilde f_i$ and the infinite chain has a top but no endpoint.

No choice is used: $P_i$ is a locally finite sum by step 2.2, the coefficients and shifts are explicit formulas in steps 4.1-6.1, and step 8.1 records that the construction uses only finite sums, unique decompositions and the DVR arithmetic of $A_0$.

The kernel identity $\tilde e_iu=0$ if and only if $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ is proved in step 7.1: forward, $\tilde e_iu=0$ forces $u_n=0$ for all $n\ge1$, so $u=u_0$ lies in $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$.

Converse of the same step 7.1 identity: if $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ then every positive coefficient vanishes by uniqueness of the expansion, so $\tilde e_iu=0$; the same computation gives injectivity of $\tilde f_i$ from $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}$.

Let $M$ be an integrable chosen $P$-graded type-1 module ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) and fix $i\in I$. By [[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]] every $u\in M_\lambda$ has a unique admissible decomposition
$$u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}=\ker(E_i)\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i},$$
with $u_n=0$ whenever $n>\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$. Define the **Kashiwara operators**
$$\tilde e_i u:=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_i u:=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n+1)}u_n .$$
Both are linear maps on $M$, shifting the label weight by $+\alpha_i$, respectively $-\alpha_i$. Along each string, $\tilde e_i$ moves $F_i^{(n)}u_n$ to $F_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ and kills the top position $n=0$, while $\tilde f_i$ moves it to $F_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ and kills a string exactly at its bottom, where $n=\langle\mathrm{wt}(u_n),h_i\rangle$.

Let $p_{\mathrm{top}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$ be the projections onto the top positions and the bottom positions of these strings:
$$p_{\mathrm{top}}u:=u_0,\qquad p_{\mathrm{bottom}}u:=\sum_{n:\,n=\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle}F_i^{(n)}u_n .$$
Then
$$\ker\tilde e_i=\ker E_i,\qquad \ker\tilde f_i=\ker F_i,\qquad \tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{top}},\qquad \tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{bottom}},$$
so $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ are inverse to each other on each existing string edge. Module homomorphisms commute with both operators, $p_{\mathrm{top}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$. On $\ker E_i$ one has $\tilde f_i=F_i$, and on $\ker F_i$ one has $\tilde e_i=E_i$. At interior positions the operators differ from the generators: in the rank-one module $L_i(2)$ with highest vector $v$ and $u=F_iv$, one has $F_iu=[2]_iF_i^{(2)}v$ while $\tilde f_iu=F_i^{(2)}v$, and $[2]_i\neq1$. No choice principle is used. The analogous Kashiwara operators on the negative half $U_q^-$ are the shifts of its unique $e_i'$-string decomposition ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]), constructed using the skew derivation of [[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]. Their strings have no bottom: $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}$ and $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-P_i$, where $P_i$ projects onto $\ker e_i'$; the second identity follows by subtracting the position-zero coefficient $u_0=P_iu$ from the string expansion. These string-shift operators are distinct from the skew derivations $e_i',e_i''$. No negative-half operator is used in the module verification below.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group
with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), with root lattice $Q$,
simple roots $\alpha_i\in P$ and integer pairing
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$, and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with generators $E_i,F_i,K_h$
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). The lattice $P$ plays
the role of the integral weights of the classical theory
([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]); the pairing need not
be perfect, and no identification $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$ is
assumed anywhere.

A **$P$-graded type-one quantum weight module** is a left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$
together with a direct sum decomposition

$$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$$

(an internal direct sum of $\mathbb Q(q)$-subspaces, only finitely many nonzero
on each vector) such that, for all $\mu\in P$, $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $i\in I$,

$$K_h\ \text{acts on}\ M_\mu\ \text{by the scalar}\ q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle},\qquad E_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu+\alpha_i},\qquad F_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu-\alpha_i}.$$

The subspaces $M_\mu$ are the **chosen label-weight spaces**: the grading is
part of the structure and is not reconstructed from the action, because the
pairing may have a kernel. **Morphisms** of $P$-graded type-one weight modules
are the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps $f\colon M\to N$ with
$f(M_\mu)\subseteq N_\mu$ for every $\mu$; the weight submodules and quotients
considered on this page are those with the induced grading (Verification, step 2.2).

The module is **integrable** if $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every
vector: for every $v\in M$ and every $i$ there are integers $N_e(v,i),N_f(v,i)\ge1$
with $E_i^{N_e(v,i)}v=0$ and $F_i^{N_f(v,i)}v=0$. The exponents may depend on
the vector and on $i$, and both directions are required independently;
integrability is not a uniform nilpotence condition.

The following are additional hypotheses, never part of the definition:
finiteness of the dimension of every $M_\mu$; boundedness of the set of $\mu$
with $M_\mu\ne0$ above (or below); finite generation of $M$. The zero module is
a $P$-graded type-one weight module with the empty grading ($M_\mu=0$ for all
$\mu$), and it is integrable.

Two remarks are recorded here and proved below. First, when the pairing
separates $P$, the spaces $M_\mu$ are exactly the simultaneous eigenspaces of
the $K_h$, and the present definition recovers the usual type-one weight
modules (Verification, steps 2.1 and 4.1). Second, when the pairing does not
separate, distinct labels $\mu\ne\mu'$ may carry the same toral character, and
a simultaneous toral eigenspace must not be equated with a single label space;
the definition therefore takes the label grading as data. The regularization of
finite-cone support and all highest-weight comparisons on this page are proved
later, not assumed here by writing $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$.
No choice principle enters this definition.

Let $q$ be transcendental over $\mathbb Q$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and let
$$A_0:=\mathbb Q[q]_{(q)}=\Big\{\frac fg\ :\ f,g\in\mathbb Q[q],\ g(0)\neq0\Big\}\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$$
be the localisation of the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q[q]$ at the prime ideal $(q)$ ([[def-localisation-at-a-prime-ideal]]). By [[ex-the-local-ring-of-polynomials-at-x]] with $F=\mathbb Q$, the ring $A_0$ is exactly the ring of rational functions regular at $q=0$, it is a local ring ([[def-local-ring]]) with unique maximal ideal $qA_0$, and evaluation at $0$ induces an isomorphism $A_0/qA_0\cong\mathbb Q$. Since $\mathbb Q[q]$ is a principal ideal domain ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-field-is-a-pid]]) with nonzero prime ideal $(q)$, the ring $A_0$ is a local principal ideal domain with nonzero maximal ideal; by the discrete valuation ring characterisations it is a discrete valuation ring with uniformiser $q/1$ ([[thm-equivalent-characterisations-of-a-dvr]], [[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]), and in particular a principal ideal domain ([[cor-dvr-is-a-pid]], [[def-principal-ideal-domain]]), with field of fractions $\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[cor-rational-function-field-as-a-fraction-field]]).

By [[def-discrete-valuation-ring]] a discrete valuation ring is the valuation ring $V_v=\{x:v(x)\ge0\}$ of a discrete valuation $v$ on its fraction field. The discrete valuation of $\mathbb Q(q)$ with $V_v=A_0$ and $v(q)=1$ is the **$q$-adic valuation**; write it $\operatorname{ord}_q$, so that
$$\operatorname{ord}_q:\mathbb Q(q)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\cup\{\infty\},\qquad A_0=\{h\in\mathbb Q(q):\operatorname{ord}_q(h)\ge0\},\qquad \operatorname{ord}_q(q)=1 .$$
Equivalently, $\operatorname{ord}_q$ is the vanishing order at $q=0$. The units of $A_0$ are exactly the fractions $f/g$ with $f(0)\neq0$ and $g(0)\neq0$, and $qA_0$ is the maximal ideal, so $q$ is a uniformiser of $A_0$ ([[thm-localisation-at-a-prime-is-local]]).

This ring $A_0$ is the **crystal limiting ring** of the crystal development below, and it is different from the Laurent ring $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ of [[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]: $q^{-1}\in A\setminus A_0$, while $(1+q)^{-1}\in A_0\setminus A$; neither ring contains the other, and both are subrings of $\mathbb Q(q)$. For every free $A_0$-module $L$ the canonical map
$$\mathbb Q\otimes_{A_0}L\longrightarrow L/qL,\qquad c\otimes\ell\mapsto c\,\ell+qL,$$
is an isomorphism, and for every $\lambda\in\mathbb Q(q)^\times$ one has $\lambda L/q\lambda L\cong L/qL$; passing from $L$ to $L/qL$ is the **crystal limit**. No freeness of any further module, no lattice and no choice principle is asserted here.

Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half of the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with its skew derivations $e_i',e_i'':U_q^-\to U_q^-$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]), fix $i\in I$, and write $f_i^{(n)}=F_i^n/[n]_i!$ for the divided powers ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]). Then:

(i) $e_i'$ is locally nilpotent on $U_q^-$, and the endomorphism
$$P_i:=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^mq_i^{-m(m-1)/2}F_i^{(m)}e_i'^{\,m}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q(q)}(U_q^-)$$
is well defined (each sum is finite on each element) and is the projection onto $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ along $f_iU_q^-$. In particular $e_i'P_i=0$, $P_iF_i=0$, $P_i^2=P_i$, $P_iu=u$ for $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$, and
$$U_q^-=\operatorname{Ker}e_i'\oplus f_iU_q^-.$$

(ii) Every $u\in U_q^-$ has a unique $i$-string decomposition
$$u=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i',\qquad u_n=0\ \text{for }n\gg0,$$
and the components are given by $u_n=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u$.

(iii) The **Kashiwara operators on the negative half**, defined on the string decomposition by
$$\tilde e_iu:=\sum_{n\ge1}f_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_iu:=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n+1)}u_n,$$
are $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear endomorphisms of $U_q^-$ with $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}_{U_q^-}$; $\tilde e_iu=0$ if and only if $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$; $\tilde f_i$ is injective and $\tilde f_i(1)=F_i$. Both operators preserve the root grading and shift its degree by $\mp\alpha_i$, that is $\tilde e_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu+\alpha_i]$ and $\tilde f_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu-\alpha_i]$.

No choice principle is used. Here $e_i'^{\,n}$ denotes the ordinary $n$-fold power of the derivation, not its divided power. The same projector and every string coefficient preserve the $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]), as proved by the integral skew-string supplier; this does not assert that lattice's freeness.

derivations.claim: Induced operators. By (iii) the operators preserve $L$ and commute with multiplication by $A_0$, so they descend to $\mathbb Q$-linear endomorphisms of $L/qL$, which is canonically $\mathbb Q\otimes_{A_0}L$ by [F3]; by [F1] they shift the label weight by $\pm\alpha_i$, so they map $L_\mu/qL_\mu$ to $L_{\mu+\alpha_i}/qL_{\mu+\alpha_i}$ and to $L_{\mu-\alpha_i}/qL_{\mu-\alpha_i}$, and axiom (v) says that they map $B$ into $B\cup\{0\}$.

Rank decomposition. Since $L=\bigoplus_\mu L_\mu$ with every $L_\mu$ free by (ii), $\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L=\sum_\mu\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L_\mu$, and applying $\mathbb Q(q)\otimes_{A_0}-$ gives $\mathbb Q(q)\otimes_{A_0}L=\bigoplus_\mu\mathbb Q(q)\otimes_{A_0}L_\mu$ with each summand of dimension $\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L_\mu$ by [F3]. The isomorphism of (i) is weight graded, because $L_\mu\subseteq M_\mu$ and the target is the direct sum of the $M_\mu$; hence $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}M_\mu=\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L_\mu$ for every $\mu$.

Residue counts. The crystal limit isomorphism of [F3] is compatible with the grading, and $L/qL=\bigoplus_\mu L_\mu/qL_\mu$; by (iv) each $B_\mu$ is contained in $L_\mu/qL_\mu$ and $B=\bigsqcup_\mu B_\mu$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $L/qL$, so $B_\mu$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $L_\mu/qL_\mu$. Hence $\#B_\mu=\dim_{\mathbb Q}L_\mu/qL_\mu=\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L_\mu=\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}M_\mu$, which is the displayed equality, and the weight function of the crystal is well defined by (iv).

The graph and the partial-inverse property. By (vi) the arrow relation $b\xrightarrow{i}b'$ is symmetric under exchanging $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$, so the crystal graph has no ambiguity: an arrow exists exactly when $\tilde f_ib=b'$, equivalently $b=\tilde e_ib'$. In a finite-dimensional piece a string may end at a bottom, where $\tilde f_ib=0$; by (v) this is allowed and no vertex is added.

The negative half. For $U_q^-$ the same discussion applies with the root grading in place of the weight grading. By [F4] the induced endomorphisms of $L/qL$ satisfy $\bar{\tilde e}_i\bar{\tilde f}_i=\mathrm{id}$, so $\bar{\tilde f}_i$ is injective and no element of $B$ is mapped to $0$ by $\tilde f_i$; with (v) this gives $\tilde f_iB\subseteq B$, the infinite-string refinement.

Choice. The definitions select no bases, no complements and no representatives; the lattice, its grading and the residue basis are given data, and all statements above are computations with them, so no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: The Definition allows the zero crystal: for $M=0$ the lattice $L=0$ satisfies (i)-(iii) vacuously and $B=\varnothing$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of the zero crystal limit, while step 2.1's identity $\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L_\mu=\#B_\mu$ reads $0=0$ on every weight.

The zero vector is not a basis element: $B$ consists of residue classes of a $\mathbb Q$-basis, and step 1.1's induced operators are well-defined maps with values in $B\cup\{0\}$, the zero value being reserved for the killed positions.

A rank-one graded piece $L_\mu=A_0e$ has $\#B_\mu=1$ by step 2.1's count $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}M_\mu=\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L_\mu=\#B_\mu$; on a single-vertex chain the partial-inverse axiom (vi) admits no arrow, as step 2.2's graph reading records.

Axiom (ii) is imposed with each graded piece $L_\mu$ free in the Definition; this is the reading under which step 1.2's scalar extension is graded and step 2.1's rank count is available without an unstated freeness theorem, and every lattice constructed on this page has free graded pieces by the DVR suppliers.

The string endpoints enter through axiom (vi): step 2.2 reads an arrow $b\to b'$ as $\tilde f_ib=b'$ exactly when $b=\tilde e_ib'$, so the top vertex (no incoming raising) and bottom vertex (no outgoing lowering) are the two ends of the same edge relation, and step 2.3 applies the reading to the negative half.

Step 3.1 records that no choice is used: the lattice, its grading, the residue basis and the operators are given data, and steps 1.1-2.3 are computations with them; no basis, complement or representative is selected.

The forward direction of axiom (vi) is the arrow definition: step 2.2 shows that the crystal graph has no ambiguity because $\tilde f_ib=b'$ holds exactly when the arrow $b\xrightarrow{i}b'$ exists, and the axiom is used in this reading throughout the page.

The reverse direction $b=\tilde e_ib'$ of axiom (vi) is the same axiom read backwards; step 2.2 uses it to identify the inverse edge, and step 2.3 applies it on the negative half, where $\tilde f_iB\subseteq B$ has no exception because $\bar{\tilde e}_i\bar{\tilde f}_i=\operatorname{id}$.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all six verification steps against the reviewed local ring and both string suppliers. Localization of the embedded free lattice gives field generation iff the canonical tensor map is an isomorphism. Given free graded pieces give ranks and residue dimensions; the given homogeneous residue basis yields exact counts, including zero pieces/empty B. Both partial-inverse directions are axiom (vi); negative-half e-tilde f-tilde=id descends to residues, so lowering cannot kill a basis vertex. No new basis selection/AC. Sources: Kashiwara pp.473–474 (2.3.1)–(2.3.6), JKK Definitions 4.4/4.6 and 6.3, Berkeley 13.3.0.1–2. Only bibliography locators changed; no mathematical defect identified.
