Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$, an index $i\in I$, and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. Let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra and let $A_i$ be the subalgebra generated by $E_i,F_i,K_i^{\pm1}$ ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]); write $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$ for the divided powers of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]].

(i) The assignment $e\mapsto E_i$, $f\mapsto F_i$, $k\mapsto K_i$, $k^{-1}\mapsto K_i^{-1}$ defines an algebra isomorphism from the standard rank-one algebra $\mathbb A$ over $\mathbb Q(q)$, presented by $e,f,k^{\pm1}$ with $kek^{-1}=q_i^2e$, $kfk^{-1}=q_i^{-2}f$ and $[e,f]=(k-k^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ onto $A_i$; the images of the monomials $F_i^aK_i^mE_i^b$ ($a,b\ge0$, $m\in\mathbb Z$) are linearly independent in $U_q(\mathfrak g)$, being images of the PBW monomials of the triangular decomposition ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]).

(ii) For all $a,b\ge0$, $K_iE_i^{(a)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{2a}E_i^{(a)}$ and $K_iF_i^{(b)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{-2b}F_i^{(b)}$, and for $b\ge1$ the divided powers satisfy the exact commutation formula
$$E_iF_i^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}E_i+\frac{F_i^{(b-1)}}{q_i^{b}-q_i^{-b}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}\bigl(q_i^{-2s}K_i-q_i^{2s}K_i^{-1}\bigr);$$
iterating it computes $E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}$ as a finite sum of monomials $F_i^{(b-t)}K_i^{m}E_i^{(a-t)}$ ($0\le t\le\min(a,b)$) with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$.

(iii) For every $N\ge0$ there is a simple $A_i$-module $L_i(N)$ of dimension $N+1$: it is the quotient of the cyclic module $\widetilde M(N):=A_i/\bigl(A_iE_i+A_i(K_i-q_i^N)\bigr)$ by the submodule generated by $F_i^{(N+1)}w_N$, where $w_N$ is the image of $1$, with basis the images $v_t$ of $F_i^{(t)}w_N$, $0\le t\le N$, on which $K_iv_t=q_i^{N-2t}v_t$, $F_iv_t=[t+1]_iv_{t+1}$ and $E_iv_t=[N-t+1]_iv_{t-1}$ (with $v_{-1}=v_{N+1}=0$); $L_i(N)$ is the unique simple $A_i$-module generated by a vector $v\ne0$ with $E_iv=0$, $K_iv=q_i^Nv$ and $F_i^{N+1}v=0$.

Let $T$ and $I_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ be the free $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and defining ideal of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], and write $K_i=K_{d_i h_i}$. Let $\Delta:T\to T\otimes_{\mathbb Q(q)}T$ and $\varepsilon:T\to\mathbb Q(q)$ be the algebra homomorphisms determined by

$$\Delta(K_h)=K_h\otimes K_h,\quad \Delta(E_i)=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes E_i,\quad \Delta(F_i)=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i,\quad \varepsilon(K_h)=1,\quad\varepsilon(E_i)=\varepsilon(F_i)=0.$$

Let $S:T\to T$ be the $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear algebra anti-homomorphism determined by

$$S(K_h)=K_{-h},\qquad S(E_i)=-E_iK_i,\qquad S(F_i)=-K_i^{-1}F_i.$$

Then

$$\Delta(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})\subseteq I_{\mathrm{DJ}}\otimes T+T\otimes I_{\mathrm{DJ}},\qquad \varepsilon(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})=0,\qquad S(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})\subseteq I_{\mathrm{DJ}}.$$

Hence these maps descend to $U_q(\mathfrak g)=T/I_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ and make it a Hopf algebra over $\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[def-bialgebra-counit-and-antipode]]): $\Delta$ is coassociative, $\varepsilon$ is a counit, and

$$m(S\otimes\operatorname{id})\Delta=\eta\circ\varepsilon=m(\operatorname{id}\otimes S)\Delta.$$

The antipode $S$ is unique for this multiplication, unit, coproduct and counit ([[lem-an-antipode-is-unique]]), and its square satisfies

$$S^2(E_i)=q_i^{-2}E_i,\qquad S^2(F_i)=q_i^{2}F_i,\qquad S^2(K_h)=K_h.$$

Let $\lambda\in P$, let $M(\lambda)$ be the Verma module with its canonical
$P$-label grading and highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]]), and let
$\sigma$ be the linear contravariant anti-involution of
[[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]]
($\sigma(K_h)=K_h$, $\sigma(E_i)=q_iF_iK_i^{-1}$,
$\sigma(F_i)=q_i^{-1}K_iE_i$).

(i) **Existence and uniqueness.** Define the $\lambda$-weight functional
$\eta\colon U_q(\mathfrak g)\to\mathbb Q(q)$ by $\eta(y):=$ the coefficient of
$v_\lambda$ in $yv_\lambda$ (so $\eta(y)$ is unchanged by adding an element of
the Verma ideal $J(\lambda)$, and $\eta(1)=1$). Then
$$B\bigl(av_\lambda,bv_\lambda\bigr):=\eta\bigl(\sigma(a)b\bigr)\qquad(a,b\in U_q^-)$$
is a well-defined bilinear form on $M(\lambda)$; it is homogeneous, normalized
($B(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$) and $\sigma$-contravariant,
$B(xu,v)=B(u,\sigma(x)v)$. It is the unique such form on $M(\lambda)$, in the
sense of [[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]].

(ii) **Radical and descent.** The radical
$\operatorname{rad}B=\{u:B(u,M(\lambda))=0\}$ equals the sum $N(\lambda)$ of all
proper graded submodules of $M(\lambda)$; consequently $B$ descends to a
nondegenerate normalized $\sigma$-contravariant form on the simple highest
weight quotient $L(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$.

(iii) **Rank-one norms and dominant singular vectors.** If
$m_i=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$ (that is, $\lambda$ dominant), then for
every $r\ge0$
$$B\bigl(F_i^{(r)}v_\lambda,F_i^{(r)}v_\lambda\bigr)=q_i^{\,r(m_i-r)}\binom{m_i}{r}_i,$$
with the Gaussian binomial interpreted as $0$ for $r>m_i$; in particular each
$F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$ lies in the radical, so $B$ factors through the Serre
quotient $M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$. (The same
computation proves the norm formula for every $\lambda$ and all $r$ for which
the right-hand side is read with $m_i=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle$.)

(iv) **Ordinary simplicity.** Let $V$ be an integrable cyclic graded quotient of
$M(\lambda)$ with support in $\lambda-Q_+$ on which the descended form is
nondegenerate. Then $V$ is simple as an ordinary module (not only as a graded
module).

(v) **Integrality of the lattice values.** If $\lambda$ is integral and
$V_A:=U_Av_\lambda=U_A^-v_\lambda\subseteq L(\lambda)$ is the highest lattice of
the Lusztig form ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]), then
$B(V_A,V_A)\subseteq A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. No perfectness of $B$ over $A$ is
asserted.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. For $m\in\mathbb N$, define the **$q_i$-integer**

$$[m]_i:=\frac{q_i^m-q_i^{-m}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}},\qquad [0]_i:=0,$$

and the **$q_i$-factorial**

$$[m]_i!:=\prod_{k=1}^m[k]_i,\qquad [0]_i!:=1.$$

For $0\le r\le m$, define the **Gaussian binomial** $\binom{m}{r}_i:=[m]_i!/([r]_i![m-r]_i!)$, and set it to $0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$. In the published one-parameter convention, write $\binom{m}{r}_t:=\binom{m}{r,m-r}_t$ for the two-part $q$-multinomial coefficient of [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]].

For an element $x$ of a unital $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and $m\ge0$, define its **divided power at $q_i$** by $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$, so $x^{(0)}=1$ and $x^{(1)}=x$.

The symmetric convention and the published asymmetric convention are related, for $m\ge0$ and $0\le r\le m$, by

$$[m]_i=q_i^{-(m-1)}[m]_{q_i^2},\qquad \binom{m}{r}_i=q_i^{-r(m-r)}\binom{m}{r}_{q_i^2}.$$

In particular $[m]_i$ is invariant under $q_i\mapsto q_i^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the symmetrizer only through $q_i=q^{d_i}$.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum and $i\in I$, and use the conventions of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $C_{m,r}:=\binom{m}{r}_i$, with $C_{m,r}=0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$.

(i) **Pascal recurrences.** For $m\ge1$ and every integer $r$,

$$C_{m,r}=q_i^{-r}C_{m-1,r}+q_i^{m-r}C_{m-1,r-1}=q_i^rC_{m-1,r}+q_i^{r-m}C_{m-1,r-1}.$$

(ii) **Symmetry.** For $0\le r\le m$, $C_{m,r}=C_{m,m-r}$.

(iii) **Gauss product formula.** For every $N\ge0$, in the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q(q)[z]$,

$$\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}(1+q_i^{2j}z)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}q_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}z^r.$$

Consequently, for $N\ge1$,

$$\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-1)^rq_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}=0.$$

(iv) **Integrality.** For $0\le r\le m$,

$$C_{m,r}\in q_i^{-r(m-r)}\mathbb Z[q_i^2]\subseteq\mathbb Z[q_i^{\pm1}].$$

Thus every Gaussian quotient is a Laurent polynomial in $q_i$ with integer coefficients, and the Pascal recurrences hold in that Laurent polynomial ring.

Let $q$ be transcendental over $\mathbb Q$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and let
$$A_0:=\mathbb Q[q]_{(q)}=\Big\{\frac fg\ :\ f,g\in\mathbb Q[q],\ g(0)\neq0\Big\}\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$$
be the localisation of the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q[q]$ at the prime ideal $(q)$ ([[def-localisation-at-a-prime-ideal]]). By [[ex-the-local-ring-of-polynomials-at-x]] with $F=\mathbb Q$, the ring $A_0$ is exactly the ring of rational functions regular at $q=0$, it is a local ring ([[def-local-ring]]) with unique maximal ideal $qA_0$, and evaluation at $0$ induces an isomorphism $A_0/qA_0\cong\mathbb Q$. Since $\mathbb Q[q]$ is a principal ideal domain ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-field-is-a-pid]]) with nonzero prime ideal $(q)$, the ring $A_0$ is a local principal ideal domain with nonzero maximal ideal; by the discrete valuation ring characterisations it is a discrete valuation ring with uniformiser $q/1$ ([[thm-equivalent-characterisations-of-a-dvr]], [[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]), and in particular a principal ideal domain ([[cor-dvr-is-a-pid]], [[def-principal-ideal-domain]]), with field of fractions $\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[cor-rational-function-field-as-a-fraction-field]]).

By [[def-discrete-valuation-ring]] a discrete valuation ring is the valuation ring $V_v=\{x:v(x)\ge0\}$ of a discrete valuation $v$ on its fraction field. The discrete valuation of $\mathbb Q(q)$ with $V_v=A_0$ and $v(q)=1$ is the **$q$-adic valuation**; write it $\operatorname{ord}_q$, so that
$$\operatorname{ord}_q:\mathbb Q(q)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\cup\{\infty\},\qquad A_0=\{h\in\mathbb Q(q):\operatorname{ord}_q(h)\ge0\},\qquad \operatorname{ord}_q(q)=1 .$$
Equivalently, $\operatorname{ord}_q$ is the vanishing order at $q=0$. The units of $A_0$ are exactly the fractions $f/g$ with $f(0)\neq0$ and $g(0)\neq0$, and $qA_0$ is the maximal ideal, so $q$ is a uniformiser of $A_0$ ([[thm-localisation-at-a-prime-is-local]]).

This ring $A_0$ is the **crystal limiting ring** of the crystal development below, and it is different from the Laurent ring $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ of [[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]: $q^{-1}\in A\setminus A_0$, while $(1+q)^{-1}\in A_0\setminus A$; neither ring contains the other, and both are subrings of $\mathbb Q(q)$. For every free $A_0$-module $L$ the canonical map
$$\mathbb Q\otimes_{A_0}L\longrightarrow L/qL,\qquad c\otimes\ell\mapsto c\,\ell+qL,$$
is an isomorphism, and for every $\lambda\in\mathbb Q(q)^\times$ one has $\lambda L/q\lambda L\cong L/qL$; passing from $L$ to $L/qL$ is the **crystal limit**. No freeness of any further module, no lattice and no choice principle is asserted here.

Let $\lambda\in P$, let $M(\lambda)$ be the Verma module with its canonical
$P$-label grading and highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]]), and let
$\sigma$ be the linear contravariant anti-involution of
[[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]]
($\sigma(K_h)=K_h$, $\sigma(E_i)=q_iF_iK_i^{-1}$,
$\sigma(F_i)=q_i^{-1}K_iE_i$).

(i) **Existence and uniqueness.** Define the $\lambda$-weight functional
$\eta\colon U_q(\mathfrak g)\to\mathbb Q(q)$ by $\eta(y):=$ the coefficient of
$v_\lambda$ in $yv_\lambda$ (so $\eta(y)$ is unchanged by adding an element of
the Verma ideal $J(\lambda)$, and $\eta(1)=1$). Then
$$B\bigl(av_\lambda,bv_\lambda\bigr):=\eta\bigl(\sigma(a)b\bigr)\qquad(a,b\in U_q^-)$$
is a well-defined bilinear form on $M(\lambda)$; it is homogeneous, normalized
($B(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$) and $\sigma$-contravariant,
$B(xu,v)=B(u,\sigma(x)v)$. It is the unique such form on $M(\lambda)$, in the
sense of [[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]].

(ii) **Radical and descent.** The radical
$\operatorname{rad}B=\{u:B(u,M(\lambda))=0\}$ equals the sum $N(\lambda)$ of all
proper graded submodules of $M(\lambda)$; consequently $B$ descends to a
nondegenerate normalized $\sigma$-contravariant form on the simple highest
weight quotient $L(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$.

(iii) **Rank-one norms and dominant singular vectors.** If
$m_i=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$ (that is, $\lambda$ dominant), then for
every $r\ge0$
$$B\bigl(F_i^{(r)}v_\lambda,F_i^{(r)}v_\lambda\bigr)=q_i^{\,r(m_i-r)}\binom{m_i}{r}_i,$$
with the Gaussian binomial interpreted as $0$ for $r>m_i$; in particular each
$F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$ lies in the radical, so $B$ factors through the Serre
quotient $M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$. (The same
computation proves the norm formula for every $\lambda$ and all $r$ for which
the right-hand side is read with $m_i=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle$.)

(iv) **Ordinary simplicity.** Let $V$ be an integrable cyclic graded quotient of
$M(\lambda)$ with support in $\lambda-Q_+$ on which the descended form is
nondegenerate. Then $V$ is simple as an ordinary module (not only as a graded
module).

(v) **Integrality of the lattice values.** If $\lambda$ is integral and
$V_A:=U_Av_\lambda=U_A^-v_\lambda\subseteq L(\lambda)$ is the highest lattice of
the Lusztig form ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]), then
$B(V_A,V_A)\subseteq A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. No perfectness of $B$ over $A$ is
asserted.

Let $T$ and $I_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ be the free $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and defining ideal of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], and write $K_i=K_{d_i h_i}$. Let $\Delta:T\to T\otimes_{\mathbb Q(q)}T$ and $\varepsilon:T\to\mathbb Q(q)$ be the algebra homomorphisms determined by

$$\Delta(K_h)=K_h\otimes K_h,\quad \Delta(E_i)=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes E_i,\quad \Delta(F_i)=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i,\quad \varepsilon(K_h)=1,\quad\varepsilon(E_i)=\varepsilon(F_i)=0.$$

Let $S:T\to T$ be the $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear algebra anti-homomorphism determined by

$$S(K_h)=K_{-h},\qquad S(E_i)=-E_iK_i,\qquad S(F_i)=-K_i^{-1}F_i.$$

Then

$$\Delta(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})\subseteq I_{\mathrm{DJ}}\otimes T+T\otimes I_{\mathrm{DJ}},\qquad \varepsilon(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})=0,\qquad S(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})\subseteq I_{\mathrm{DJ}}.$$

Hence these maps descend to $U_q(\mathfrak g)=T/I_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ and make it a Hopf algebra over $\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[def-bialgebra-counit-and-antipode]]): $\Delta$ is coassociative, $\varepsilon$ is a counit, and

$$m(S\otimes\operatorname{id})\Delta=\eta\circ\varepsilon=m(\operatorname{id}\otimes S)\Delta.$$

The antipode $S$ is unique for this multiplication, unit, coproduct and counit ([[lem-an-antipode-is-unique]]), and its square satisfies

$$S^2(E_i)=q_i^{-2}E_i,\qquad S^2(F_i)=q_i^{2}F_i,\qquad S^2(K_h)=K_h.$$

derivations.claim: Tensor contravariance and divided coproduct. Since $\Delta$ is an algebra map, $\Delta(\sigma(E_i))=z\Delta(F_i)\Delta(K_i^{-1})=zF_iK_i^{-1}\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes zF_iK_i^{-1}=(\sigma\otimes\sigma)\Delta(E_i)$, and $\Delta(\sigma(F_i))=z^{-1}\Delta(K_i)\Delta(E_i)=z^{-1}K_iE_i\otimes1+z^{-1}K_i\otimes K_iE_i=(\sigma\otimes\sigma)\Delta(F_i)$; the equality for $K_i^{\pm1}$ is immediate. Both $\Delta\sigma$ and $(\sigma\otimes\sigma)\Delta$ reverse products, so equality on generators proves equality on the rank-one algebra. Factor contravariance then gives $B(\Delta(X)(x\otimes y),x'\otimes y')=B(x\otimes y,(\sigma\otimes\sigma)\Delta(X)(x'\otimes y'))=B(x\otimes y,\Delta(\sigma(X))(x'\otimes y'))$ for all $X$; extend by bilinearity to all tensor vectors. This proves the tensor contravariance of the product form. From $\Delta F_i=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i$ and the $q$-commutation $(K_i\otimes F_i)(F_i\otimes1)=z^{-2}(F_i\otimes1)(K_i\otimes F_i)$, expanding the $n$-th power gives $\Delta F_i^{(n)}=\sum_{s=0}^{n}z^{-s(n-s)}F_i^{(n-s)}K_i^s\otimes F_i^{(s)}$: the coefficient of $(F_i\otimes1)^{n-s}(K_i\otimes F_i)^s$ in $(\Delta F_i)^n$ is $z^{-s(n-s)}\binom{n}{s}_z$, and division by $[n]_z!$ cancels the Gaussian binomials as $[n]_z!=\binom{n}{s}_z[s]_z![n-s]_z!$.

The highest vectors. For $0\le t\le\min(a,b)$ define $c_0=1$ and $c_{l+1}=-c_lz^{b-2t+2l+2}\frac{[b-t+l+1]_z}{[a-l]_z}$ for $0\le l<t$; all denominators are nonzero since $l<t\le a$, and set $h_t:=\sum_{l=0}^{t}c_l\,v_l\otimes w_{t-l}$. Substituting $\Delta E_i$ and comparing the coefficient of $v_{l-1}\otimes w_{t-l}$ for $1\le l\le t$ gives $c_l[a-l+1]_zz^{2(t-l)-b}+c_{l-1}[b-t+l]_z$, which is zero by the recurrence; the coefficients of $v_{-1}\otimes w_t$ and $v_t\otimes w_{-1}$ vanish because those basis vectors do not exist. Hence $\Delta E_ih_t=0$, and $h_t$ has weight $a+b-2t$ since $K_i$ acts on $v_l\otimes w_{t-l}$ by $z^{a-2l}z^{b-2(t-l)}=z^{a+b-2t}$.

The norm criterion. For $x=\sum_{j,k}\alpha_{j,k}v_j\otimes w_k$ one has $B(x,x)=\sum_{j,k}\alpha_{j,k}^2d(a,j)d(b,k)$, so $x\in L$ implies $B(x,x)\in A_0$ because $d(a,j)d(b,k)\in A_0$; conversely, if $B(x,x)\in A_0$ but $x\notin L$, take the minimal $N\ge1$ with $q^Nx\in L$ and let $\overline{x}\neq0$ be its residue in $L/qL$. Then $B(q^Nx,q^Nx)=q^{2N}B(x,x)\in qA_0$, while on residues the form $\overline B$ is diagonal with all entries congruent to $1$ modulo $q$, so $\overline B(\overline x,\overline x)$ is the sum of the squares of the rational residues of the coordinates of $\overline x$, a positive rational, contradicting $\overline B(\overline x,\overline x)=0$. Hence $L=\{x:B(x,x)\in A_0\}$.

Valuations. By [F4], $\operatorname{ord}_zc_{l+1}-\operatorname{ord}_zc_l=(b-2t+2l+2)+(1-(b-t+l+1))-(1-(a-l))=a-t+1$ for every $l$, so the orders telescope to $\operatorname{ord}_zc_l=l(a-t+1)>0$ for $l\ge1$, with $\operatorname{ord}_zc_0=0$; hence $c_l\in A_0$, $c_0=1$ and $c_l\in qA_0$ for $l>0$. Therefore $h_t\equiv v_0\otimes w_t\pmod{qL}$, and by [F6] $B(h_t,h_t)=\sum_lc_l^2d(a,l)d(b,t-l)\equiv d(b,t)\equiv1\pmod q$, since $d(a,l)\in1+qA_0$ and the $l>0$ terms lie in $qA_0$.

Coefficients. Put $u_{t,n}:=F_i^{(n)}h_t$ and write $u_{t,n}=\sum_{j,k}\gamma_{j,k}\,v_j\otimes w_k$; by weight, $\gamma_{j,k}=0$ unless $j+k=t+n$. Applying $\Delta F_i^{(n)}=\sum_sz^{-s(n-s)}F_i^{(n-s)}K_i^s\otimes F_i^{(s)}$ of step 1.1 to $h_t$ and using [F1] gives the finite sum $\gamma_{j,k}=\sum_{l}c_l\,z^{-s(n-s)+s(a-2l)}\binom{j}{l}_z\binom{k}{t-l}_z$ with $s=k-t+l$, over the integers $l$ with $0\le l\le\min(t,j)$ and $0\le s\le n$ (the symmetry of the Gaussian binomials rewrites the divided-power coefficients).

The tensored strings lie in $L$. Let $A:=a+b-2t$ and $u_{t,n}:=F_i^{(n)}h_t$ for $0\le n\le A$. By [F5](ii), $F_i^{(n)}h_t\ne0$ for $0\le n\le A$; the span of these $A+1$ vectors is generated by $h_t$ and stable under $E_i,F_i,K_i$, so it is the simple rank-one module of highest weight $A$ by [F1], and the form restricted to it is a nonzero contravariant form, hence by [F3] a multiple of the normalized form, with factor $B(h_t,h_t)$; hence $B(u_{t,n},u_{t,n})=d(A,n)B(h_t,h_t)\in A_0$ by step 2.1 and [F4]. The norm criterion of step 1.3 therefore gives $u_{t,n}\in L$.

Integrality of the residue. Every summand in step 2.2 is an integer Laurent series in $z$: its factors $c_l$, $[m]_z$ and $\binom{N}{R}_z$ are quotients of Laurent polynomials whose denominator factors $[m]_z$ have leading coefficient $\pm1$, so their inverses are Laurent series with integer coefficients with finitely many negative terms. Since $u_{t,n}\in L$ by step 3.1, each $\gamma_{j,k}$ lies in $A_0$; an element of $A_0$ that is also an integer Laurent series has an integer residue, and the sum of the squares of the residues is $1$ because $B(u_{t,n},u_{t,n})\equiv1\pmod q$ by step 2.1 and [F4], while the Gram entries are congruent to $1$.

Distinguished coefficient. If $n\le a-t$, take $(j,k)=(n,t)$. The summand with $l=0$ is $c_0z^0\binom{n}{0}_z\binom{t}{t}_z=1$; a summand with $l\ge1$ has $s=l$ and valuation $l(a-t+1)+l(a-2l)-l(n-l)-l(t-l)-l(n-l)=l(2a-2n-2t+1)+l^2\ge l+l^2>0$ by the additivity of $\operatorname{ord}_z$ in [F4] (here $a-t-n\ge0$). Hence $\gamma_{n,t}\equiv1\pmod q$.

Second distinguished coefficient. If $n\ge a-t$, take $(j,k)=(a-t,\,n-a+2t)$. The summand with $l=0$ is $z^{t(n-a+t)}\binom{n-a+2t}{t}_z$, of valuation $t(n-a+t)-t(n-a+t)=0$ and leading coefficient $1$ by [F4]; a summand with $l\ge1$ and $\binom{j}{l}_z\neq0$, so $l\le a-t$, has $s=n-a+t+l$ and valuation $l(a-t+1)-s(n-s)+s(a-2l)-l(j-l)-(t-l)(k-t+l)=l+l^2>0$, where the exponent identity uses $k-t+l=s$. Hence $\gamma_{a-t,\,n-a+2t}\equiv1\pmod q$.

The residues are the chain positions. By steps 5.1-5.2 the distinguished coefficient of $u_{t,n}$ has residue $1$. Since all residues are integers and their squares sum to $1$ by step 4.1, every other coefficient has residue $0$. Hence the residue of $u_{t,n}$ is the single basis element $v_j\otimes w_k$ with $(j,k)=(n,t)$ when $n\le a-t$ and $(j,k)=(a-t,n-a+2t)$ when $n\ge a-t$.

Partition into chains. Fixing $t$ and letting $n$ run over $0,\dots,a+b-2t$, the positions of step 6.1 are $(0,t),(1,t),\dots,(a-t,t),(a-t,t+1),\dots,(a-t,b)$. These are the chains of the statement, and they partition the rectangle $0\le j\le a$, $0\le k\le b$: a cell $(j,k)$ lies on the chain of $t=\min(k,a-j)$, and then it is the position $n=j$ if $k=t$ and $n=a-t+k-t$ if $k>t$ (then $j=a-t$), which determines the position uniquely. The total number of vectors $u_{t,n}$ is $\sum_{t=0}^{\min(a,b)}(a+b-2t+1)=(a+1)(b+1)$.

$A_0$-basis. The matrix expressing the family $\{u_{t,n}\}$ in the product basis reduces modulo $q$ to a permutation matrix by steps 6.1-7.1, hence has determinant congruent to $\pm1$ modulo $q$, a unit of $A_0$; the adjugate identity over $A_0$ makes the matrix invertible over $A_0$. Since $\{u_{t,n}\}\subseteq L$ by step 3.1 and both families have $(a+1)(b+1)$ members, $\{u_{t,n}\}$ is an $A_0$-basis of $L$.

The crystal rule. By [F5] the operators act on the strings by $\tilde e_iF_i^{(n)}h_t=F_i^{(n-1)}h_t$ and $\tilde f_iF_i^{(n)}h_t=F_i^{(n+1)}h_t$, with the endpoint terms zero; since the strings form the $A_0$-basis of $L$ by step 8.1, both operators preserve $L$ and shift the residues along the chains of step 7.1. Reading off which tensor factor changes gives the two displayed rules: along $(n,t)\mapsto(n+1,t)$ the first factor moves exactly when $a-(n)>\ t$, that is $a-j>k$, and along $(a-t,k)\mapsto(a-t,k+1)$ the second factor moves, which is the case $a-j\le k$; the $\tilde e_i$-rule is read in the reverse direction, where the first factor moves exactly when $a-j\ge k$. Terms leaving the ranges are $0$. For residues $b=v_j\otimes w_k$ and $b'$: if $a-j>k$ then $\tilde f_ib=v_{j+1}\otimes w_k$ and $a-(j+1)\ge k$, so $\tilde e_ib'=b$; if $a-j\le k$ then $\tilde f_ib=v_j\otimes w_{k+1}$ and $a-j<k+1$, so $\tilde e_ib'=b$; the converse implications follow by the same two evaluations of the displayed rules. Hence $\tilde f_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde e_ib'$. No choice is used, and neither the grand loop nor any freeness over $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ enters.

boundaries.evidence: The rectangle $0\le j\le a$, $0\le k\le b$ is nonempty for all $a,b\ge0$ and the tensor product is nonzero, so the empty cases occur only inside sums: step 2.2's coefficient formula omits all $l$ outside $0\le l\le\min(t,j)$, and step 5.1 has the single summand $l=0$ equal to $1$ when the sum is otherwise empty.

The zero values are the endpoint terms of the rules (ii): $F_i^{(-1)}=F_i^{(A+1)}=0$ on a string of length $A$ by [F5], and step 9.1 reads the two displayed rules with all terms leaving the divided-basis ranges equal to $0$.

The chain with $t=0$ is the highest chain of length $a+b+1$ starting at $v_0\otimes w_0$, and the smallest nontrivial cases $a=0$ or $b=0$ reduce the tensor to a single rank-one module: the recurrence of step 1.2 is empty for $t=0$, and steps 5.1 and 5.2 give the residue $1$ at both ends of the split.

When $a=0$ the factor $V(a)$ is one-dimensional, the rectangle is the single row $j=0$, and the chains of (iii) are the strings of $V(b)$; step 1.3's norm criterion reduces to $L=A_0$-span of the product basis and step 3.1's rank-one module has length $b+1$, so the degenerate factor is a genuine boundary of the computation rather than an excluded case.

The endpoint vertices $j=0$, $j=a$, $k=0$, $k=b$: the comparison split at $a-j=k$ is evaluated on both sides in step 9.1, including the tie, and the two distinguished coefficients of steps 5.1 and 5.2 cover the ends $n\le a-t$ and $n\ge a-t$ of every chain.

No choice is used: the coefficients $c_l$ are determined by the recurrence of step 1.2, the product basis is fixed data, and the string family is indexed by the integer points of the rectangle; step 9.1 records that neither the grand loop nor any freeness over $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ enters.

The forward direction $\tilde f_ib=b'$ implies $b=\tilde e_ib'$: on the first branch $a-j>k$ of step 9.1, $\tilde f_i$ moves to $(j+1,k)$ with $a-(j+1)\ge k$, so applying the displayed $\tilde e_i$-rule returns $b$; step 9.1 computes this for both branches, tie included.

The converse $b=\tilde e_ib'$ implies $\tilde f_ib=b'$ is the same two evaluations of the displayed rules read in reverse: on the branch $a-j\le k$ the second factor moves, and step 9.1 states both implications and records the partial-inverse property for all residue pairs.

risk_review.notes: Read all 13 steps and exact coproduct/form suppliers. Independently expanded divided coproduct, highest recurrence and both coefficient valuations: first distinguished extra terms have l(2a-2n-2t+1)+l^2>0; second have l+l^2>0. Sigma commutes with coproduct by generator calculation, giving the product form and unit norms. Rational sums of squares detect the lattice, integer Laurent residues with squared norm 1 identify a single coordinate, and determinant-unit inversion gives an A0 basis. Rectangle cell chain t=min(k,a-j) yields the strict lowering/non-strict raising boundary, including a=0,b=0, top, bottom and equality. Berkeley pp.332–334 and JKK pp.19–21 confirm coproduct orientation/rule, though Berkeley displays contain evident typographic errors; local formulas are used. Current reader arithmetic and chain-index corrections are sound; no AC or circular grand-loop use.

citations.quote:
Let $M$ be an integrable chosen $P$-graded type-1 module ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) and fix $i\in I$. By [[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]] every $u\in M_\lambda$ has a unique admissible decomposition
$$u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}=\ker(E_i)\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i},$$
with $u_n=0$ whenever $n>\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$. Define the **Kashiwara operators**
$$\tilde e_i u:=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_i u:=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n+1)}u_n .$$
Both are linear maps on $M$, shifting the label weight by $+\alpha_i$, respectively $-\alpha_i$. Along each string, $\tilde e_i$ moves $F_i^{(n)}u_n$ to $F_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ and kills the top position $n=0$, while $\tilde f_i$ moves it to $F_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ and kills a string exactly at its bottom, where $n=\langle\mathrm{wt}(u_n),h_i\rangle$.

Let $p_{\mathrm{top}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$ be the projections onto the top positions and the bottom positions of these strings:
$$p_{\mathrm{top}}u:=u_0,\qquad p_{\mathrm{bottom}}u:=\sum_{n:\,n=\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle}F_i^{(n)}u_n .$$
Then
$$\ker\tilde e_i=\ker E_i,\qquad \ker\tilde f_i=\ker F_i,\qquad \tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{top}},\qquad \tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{bottom}},$$
so $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ are inverse to each other on each existing string edge. Module homomorphisms commute with both operators, $p_{\mathrm{top}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$. On $\ker E_i$ one has $\tilde f_i=F_i$, and on $\ker F_i$ one has $\tilde e_i=E_i$. At interior positions the operators differ from the generators: in the rank-one module $L_i(2)$ with highest vector $v$ and $u=F_iv$, one has $F_iu=[2]_iF_i^{(2)}v$ while $\tilde f_iu=F_i^{(2)}v$, and $[2]_i\neq1$. No choice principle is used. The analogous Kashiwara operators on the negative half $U_q^-$ are the shifts of its unique $e_i'$-string decomposition ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]), constructed using the skew derivation of [[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]. Their strings have no bottom: $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}$ and $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-P_i$, where $P_i$ projects onto $\ker e_i'$; the second identity follows by subtracting the position-zero coefficient $u_0=P_iu$ from the string expansion. These string-shift operators are distinct from the skew derivations $e_i',e_i''$. No negative-half operator is used in the module verification below.

Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half of the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with its skew derivations $e_i',e_i'':U_q^-\to U_q^-$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]), fix $i\in I$, and write $f_i^{(n)}=F_i^n/[n]_i!$ for the divided powers ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]). Then:

(i) $e_i'$ is locally nilpotent on $U_q^-$, and the endomorphism
$$P_i:=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^mq_i^{-m(m-1)/2}F_i^{(m)}e_i'^{\,m}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q(q)}(U_q^-)$$
is well defined (each sum is finite on each element) and is the projection onto $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ along $f_iU_q^-$. In particular $e_i'P_i=0$, $P_iF_i=0$, $P_i^2=P_i$, $P_iu=u$ for $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$, and
$$U_q^-=\operatorname{Ker}e_i'\oplus f_iU_q^-.$$

(ii) Every $u\in U_q^-$ has a unique $i$-string decomposition
$$u=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i',\qquad u_n=0\ \text{for }n\gg0,$$
and the components are given by $u_n=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u$.

(iii) The **Kashiwara operators on the negative half**, defined on the string decomposition by
$$\tilde e_iu:=\sum_{n\ge1}f_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_iu:=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n+1)}u_n,$$
are $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear endomorphisms of $U_q^-$ with $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}_{U_q^-}$; $\tilde e_iu=0$ if and only if $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$; $\tilde f_i$ is injective and $\tilde f_i(1)=F_i$. Both operators preserve the root grading and shift its degree by $\mp\alpha_i$, that is $\tilde e_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu+\alpha_i]$ and $\tilde f_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu-\alpha_i]$.

No choice principle is used. Here $e_i'^{\,n}$ denotes the ordinary $n$-fold power of the derivation, not its divided power. The same projector and every string coefficient preserve the $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]), as proved by the integral skew-string supplier; this does not assert that lattice's freeness.

derivations.claim: Finiteness. Let $b\in B$ and let $x\in L$ be a lift of $b$. By [F2] the vector $x$ is a finite sum of string positions $F_i^{(n)}u_n$; along each of the finitely many strings both $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ move one position and kill the ends, so there are integers $N,M$ with $\tilde f_i^Nx=0$ and $\tilde e_i^Mx=0$. The operators preserve $L$ and descend to the quotient, so $\tilde f_i^Nb=0$ and $\tilde e_i^Mb=0$; hence $\varepsilon_i(b)$ and $\varphi_i(b)$ are finite.

A highest lift. Let $b_{\mathrm{top}}:=\tilde e_i^{\varepsilon_i(b)}b$ and let $y\in L_{\mathrm{wt}(b_{\mathrm{top}})}$ be a homogeneous lift of $b_{\mathrm{top}}$. Since $\tilde e_ib_{\mathrm{top}}=0$, the element $\tilde e_iy$ lies in $qL$, hence so does $\tilde f_i\tilde e_iy$; by [F2], $h:=(\mathrm{id}-\tilde f_i\tilde e_i)(y)=y-\tilde f_i\tilde e_iy$ is a lift of $b_{\mathrm{top}}$ that lies in the image of $p_{\mathrm{top}}=\mathrm{id}-\tilde f_i\tilde e_i$, that is, in $\ker\tilde e_i=\ker E_i$; it is nonzero because its class $b_{\mathrm{top}}$ is nonzero. Thus $h$ is a nonzero $E_i$-highest vector of $M$, and its weight is $\mu:=\mathrm{wt}(b_{\mathrm{top}})=\mathrm{wt}(b)+\varepsilon_i(b)\alpha_i$ by [F2].

The negative half. For $U_q^-$ and a residue class $b$ of root degree $-
u$, the operator $	ilde e_i$ raises the root degree by $\alpha_i$ and hence lowers the height $\operatorname{ht}(
u)$ by one; iterating, $	ilde e_i^{\,\operatorname{ht}(
u)+1}b=0$, so $\varepsilon_i(b)$ is finite. The operator $	ilde f_i$ is injective by [F4], so $	ilde f_i^{\,n}b
e0$ for every $n\ge0$; the actual lowering-chain length is therefore $\ell_i^-=+\infty$. The formal quantity $\varphi_i:=\varepsilon_i+\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}angle$ is an integer, well defined on the root-graded crystal, and along a lowering edge it changes by $+1-2=-1$: indeed $\varepsilon_i$ increases by one and $\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}angle$ decreases by $\langle h_i,\alpha_iangle=2$. It can be negative (for example $\varphi_i=0$ at the unit, and $\varphi_i=\varepsilon_i-\sum_j a_{ij}
u_j$ at degree $-
u=-\sum_j
u_j\alpha_j$), and it is not the length of the lowering chain. No integrability or finite-string property of the whole negative half is used.

The component is a finite chain. By [F1] the relation $b\sim b'$ if $\tilde f_i^mb=b'$ or $\tilde f_i^mb'=b$ for some $m\ge0$ is symmetric and transitive, and each vertex has at most one $\tilde f_i$-image and at most one $\tilde f_i$-preimage in $B$; by step 1.1 every class is finite, so the component of $b$ is a finite path. It has a unique top, where $\tilde e_i$ acts by $0$, and a unique bottom, where $\tilde f_i$ acts by $0$; writing $\varepsilon_i$ and $\varphi_i$ for the distances from the top and to the bottom gives $\varepsilon_i(b)+\varphi_i(b)+1=\#$ of vertices of the component.

The chain has length $a+1$. Put $a:=\langle\mu,h_i\rangle$, so $a\ge0$ and $h\in H_\mu$. By [F3], $F_i^{(n)}h\ne0$ for $0\le n\le a$ and $F_i^{(n)}h=0$ for $n>a$, so exactly $a+1$ positions of this string are nonzero. Their classes are also nonzero: if $F_i^{(n)}h=\tilde f_i^nh\in qL$ for $n\le a$, then applying the lattice-preserving $\tilde e_i^n$ gives $h\in qL$, contradicting its nonzero top residue. Thus their classes are the vertices reached from $b_{\mathrm{top}}$ by $\tilde f_i$ (while nonzero), and by step 2.1 they are precisely the vertices of the component of $b$. Hence the component of $b$ has $a+1$ vertices.

The formulas. If $b$ is the position $n$ of the chain, counted from the top, then $\varepsilon_i(b)=n$ and, by step 3.1, $\varphi_i(b)=a-n$. Since $a=\langle\mu,h_i\rangle=\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle+2n$ by step 1.2, this gives $\varphi_i(b)=\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle+n=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle$, and also $\varepsilon_i(b)+\varphi_i(b)=a=\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle+2\varepsilon_i(b)$, which is the highest rank-one integer of the top label.

Edges. On an existing arrow $b\to\tilde f_ib$, the position increases by one, so $\varepsilon_i$ increases by $1$ and $\varphi_i$ decreases by $1$, while the weight decreases by $\alpha_i$; conversely, $\tilde e_i$ moves one position up whenever $b$ is not the top. By step 2.1 the chain has exactly $\varepsilon_i(b)+\varphi_i(b)+1$ vertices.

Choice. The data $(L,B)$, the operators and the chain positions are given or uniquely determined; all constructions above use finite sums and the unique string decomposition, so no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: Every claim is pointwise in $b\in B$; for the empty crystal there is no vertex to test and both maxima are undefined, while the Definition's parenthetical finiteness is proved for each fixed vertex in step 1.1 by lifting it into the lattice.

The value $0$ is attained at string ends: a top vertex has $\varepsilon_i=0$ and a bottom vertex has $\varphi_i=0$, and the convention $\tilde e_iB\subseteq B\cup\{0\}$ is used in step 1.1 where the powers are eventually killed (with $0\notin B$).

A one-vertex chain has $a=\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle=0$, hence $\varepsilon_i(b)=\varphi_i(b)=0$ and highest rank-one integer $0$; this is the case $a=0$ of step 3.1 and of the formula $\varphi_i=\varepsilon_i+\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}\rangle$ in step 4.1.

The negative half is the degenerate case handled in step 1.3: $\varepsilon_i(b)$ is finite because raising lowers the positive-root height, while the formal $\varphi_i=\varepsilon_i+\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}\rangle$ may be negative and the actual lowering length is $\ell_i^-=\infty$ because $\tilde f_i$ is injective; the Definition states explicitly that the formal value is not the chain length.

Top and bottom vertices: step 5.1 shows that along an existing edge $\varepsilon_i$ increases by $1$, $\varphi_i$ decreases by $1$ and the weight drops by $\alpha_i$, and the chain stops where the corresponding operator is $0$ by the partial-inverse axiom [F1]; step 2.1 makes the component a finite chain with two ends.

No choice is used: step 6.1 records that the crystal basis, its operators and the chain positions are given or uniquely determined, and steps 1.1-5.1 use finite sums, lifts of residues and the unique string decomposition.

The forward direction of the partial-inverse axiom, $\tilde f_ib=b'$ implies $b=\tilde e_ib'$, is an input from [F1]; step 2.1 reads the crystal graph so that an edge $b\to b'$ means exactly $\tilde f_ib=b'$, and step 4.1 uses this reading to place positions on a chain.

The reverse direction $b=\tilde e_ib'$ implies $\tilde f_ib=b'$ is the same axiom read backwards; step 5.1 uses it to move one position up whenever $b$ is not the top, so both directions of the biconditional are consumed rather than re-proved.

risk_review.notes: Read all eight steps against reviewed crystal and string suppliers. A homogeneous top lift h=y-f-tilde e-tilde y is nonzero and highest; raising back from each nonzero field position excludes a zero residue. Thus module chain length is a+1 and phi=epsilon+coroot label in both endpoint cases, including trivial strings. Negative-half height bounds raising, e-tilde f-tilde=id holds on residues and yields infinite actual lowering; formal phi is the finite integer epsilon-sum_j a_ij nu_j. Corrected full Cartan row and highest-lift argument are sound. JKK p.18 (4.7), Proposition 4.8, p.19 Example 5.1(a) and Kashiwara pp.474–475 confirm module convention. Added explicit reversed-bracket notation to retain the displayed conventional dual pairing without a typing ambiguity; it denotes the existing pairing and changes no mathematical interface.

citations.quote:
Let $M$ be an integrable chosen $P$-graded type-1 module ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) and fix $i\in I$. By [[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]] every $u\in M_\lambda$ has a unique admissible decomposition
$$u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}=\ker(E_i)\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i},$$
with $u_n=0$ whenever $n>\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$. Define the **Kashiwara operators**
$$\tilde e_i u:=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_i u:=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n+1)}u_n .$$
Both are linear maps on $M$, shifting the label weight by $+\alpha_i$, respectively $-\alpha_i$. Along each string, $\tilde e_i$ moves $F_i^{(n)}u_n$ to $F_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ and kills the top position $n=0$, while $\tilde f_i$ moves it to $F_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ and kills a string exactly at its bottom, where $n=\langle\mathrm{wt}(u_n),h_i\rangle$.

Let $p_{\mathrm{top}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$ be the projections onto the top positions and the bottom positions of these strings:
$$p_{\mathrm{top}}u:=u_0,\qquad p_{\mathrm{bottom}}u:=\sum_{n:\,n=\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle}F_i^{(n)}u_n .$$
Then
$$\ker\tilde e_i=\ker E_i,\qquad \ker\tilde f_i=\ker F_i,\qquad \tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{top}},\qquad \tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{bottom}},$$
so $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ are inverse to each other on each existing string edge. Module homomorphisms commute with both operators, $p_{\mathrm{top}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$. On $\ker E_i$ one has $\tilde f_i=F_i$, and on $\ker F_i$ one has $\tilde e_i=E_i$. At interior positions the operators differ from the generators: in the rank-one module $L_i(2)$ with highest vector $v$ and $u=F_iv$, one has $F_iu=[2]_iF_i^{(2)}v$ while $\tilde f_iu=F_i^{(2)}v$, and $[2]_i\neq1$. No choice principle is used. The analogous Kashiwara operators on the negative half $U_q^-$ are the shifts of its unique $e_i'$-string decomposition ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]), constructed using the skew derivation of [[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]. Their strings have no bottom: $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}$ and $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-P_i$, where $P_i$ projects onto $\ker e_i'$; the second identity follows by subtracting the position-zero coefficient $u_0=P_iu$ from the string expansion. These string-shift operators are distinct from the skew derivations $e_i',e_i''$. No negative-half operator is used in the module verification below.

Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half of the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with its skew derivations $e_i',e_i'':U_q^-\to U_q^-$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]), fix $i\in I$, and write $f_i^{(n)}=F_i^n/[n]_i!$ for the divided powers ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]). Then:

(i) $e_i'$ is locally nilpotent on $U_q^-$, and the endomorphism
$$P_i:=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^mq_i^{-m(m-1)/2}F_i^{(m)}e_i'^{\,m}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q(q)}(U_q^-)$$
is well defined (each sum is finite on each element) and is the projection onto $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ along $f_iU_q^-$. In particular $e_i'P_i=0$, $P_iF_i=0$, $P_i^2=P_i$, $P_iu=u$ for $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$, and
$$U_q^-=\operatorname{Ker}e_i'\oplus f_iU_q^-.$$

(ii) Every $u\in U_q^-$ has a unique $i$-string decomposition
$$u=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i',\qquad u_n=0\ \text{for }n\gg0,$$
and the components are given by $u_n=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u$.

(iii) The **Kashiwara operators on the negative half**, defined on the string decomposition by
$$\tilde e_iu:=\sum_{n\ge1}f_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_iu:=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n+1)}u_n,$$
are $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear endomorphisms of $U_q^-$ with $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}_{U_q^-}$; $\tilde e_iu=0$ if and only if $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$; $\tilde f_i$ is injective and $\tilde f_i(1)=F_i$. Both operators preserve the root grading and shift its degree by $\mp\alpha_i$, that is $\tilde e_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu+\alpha_i]$ and $\tilde f_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu-\alpha_i]$.

No choice principle is used. Here $e_i'^{\,n}$ denotes the ordinary $n$-fold power of the derivation, not its divided power. The same projector and every string coefficient preserve the $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]), as proved by the integral skew-string supplier; this does not assert that lattice's freeness.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group
with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), with root lattice $Q$,
simple roots $\alpha_i\in P$ and integer pairing
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$, and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with generators $E_i,F_i,K_h$
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). The lattice $P$ plays
the role of the integral weights of the classical theory
([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]); the pairing need not
be perfect, and no identification $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$ is
assumed anywhere.

A **$P$-graded type-one quantum weight module** is a left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$
together with a direct sum decomposition

$$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$$

(an internal direct sum of $\mathbb Q(q)$-subspaces, only finitely many nonzero
on each vector) such that, for all $\mu\in P$, $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $i\in I$,

$$K_h\ \text{acts on}\ M_\mu\ \text{by the scalar}\ q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle},\qquad E_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu+\alpha_i},\qquad F_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu-\alpha_i}.$$

The subspaces $M_\mu$ are the **chosen label-weight spaces**: the grading is
part of the structure and is not reconstructed from the action, because the
pairing may have a kernel. **Morphisms** of $P$-graded type-one weight modules
are the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps $f\colon M\to N$ with
$f(M_\mu)\subseteq N_\mu$ for every $\mu$; the weight submodules and quotients
considered on this page are those with the induced grading (Verification, step 2.2).

The module is **integrable** if $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every
vector: for every $v\in M$ and every $i$ there are integers $N_e(v,i),N_f(v,i)\ge1$
with $E_i^{N_e(v,i)}v=0$ and $F_i^{N_f(v,i)}v=0$. The exponents may depend on
the vector and on $i$, and both directions are required independently;
integrability is not a uniform nilpotence condition.

The following are additional hypotheses, never part of the definition:
finiteness of the dimension of every $M_\mu$; boundedness of the set of $\mu$
with $M_\mu\ne0$ above (or below); finite generation of $M$. The zero module is
a $P$-graded type-one weight module with the empty grading ($M_\mu=0$ for all
$\mu$), and it is integrable.

Two remarks are recorded here and proved below. First, when the pairing
separates $P$, the spaces $M_\mu$ are exactly the simultaneous eigenspaces of
the $K_h$, and the present definition recovers the usual type-one weight
modules (Verification, steps 2.1 and 4.1). Second, when the pairing does not
separate, distinct labels $\mu\ne\mu'$ may carry the same toral character, and
a simultaneous toral eigenspace must not be equated with a single label space;
the definition therefore takes the label grading as data. The regularization of
finite-cone support and all highest-weight comparisons on this page are proved
later, not assumed here by writing $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$.
No choice principle enters this definition.

Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half of the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with its skew derivations $e_i',e_i'':U_q^-\to U_q^-$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]), fix $i\in I$, and write $f_i^{(n)}=F_i^n/[n]_i!$ for the divided powers ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]). Then:

(i) $e_i'$ is locally nilpotent on $U_q^-$, and the endomorphism
$$P_i:=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^mq_i^{-m(m-1)/2}F_i^{(m)}e_i'^{\,m}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q(q)}(U_q^-)$$
is well defined (each sum is finite on each element) and is the projection onto $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ along $f_iU_q^-$. In particular $e_i'P_i=0$, $P_iF_i=0$, $P_i^2=P_i$, $P_iu=u$ for $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$, and
$$U_q^-=\operatorname{Ker}e_i'\oplus f_iU_q^-.$$

(ii) Every $u\in U_q^-$ has a unique $i$-string decomposition
$$u=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i',\qquad u_n=0\ \text{for }n\gg0,$$
and the components are given by $u_n=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u$.

(iii) The **Kashiwara operators on the negative half**, defined on the string decomposition by
$$\tilde e_iu:=\sum_{n\ge1}f_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_iu:=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n+1)}u_n,$$
are $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear endomorphisms of $U_q^-$ with $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}_{U_q^-}$; $\tilde e_iu=0$ if and only if $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$; $\tilde f_i$ is injective and $\tilde f_i(1)=F_i$. Both operators preserve the root grading and shift its degree by $\mp\alpha_i$, that is $\tilde e_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu+\alpha_i]$ and $\tilde f_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu-\alpha_i]$.

No choice principle is used. Here $e_i'^{\,n}$ denotes the ordinary $n$-fold power of the derivation, not its divided power. The same projector and every string coefficient preserve the $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]), as proved by the integral skew-string supplier; this does not assert that lattice's freeness.

Fix a minimal realization $(\mathfrak h,(h_i),(\alpha_i))$ of a finite GCM $A$, with the row-coroot convention $\alpha_j(h_i)=a_{ij}$ from [[def-realization-of-a-generalized-cartan-matrix]]. Define

$$P=\{\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*: \lambda(h_i)\in\mathbb Z\text{ for every }i\},\qquad P^+=\{\lambda\in P:\lambda(h_i)\geq0\text{ for every }i\}.$$

Elements of $P$ are **integral weights**; elements of $P^+$ are **dominant integral weights**. Their simple-coroot labels are the integers $\lambda(h_i)$. Zero labels are allowed, and the zero functional is dominant integral.

The independent coroots can be extended to a finite basis of $\mathfrak h$. Prescribing integral labels on the coroots and arbitrary complex values on the remaining basis vectors specifies a unique functional. Thus complementary Cartan values are unrestricted; $P$ need not be a discrete lattice in $\mathfrak h^*$. The inequalities only concern the integral coroot labels, not an ordering of arbitrary complex Cartan values. This definition uses finite linear algebra and no AC.
Every finitely generated torsion-free module over a principal ideal domain is finite free.

Let $q$ be transcendental over $\mathbb Q$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and let
$$A_0:=\mathbb Q[q]_{(q)}=\Big\{\frac fg\ :\ f,g\in\mathbb Q[q],\ g(0)\neq0\Big\}\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$$
be the localisation of the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q[q]$ at the prime ideal $(q)$ ([[def-localisation-at-a-prime-ideal]]). By [[ex-the-local-ring-of-polynomials-at-x]] with $F=\mathbb Q$, the ring $A_0$ is exactly the ring of rational functions regular at $q=0$, it is a local ring ([[def-local-ring]]) with unique maximal ideal $qA_0$, and evaluation at $0$ induces an isomorphism $A_0/qA_0\cong\mathbb Q$. Since $\mathbb Q[q]$ is a principal ideal domain ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-field-is-a-pid]]) with nonzero prime ideal $(q)$, the ring $A_0$ is a local principal ideal domain with nonzero maximal ideal; by the discrete valuation ring characterisations it is a discrete valuation ring with uniformiser $q/1$ ([[thm-equivalent-characterisations-of-a-dvr]], [[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]), and in particular a principal ideal domain ([[cor-dvr-is-a-pid]], [[def-principal-ideal-domain]]), with field of fractions $\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[cor-rational-function-field-as-a-fraction-field]]).

By [[def-discrete-valuation-ring]] a discrete valuation ring is the valuation ring $V_v=\{x:v(x)\ge0\}$ of a discrete valuation $v$ on its fraction field. The discrete valuation of $\mathbb Q(q)$ with $V_v=A_0$ and $v(q)=1$ is the **$q$-adic valuation**; write it $\operatorname{ord}_q$, so that
$$\operatorname{ord}_q:\mathbb Q(q)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\cup\{\infty\},\qquad A_0=\{h\in\mathbb Q(q):\operatorname{ord}_q(h)\ge0\},\qquad \operatorname{ord}_q(q)=1 .$$
Equivalently, $\operatorname{ord}_q$ is the vanishing order at $q=0$. The units of $A_0$ are exactly the fractions $f/g$ with $f(0)\neq0$ and $g(0)\neq0$, and $qA_0$ is the maximal ideal, so $q$ is a uniformiser of $A_0$ ([[thm-localisation-at-a-prime-is-local]]).

This ring $A_0$ is the **crystal limiting ring** of the crystal development below, and it is different from the Laurent ring $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ of [[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]: $q^{-1}\in A\setminus A_0$, while $(1+q)^{-1}\in A_0\setminus A$; neither ring contains the other, and both are subrings of $\mathbb Q(q)$. For every free $A_0$-module $L$ the canonical map
$$\mathbb Q\otimes_{A_0}L\longrightarrow L/qL,\qquad c\otimes\ell\mapsto c\,\ell+qL,$$
is an isomorphism, and for every $\lambda\in\mathbb Q(q)^\times$ one has $\lambda L/q\lambda L\cong L/qL$; passing from $L$ to $L/qL$ is the **crystal limit**. No freeness of any further module, no lattice and no choice principle is asserted here.

Let $\lambda\in P$ be a dominant integral label weight, put
$m_i:=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$, and let $M(\lambda)$ be the quantum Verma
module with highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]],
[[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]).

(i) The quotient $\tilde L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$
is nonzero, has finite-dimensional label weights and support contained in
$\lambda-Q_+$, is integrable, and equals the canonical simple highest weight
module $L(\lambda)$, which is simple also as an ordinary (not assumed graded)
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module.

(ii) **Universality.** Every integrable cyclic highest weight module $V$ of
highest weight $\lambda$ with highest vector $v\ne0$ receives a
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $\tilde L(\lambda)\to V$ with
$\bar v_\lambda\mapsto v$, and this map is unique; every nonzero such $V$ is
isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$.

(iii) Its character equals the classical integrable highest weight character of
the explicitly regularized realization of the datum. No global
$\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness and no crystal or global basis is used.

derivations.claim: Grading (a). Each generator $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda$ is homogeneous of weight $\lambda-\alpha_{i_1}-\cdots-\alpha_{i_r}$, and each generator of $\mathcal L(\infty)$ is homogeneous of root degree $-\alpha_{i_1}-\cdots-\alpha_{i_r}$, by [F3]. Taking $A_0$-linear combinations and using [F2], every element of $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ lies in $\bigoplus_\mu V(\lambda)_\mu$ with only finitely many nonzero components, and its weight components lie in $\mathcal L(\lambda)$; hence $\mathcal L(\lambda)=\bigoplus_\mu\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu$ with $\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu=\mathcal L(\lambda)\cap V(\lambda)_\mu$, and similarly $\mathcal L(\infty)=\bigoplus_\nu\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}$. The residue sets decompose accordingly by their definition.

Stability (b). A generator is carried by $\tilde f_i$ to the generator with the color $i$ prepended; since $\tilde f_i$ is $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear, it commutes with $A_0$-coefficients, so $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)$ and $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\infty)\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)$.

Recursive spanning (c). Let $\alpha\in Q_+\setminus\{0\}$ and let $w$ be a word of total degree $\alpha$; writing $w=\tilde f_{i_1}w'$ exhibits the class of $w$ as $\tilde f_{i_1}$ of the class of the shorter word $w'$, which is a generator of degree $\alpha-\alpha_{i_1}$. This gives $\subseteq$; the reverse inclusion holds because $\tilde f_i$ preserves $\mathcal L$ by step 1.2 and lowers the degree by $\alpha_i$. For the residue sets, a word class that is nonzero remains nonzero when shortened (if $w'\in q\mathcal L$ then $w=\tilde f_{i_1}w'\in q\mathcal L$), and the displayed union minus zero therefore equals $\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$; the same argument applies to $\mathcal B(\infty)$.

Finite generation and freeness. Iterating (c) from degree $\alpha$ down to degree $0$ expresses every $\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$ as the sum of the images of $A_0v_\lambda$ under the words of length exactly $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$; there are finitely many such words because $I$ is finite, and for $\alpha=0$ the component is $A_0v_\lambda$. Hence each component is finitely generated over $A_0$ by monomials of length at most $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$. It is torsionfree because it is contained in the $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector space $V(\lambda)$, respectively $U_q^-$, so [F4] makes it a free $A_0$-module.

Choice and the field map. The words are indexed by finite sequences in the finite set $I$, so no choice is needed to name the generators. The map $\pi_\lambda$ is surjective by [F5], because $U_q^-$ generates $V(\lambda)$ over $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ from $v_\lambda$; no equality between $\pi_\lambda$ and the lattice projections, and no spanning over $A_0$ of the field-spanning property, is asserted here.

No crystal-lattice claim yet. The statements proved above are the graded decompositions, stability, recursive spanning, finite generation and freeness of the components; whether $\mathcal B(\lambda)$ and $\mathcal B(\infty)$ are crystal bases, and whether $\mathcal L(\lambda)\otimes_{A_0}\mathbb Q(q)\to V(\lambda)$ is an isomorphism, is not asserted and is deferred to the grand loop.

boundaries.evidence: The generating families include the empty word by convention ($r=0$), so they are never empty: $v_\lambda$ and $\mathbf 1$ are generators, the degree-zero components are $A_0v_\lambda$ and $A_0\mathbf 1$ by step 1.1, and the sums defining the lattices are over the words of each degree.

Step 3.1: The degree-zero components are $A_0v_\lambda$ at label $\lambda$ and $A_0\mathbf1$ at root degree zero. The label-zero space of a highest module need not be its highest line. Recursive spanning applies only to nonzero root degree.

A single-word image is the smallest nontrivial component: step 2.1 writes the class of a word as $\tilde f_{i_1}$ of the class of the shorter word, and step 3.1 expresses each component as the finite sum over the finitely many words of exactly the given length, the length-one case being simple-root components.

The deliberate non-claims are recorded in step 5.1: the definition asserts neither that $(\mathcal L(\lambda),\mathcal B(\lambda))$ is a crystal basis nor that the components are spanned by the residue sets, so the potentially degenerate outcomes are open questions here, resolved later in the grand loop; the proved content is the graded decomposition, stability, recursive spanning and freeness of steps 1.1-3.1.

The endpoint of a word is its $r=0$ case: the highest vector $v_\lambda$ and the unit $\mathbf 1$ are words of length zero, and step 2.1 peels letters from an arbitrary word until that case is reached; step 4.1 records the surjectivity of $\pi_\lambda$ without asserting an isomorphism, so no boundary equality is claimed.

No choice is used: step 4.1 records that the words are finite sequences in the finite index set $I$ and can be listed, and the map $\pi_\lambda$ is fixed by the universal property of $V(\lambda)$; the freeness argument of step 3.1 uses the DVR structure of $A_0$ only.

boundaries.reason: The Definition asserts spanning inclusions and a surjectivity, not a biconditional; step 2.1 proves the recursive spanning as an equality of submodules (both inclusions stated in the step), which is set equality rather than an implication pair.

No claim of the item has two mutually converse implication directions: step 4.1's $\pi_\lambda$ is a single surjectivity statement ($U_q^-v_\lambda=V(\lambda)$), and the graded decompositions of step 1.1 are equalities; the iff axes are therefore genuinely absent.

risk_review.notes: Read all six steps and exact highest-module, free-PID and weight-module statements. Word homogeneity gives direct graded pieces; prepending a color gives lowering stability and recursive spanning in both directions. Zero residues cannot become nonzero when prepended. Finite I gives finitely many words in each fixed height, embedded modules are torsionfree, so the finite PID supplier gives each component free; no field spanning, residue independence or premature crystal existence is assumed. Height zero is the normalized line and absent weights have zero component. JKK pp.24–25 and Berkeley p.329 state these lowering-word constructions. Reader change is bibliography-only; no AC is used by this construction.

Let $\lambda\in P$ be a dominant integral label weight, put
$m_i:=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$, and let $M(\lambda)$ be the quantum Verma
module with highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]],
[[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]).

(i) The quotient $\tilde L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$
is nonzero, has finite-dimensional label weights and support contained in
$\lambda-Q_+$, is integrable, and equals the canonical simple highest weight
module $L(\lambda)$, which is simple also as an ordinary (not assumed graded)
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module.

(ii) **Universality.** Every integrable cyclic highest weight module $V$ of
highest weight $\lambda$ with highest vector $v\ne0$ receives a
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $\tilde L(\lambda)\to V$ with
$\bar v_\lambda\mapsto v$, and this map is unique; every nonzero such $V$ is
isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$.

(iii) Its character equals the classical integrable highest weight character of
the explicitly regularized realization of the datum. No global
$\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness and no crystal or global basis is used.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum with $a_{ii}=2$ for
all $i$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]) with Borel subalgebra
$U_q^{\ge0}=U_q^0U_q^+$ and negative half $U_q^-$
([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]). Fix
$\lambda\in P$ and let $\mathbb Q(q)_\lambda=\mathbb Q(q)$ be the
**Borel character module** on which $K_h$ acts by the scalar
$q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}$ and every $E_i$ acts as $0$ (the character is a
well-defined $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra homomorphism
$\chi_\lambda\colon U_q^{\ge0}\to\mathbb Q(q)$, Verification, step 1.1). The
**quantum Verma module** is the induced module

$$M(\lambda):=U_q(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U_q^{\ge0}}\mathbb Q(q)_\lambda,$$

a left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module, with distinguished vector
$v_\lambda:=1\otimes1$ ([[def-quotient-ring]] for the quotient/induction
conventions).

Then (Verification, steps 2.1 and 3.1):

(i) $M(\lambda)$ carries the **canonical $P$-label grading**
$M(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M(\lambda)_\mu$ with
$M(\lambda)_{\lambda-\nu}=U_q^-[-\nu]v_\lambda$ for $\nu\in Q_+$ and
$M(\lambda)_\mu=0$ otherwise; each $M(\lambda)_\mu$ is finite dimensional
(there are only finitely many words in the $F_i$ of a given root degree), and
$M(\lambda)_\lambda=\mathbb Q(q)v_\lambda$ is the highest line. With this
grading $M(\lambda)$ is a $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module
([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) and $v_\lambda$ is a highest
weight vector: $K_hv_\lambda=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}v_\lambda$,
$E_iv_\lambda=0$, $M(\lambda)=U_q(\mathfrak g)v_\lambda$.

(ii) (Universal property) For every left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $V$ and every
$v\in V$ with $K_hv=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}v$ and $E_iv=0$ for all $h,i$
there is a unique $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $M(\lambda)\to V$ with
$v_\lambda\mapsto v$; if $V=U_q(\mathfrak g)v$ is cyclic, this map is
surjective. When $V$ is a $P$-graded type-one module and $v\in V_\lambda$, the
map is grading-preserving.

(iii) The sum $N(\lambda)$ of all proper graded submodules of $M(\lambda)$ is a
proper graded submodule, and

$$L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$$

is the **simple highest weight quotient**: it has no nonzero proper graded
submodule, and it is the unique simple graded quotient of $M(\lambda)$ up to
isomorphism ([[def-submodule]]). Thus the maximal proper submodule occurring
here is the sum of *all* proper graded submodules, not an arbitrarily chosen
maximal one; no choice is used.

If the pairing separates $P$, then every submodule of $M(\lambda)$ is graded,
$N(\lambda)$ is the unique maximal proper submodule, and $L(\lambda)$ is the
ordinary simple (not only graded-simple) quotient: this is the usual simple
weight-module quotient of the Verma module over a separating torus
(Verification, step 4.1).

The contravariant Cartan-projection lemma
`lem-cartan-projection-constructs-the-quantum-verma-contravariant-form`
identifies $N(\lambda)$ with the radical of the normalized Verma contravariant
form and gives the canonical normalized form on $L(\lambda)$; for $\lambda$
dominant integral, the existence theorem
`thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique` proves the
ordinary simplicity and the universal integrable conclusions. Both are
declared obligations of those later items, not assumptions here.

Let $T$ and $I_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ be the free $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and defining ideal of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], and write $K_i=K_{d_i h_i}$. Let $\Delta:T\to T\otimes_{\mathbb Q(q)}T$ and $\varepsilon:T\to\mathbb Q(q)$ be the algebra homomorphisms determined by

$$\Delta(K_h)=K_h\otimes K_h,\quad \Delta(E_i)=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes E_i,\quad \Delta(F_i)=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i,\quad \varepsilon(K_h)=1,\quad\varepsilon(E_i)=\varepsilon(F_i)=0.$$

Let $S:T\to T$ be the $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear algebra anti-homomorphism determined by

$$S(K_h)=K_{-h},\qquad S(E_i)=-E_iK_i,\qquad S(F_i)=-K_i^{-1}F_i.$$

Then

$$\Delta(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})\subseteq I_{\mathrm{DJ}}\otimes T+T\otimes I_{\mathrm{DJ}},\qquad \varepsilon(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})=0,\qquad S(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})\subseteq I_{\mathrm{DJ}}.$$

Hence these maps descend to $U_q(\mathfrak g)=T/I_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ and make it a Hopf algebra over $\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[def-bialgebra-counit-and-antipode]]): $\Delta$ is coassociative, $\varepsilon$ is a counit, and

$$m(S\otimes\operatorname{id})\Delta=\eta\circ\varepsilon=m(\operatorname{id}\otimes S)\Delta.$$

The antipode $S$ is unique for this multiplication, unit, coproduct and counit ([[lem-an-antipode-is-unique]]), and its square satisfies

$$S^2(E_i)=q_i^{-2}E_i,\qquad S^2(F_i)=q_i^{2}F_i,\qquad S^2(K_h)=K_h.$$

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. $$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group
with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), with root lattice $Q$,
simple roots $\alpha_i\in P$ and integer pairing
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$, and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with generators $E_i,F_i,K_h$
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). The lattice $P$ plays
the role of the integral weights of the classical theory
([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]); the pairing need not
be perfect, and no identification $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$ is
assumed anywhere.

A **$P$-graded type-one quantum weight module** is a left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$
together with a direct sum decomposition

$$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$$

(an internal direct sum of $\mathbb Q(q)$-subspaces, only finitely many nonzero
on each vector) such that, for all $\mu\in P$, $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $i\in I$,

$$K_h\ \text{acts on}\ M_\mu\ \text{by the scalar}\ q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle},\qquad E_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu+\alpha_i},\qquad F_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu-\alpha_i}.$$

The subspaces $M_\mu$ are the **chosen label-weight spaces**: the grading is
part of the structure and is not reconstructed from the action, because the
pairing may have a kernel. **Morphisms** of $P$-graded type-one weight modules
are the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps $f\colon M\to N$ with
$f(M_\mu)\subseteq N_\mu$ for every $\mu$; the weight submodules and quotients
considered on this page are those with the induced grading (Verification, step 2.2).

The module is **integrable** if $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every
vector: for every $v\in M$ and every $i$ there are integers $N_e(v,i),N_f(v,i)\ge1$
with $E_i^{N_e(v,i)}v=0$ and $F_i^{N_f(v,i)}v=0$. The exponents may depend on
the vector and on $i$, and both directions are required independently;
integrability is not a uniform nilpotence condition.

The following are additional hypotheses, never part of the definition:
finiteness of the dimension of every $M_\mu$; boundedness of the set of $\mu$
with $M_\mu\ne0$ above (or below); finite generation of $M$. The zero module is
a $P$-graded type-one weight module with the empty grading ($M_\mu=0$ for all
$\mu$), and it is integrable.

Two remarks are recorded here and proved below. First, when the pairing
separates $P$, the spaces $M_\mu$ are exactly the simultaneous eigenspaces of
the $K_h$, and the present definition recovers the usual type-one weight
modules (Verification, steps 2.1 and 4.1). Second, when the pairing does not
separate, distinct labels $\mu\ne\mu'$ may carry the same toral character, and
a simultaneous toral eigenspace must not be equated with a single label space;
the definition therefore takes the label grading as data. The regularization of
finite-cone support and all highest-weight comparisons on this page are proved
later, not assumed here by writing $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$.
No choice principle enters this definition.

Let $\lambda\in P$, let $M(\lambda)$ be the Verma module with its canonical
$P$-label grading and highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]]), and let
$\sigma$ be the linear contravariant anti-involution of
[[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]]
($\sigma(K_h)=K_h$, $\sigma(E_i)=q_iF_iK_i^{-1}$,
$\sigma(F_i)=q_i^{-1}K_iE_i$).

(i) **Existence and uniqueness.** Define the $\lambda$-weight functional
$\eta\colon U_q(\mathfrak g)\to\mathbb Q(q)$ by $\eta(y):=$ the coefficient of
$v_\lambda$ in $yv_\lambda$ (so $\eta(y)$ is unchanged by adding an element of
the Verma ideal $J(\lambda)$, and $\eta(1)=1$). Then
$$B\bigl(av_\lambda,bv_\lambda\bigr):=\eta\bigl(\sigma(a)b\bigr)\qquad(a,b\in U_q^-)$$
is a well-defined bilinear form on $M(\lambda)$; it is homogeneous, normalized
($B(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$) and $\sigma$-contravariant,
$B(xu,v)=B(u,\sigma(x)v)$. It is the unique such form on $M(\lambda)$, in the
sense of [[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]].

(ii) **Radical and descent.** The radical
$\operatorname{rad}B=\{u:B(u,M(\lambda))=0\}$ equals the sum $N(\lambda)$ of all
proper graded submodules of $M(\lambda)$; consequently $B$ descends to a
nondegenerate normalized $\sigma$-contravariant form on the simple highest
weight quotient $L(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$.

(iii) **Rank-one norms and dominant singular vectors.** If
$m_i=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$ (that is, $\lambda$ dominant), then for
every $r\ge0$
$$B\bigl(F_i^{(r)}v_\lambda,F_i^{(r)}v_\lambda\bigr)=q_i^{\,r(m_i-r)}\binom{m_i}{r}_i,$$
with the Gaussian binomial interpreted as $0$ for $r>m_i$; in particular each
$F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$ lies in the radical, so $B$ factors through the Serre
quotient $M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$. (The same
computation proves the norm formula for every $\lambda$ and all $r$ for which
the right-hand side is read with $m_i=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle$.)

(iv) **Ordinary simplicity.** Let $V$ be an integrable cyclic graded quotient of
$M(\lambda)$ with support in $\lambda-Q_+$ on which the descended form is
nondegenerate. Then $V$ is simple as an ordinary module (not only as a graded
module).

(v) **Integrality of the lattice values.** If $\lambda$ is integral and
$V_A:=U_Av_\lambda=U_A^-v_\lambda\subseteq L(\lambda)$ is the highest lattice of
the Lusztig form ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]), then
$B(V_A,V_A)\subseteq A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. No perfectness of $B$ over $A$ is
asserted.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum with $a_{ii}=2$ for
all $i$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). The **linear
contravariant anti-involution** $\sigma$ of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ is defined on
generators by

$$\sigma(q)=q,\qquad\sigma(K_h)=K_h,\qquad\sigma(E_i)=q_iF_iK_i^{-1},\qquad\sigma(F_i)=q_i^{-1}K_iE_i,$$

extended as an anti-algebra map, $\sigma(xy)=\sigma(y)\sigma(x)$. It is
$\mathbb Q(q)$-linear, preserves the torus (it does not invert it), and is an
involution (Verification, step 1.1). It is distinct from the semilinear
contravariant anti-involution $\tau$ with $\tau(q)=q^{-1}$,
$\tau(E_i)=F_i$, $\tau(F_i)=E_i$, $\tau(K_h)=K_{-h}$ of
[[lem-quantum-serre-relations-are-stable-under-the-chevalley-involutions]].

Let $\lambda\in P$ be dominant integral ([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]),
so $\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$ for all $i$, and let $(M,v_\lambda)$ be a
**normalized highest weight module**: $M$ is a $P$-graded type-one quantum
weight module ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) with
$v_\lambda\in M_\lambda$, $E_iv_\lambda=0$ for all $i$, and $M=U_q(\mathfrak g)v_\lambda$.
(The normalized simple highest weight module $L(\lambda)$ is the companion
construction later on this page; the present definition applies to any
normalized highest weight module, in particular to the Verma module and to its
simple quotient.)

A **contravariant form** on $(M,v_\lambda)$ is a bilinear form
$B\colon M\times M\to\mathbb Q(q)$ such that

(i) $B$ is symmetric: $B(u,v)=B(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in M$;

(ii) $B$ is **homogeneous** for the label grading: $B(M_\mu,M_\tau)=0$
whenever the two labels have different toral characters, that is, whenever
$\langle\mu,h\rangle\ne\langle\tau,h\rangle$ for some $h\in P^{\vee}$;

(iii) $B(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$ (the normalization);

(iv) $B$ is $\sigma$-invariant: $B(xu,v)=B(u,\sigma(x)v)$ for all
$x\in U_q(\mathfrak g)$ and all $u,v\in M$.

Because $\sigma$ is $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear and fixes the torus, condition (iv)
is equivalent to the adjunction displays

$$B(K_hu,v)=B(u,K_hv),\qquad B(E_iu,v)=B(u,q_iF_iK_i^{-1}v),\qquad B(F_iu,v)=B(u,q_i^{-1}K_iE_iv),$$

for all $u,v\in M$, $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $i\in I$ (Verification, step 2.1).

For $\lambda$ dominant and $L(\lambda)$ the normalized simple highest weight
module, such a form exists, is unique, and is nondegenerate on $L(\lambda)$;
moreover distinct label-weight spaces with distinct characters are orthogonal
by (ii). Uniqueness is proved here (Verification, step 2.2), as is the
orthogonality; consequently, when the pairing separates $P$, the distinct
label-weight spaces of $L(\lambda)$ are orthogonal and the restriction of $B$
to each finite-dimensional label-weight space is nondegenerate (Verification,
step 4.1). The
existence, the identification of the radical on the Verma module and the
descent to $L(\lambda)$ are proved in the local Cartan-projection lemma
`lem-cartan-projection-constructs-the-quantum-verma-contravariant-form`, which
is the declared justification of this definition. That lemma is proved on this
page, and its statement is the supplier of the existence and nondegeneracy
clauses above; establishing those clauses is its content rather than a claim of
this definition.
