integrability is not a uniform nilpotence condition.

The following are additional hypotheses, never part of the definition:
finiteness of the dimension of every $M_\mu$; boundedness of the set of $\mu$
with $M_\mu\ne0$ above (or below); finite generation of $M$. The zero module is
a $P$-graded type-one weight module with the empty grading ($M_\mu=0$ for all
$\mu$), and it is integrable.

Two remarks are recorded here and proved below. First, when the pairing
separates $P$, the spaces $M_\mu$ are exactly the simultaneous eigenspaces of
the $K_h$, and the present definition recovers the usual type-one weight
modules (Verification, steps 2.1 and 4.1). Second, when the pairing does not
separate, distinct labels $\mu\ne\mu'$ may carry the same toral character, and
a simultaneous toral eigenspace must not be equated with a single label space;
the definition therefore takes the label grading as data. The regularization of
finite-cone support and all highest-weight comparisons on this page are proved
later, not assumed here by writing $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$.
No choice principle enters this definition.

derivations.claim: The highest vector. By [F2], $\Delta E_i(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=E_iv_\lambda\otimes K_i^{-1}v_\mu+v_\lambda\otimes E_iv_\mu=0$ and $\Delta K_h(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle}v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$, so $v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$ is a highest weight vector of weight $\lambda+\mu$; it is nonzero.

Integrability and finite weight spaces of the tensor product. Write $A:=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}$ and $B:=1\otimes E_i$, so $\Delta E_i=A+B$ and $AB=q^{-\langle\alpha_i,d_ih_i\rangle}BA=z^{-2}BA$ with $z=q_i$; for a pure tensor $x\otimes y$ choose $N,M$ with $E_i^Nx=0$ and $E_i^My=0$ (local nilpotence of $E_i$ on $V(\lambda),V(\mu)$), then $A^N$ and $B^M$ kill $x\otimes y$, and expanding $(A+B)^{N+M}$ into $q$-commuting monomials $A^{N+M-s}B^s$ shows that every term contains either $A^N$ or $B^M$; hence $\Delta E_i$ is locally nilpotent, and the same argument with $\Delta F_i=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i$ gives local nilpotence of $\Delta F_i$. A fixed tensor weight $\nu$ is a sum $\beta+\gamma$ of weights; a fixed root degree $\alpha$ has only finitely many decompositions $\alpha=\beta+\gamma$ with $\beta,\gamma\in Q_+$ (each $\beta_i\le\alpha_i$ for the finite index set $I$), and the contributing spaces $V(\lambda)_{\lambda-\beta}\otimes V(\mu)_{\mu-\gamma}$ are finite-dimensional by [F1]; hence every tensor weight space is finite-dimensional.

The product form is contravariant. Define $(x\otimes y,x'\otimes y'):=(x,x')(y,y')$; this is symmetric and bilinear, and for $X\in U_q(\mathfrak g)$ one has $(\Delta(X)(x\otimes y),x'\otimes y')=((x\otimes y),(\sigma\otimes\sigma)(\Delta X)(x'\otimes y'))=((x\otimes y),\Delta(\sigma X)(x'\otimes y'))$ by [F4], because $\sigma$-contravariance holds on each factor. Hence the product form is $\sigma$-contravariant for the tensor action, and the three displayed identities follow from the values of $\sigma$ on $K_h,E_i,F_i$ recalled in [F3].

Part (iv): well-definedness. By [F5], $V(\mu)=\mathbb Q(q)v_\mu\oplus\sum_iF_iV(\mu)$, so every $w\in V(\mu)$ has a unique decomposition $w=cv_\mu+w'$ with $c\in\mathbb Q(q)$ and $w'\in\sum_iF_iV(\mu)$; setting $S_{\lambda,\mu}(u\otimes w):=cu$ and extending bilinearly gives the stated well-defined linear map.

Part (i). By steps 1.1-1.2 the cyclic submodule $N:=U_q(\mathfrak g)(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)$ is an integrable cyclic highest weight module of weight $\lambda+\mu$ with highest vector $v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$, so the universality in [F1] gives a $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $V(\lambda+\mu)\to N$ with $v_{\lambda+\mu}\mapsto v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$; it is nonzero, and its kernel is a submodule of the simple module $V(\lambda+\mu)$ not containing the highest vector, hence zero. Therefore $V(\lambda+\mu)\cong N$.

Part (iv): $U_q^-$-linearity. For $w\in\sum_iF_iV(\mu)$ and any $u\in V(\lambda)$ one has $\Delta F_j(u\otimes w)=F_ju\otimes w+K_ju\otimes F_jw$ with both second factors in $\sum_iF_iV(\mu)$, so both terms are killed by $S_{\lambda,\mu}$ and $S_{\lambda,\mu}(\Delta F_j\cdot u\otimes w)=0=F_jS_{\lambda,\mu}(u\otimes w)$; for $w=v_\mu$, $\Delta F_j(u\otimes v_\mu)=F_ju\otimes v_\mu+K_ju\otimes F_jv_\mu$ has first term mapped to $F_ju$ and second term killed, so $S_{\lambda,\mu}\Delta F_j=F_jS_{\lambda,\mu}$ on $V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)$. Since the $F_j$ generate $U_q^-$ and the actions are linear, $S_{\lambda,\mu}$ is $U_q^-$-linear.

Part (ii), existence and uniqueness. The same universality gives $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ with $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}(v_{\lambda+\mu})=v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$; by step 2.1 its image is exactly $N$, and $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is injective since $V(\lambda+\mu)$ is simple. It is unique because $V(\lambda+\mu)$ is generated by its highest vector.

Part (iv): the composite. $S_{\lambda,\mu}\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is $U_q^-$-linear and sends $v_{\lambda+\mu}$ to $S_{\lambda,\mu}(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=v_\lambda$; it is surjective because $U_q^-v_\lambda=V(\lambda)$ by [F1]. Any $U_q^-$-linear map $V(\lambda+\mu)\to V(\lambda)$ with $v_{\lambda+\mu}\mapsto v_\lambda$ agrees with it on the cyclic vector and hence everywhere, since $V(\lambda+\mu)=U_q^-v_{\lambda+\mu}$; this is the asserted uniqueness.

The adjoint $\Psi$ and Part (iii). The Cartan construction is homogeneous for the chosen labels, even when toral characters coincide; hence the product form is likewise label-homogeneous. For each weight $
u$, the form on $V(\lambda+\mu)_
u$ is nondegenerate by [F3], and $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ maps $V(\lambda+\mu)_
u$ injectively into the finite-dimensional space $(V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu))_
u$; the prescription $(\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}u,v):=(u,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v)$ for $v\in V(\lambda+\mu)$ therefore defines $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$ uniquely and $\mathbb Q(q)$-linearly. It is a $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map because for $X\in U_q(\mathfrak g)$, $(\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}Xu,v)=(Xu,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v)=(u,\sigma(X)\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v)=(u,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}\sigma(X)v)=(\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}u,\sigma(X)v)=(X\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}u,v)$. The pullback form $(v,v')\mapsto(\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v')$ is a homogeneous $\sigma$-contravariant form on $V(\lambda+\mu)$ with top norm $(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)(v_\mu,v_\mu)=1$, so by uniqueness in [F3] it equals the normalized form of $V(\lambda+\mu)$; hence $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is an isometry onto its image. Then $(\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v,v')=(\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v')=(v,v')$ for all $v'$, so $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}=\mathrm{id}$ and $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is surjective with the stated adjunction. The endomorphism $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is idempotent with image $\operatorname{Im}\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ and kernel $\ker\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$, which gives the direct splitting of (ii).

Uniqueness of $\Psi$. Let $\Psi'$ be a grading-preserving $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map with $\Psi'(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=v_{\lambda+\mu}$, and let $(\Psi')^{*}$ be its adjoint defined by $((\Psi')^{*}v,u)=(v,\Psi'u)$. Then $(\Psi')^{*}$ is a module map and $((\Psi')^{*}v_{\lambda+\mu},v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=(v_{\lambda+\mu},v_{\lambda+\mu})=1$, so $(\Psi')^{*}v_{\lambda+\mu}=v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$ because the $(\lambda+\mu)$-weight space of the tensor product is the one-dimensional space $\mathbb Q(q)(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)$; by uniqueness in step 3.1, $(\Psi')^{*}=\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$, and taking adjoints gives $\Psi'=\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$.

Choice. The maps are defined by universal properties (determined by the image of the highest vector) and by adjunction against nondegenerate forms on finite-dimensional spaces; no basis, complement or lift is selected, so no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: When all $\mu(h_i)=0$, the highest module is one-dimensional and $\sum_iF_iV(\mu)=0$; its label may be nonzero in a central direction. Step 1.4 still defines $S$ by its second-top coefficient.

The zero values are structural: step 1.4 sets $S_{\lambda,\mu}(u\otimes w)=0$ for $w\in\sum_iF_iV(\mu)$, and step 4.1's adjoint $\Psi$ vanishes on the orthogonal complement of the cyclic highest summand because $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is an isometry onto it.

Step 1.1: One-dimensional highest modules occur when every simple-coroot label is zero, including nonzero central labels. For two such modules, Phi and Psi identify their one-dimensional tensor with the module of the sum label.

No finiteness of the tensor product is assumed: only the finite-dimensional weight spaces of [F2] are used, and the maps are defined weight by weight in step 4.1; the Cartan pairing may have a kernel because the $P$-grading is chosen data, and no nondegeneracy beyond the forms of [F3] is required.

The weight support of $V(\lambda+\mu)$ is $\lambda+\mu-Q_+$ with one-dimensional top: step 1.1 computes the top vector, and step 4.1 defines the adjoint on every finite-dimensional weight space, so the top weight and all lower weights are covered; the $U_q^-$-retraction of steps 1.4 and 3.2 is anchored at the top vector $v_{\lambda+\mu}$.

No choice is used: the maps $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ and $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$ are determined by prescribed images of cyclic vectors (steps 2.1-3.1) and by adjunction against nondegenerate forms on finite-dimensional weight spaces (steps 4.1-5.1); step 6.1 records that no basis, complement or lift is selected.

boundaries.reason: The item proves existence plus uniqueness of maps with prescribed top images rather than a biconditional; uniqueness for $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is step 3.1 and for $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is step 5.1, each a single statement.

There is no converse implication to separate: the defining properties are the images of the highest vectors, and step 3.1 notes that a module map out of the simple module $V(\lambda+\mu)$ is determined by that image alone.

citations.quote:
Let $\lambda\in P$ be a dominant integral label weight, put
$m_i:=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$, and let $M(\lambda)$ be the quantum Verma
module with highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]],
[[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]).

(i) The quotient $\tilde L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$
is nonzero, has finite-dimensional label weights and support contained in
$\lambda-Q_+$, is integrable, and equals the canonical simple highest weight
module $L(\lambda)$, which is simple also as an ordinary (not assumed graded)
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module.

(ii) **Universality.** Every integrable cyclic highest weight module $V$ of
highest weight $\lambda$ with highest vector $v\ne0$ receives a
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $\tilde L(\lambda)\to V$ with
$\bar v_\lambda\mapsto v$, and this map is unique; every nonzero such $V$ is
isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$.

(iii) Its character equals the classical integrable highest weight character of
the explicitly regularized realization of the datum. No global
$\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness and no crystal or global basis is used.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum with $a_{ii}=2$ for
all $i$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]) with Borel subalgebra
$U_q^{\ge0}=U_q^0U_q^+$ and negative half $U_q^-$
([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]). Fix
$\lambda\in P$ and let $\mathbb Q(q)_\lambda=\mathbb Q(q)$ be the
**Borel character module** on which $K_h$ acts by the scalar
$q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}$ and every $E_i$ acts as $0$ (the character is a
well-defined $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra homomorphism
$\chi_\lambda\colon U_q^{\ge0}\to\mathbb Q(q)$, Verification, step 1.1). The
**quantum Verma module** is the induced module

$$M(\lambda):=U_q(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U_q^{\ge0}}\mathbb Q(q)_\lambda,$$

a left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module, with distinguished vector
$v_\lambda:=1\otimes1$ ([[def-quotient-ring]] for the quotient/induction
conventions).

Then (Verification, steps 2.1 and 3.1):

(i) $M(\lambda)$ carries the **canonical $P$-label grading**
$M(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M(\lambda)_\mu$ with
$M(\lambda)_{\lambda-\nu}=U_q^-[-\nu]v_\lambda$ for $\nu\in Q_+$ and
$M(\lambda)_\mu=0$ otherwise; each $M(\lambda)_\mu$ is finite dimensional
(there are only finitely many words in the $F_i$ of a given root degree), and
$M(\lambda)_\lambda=\mathbb Q(q)v_\lambda$ is the highest line. With this
grading $M(\lambda)$ is a $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module
([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) and $v_\lambda$ is a highest
weight vector: $K_hv_\lambda=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}v_\lambda$,
$E_iv_\lambda=0$, $M(\lambda)=U_q(\mathfrak g)v_\lambda$.

(ii) (Universal property) For every left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $V$ and every
$v\in V$ with $K_hv=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}v$ and $E_iv=0$ for all $h,i$
there is a unique $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $M(\lambda)\to V$ with
$v_\lambda\mapsto v$; if $V=U_q(\mathfrak g)v$ is cyclic, this map is
surjective. When $V$ is a $P$-graded type-one module and $v\in V_\lambda$, the
map is grading-preserving.

(iii) The sum $N(\lambda)$ of all proper graded submodules of $M(\lambda)$ is a
proper graded submodule, and

$$L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$$

is the **simple highest weight quotient**: it has no nonzero proper graded
submodule, and it is the unique simple graded quotient of $M(\lambda)$ up to
isomorphism ([[def-submodule]]). Thus the maximal proper submodule occurring
here is the sum of *all* proper graded submodules, not an arbitrarily chosen
maximal one; no choice is used.

If the pairing separates $P$, then every submodule of $M(\lambda)$ is graded,
$N(\lambda)$ is the unique maximal proper submodule, and $L(\lambda)$ is the
ordinary simple (not only graded-simple) quotient: this is the usual simple
weight-module quotient of the Verma module over a separating torus
(Verification, step 4.1).

The contravariant Cartan-projection lemma
`lem-cartan-projection-constructs-the-quantum-verma-contravariant-form`
identifies $N(\lambda)$ with the radical of the normalized Verma contravariant
form and gives the canonical normalized form on $L(\lambda)$; for $\lambda$
dominant integral, the existence theorem
`thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique` proves the
ordinary simplicity and the universal integrable conclusions. Both are
declared obligations of those later items, not assumptions here.

Let $\lambda\in P^+$ and let $L(\lambda)$ be the simple integrable highest weight module with highest weight vector $v_\lambda$ ([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]); in this page we write $V(\lambda):=L(\lambda)$, following the notation of the crystal sources. Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half with its Kashiwara operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]), and let $A_0$ be the crystal limiting ring ([[def-the-local-ring-at-q-zero]]).

Define $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ to be the $A_0$-submodule of $V(\lambda)$ generated by all vectors $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda$ ($r\ge0$, $i_1,\dots,i_r\in I$), where for $r=0$ the vector is $v_\lambda$; and $\mathcal L(\infty)$ to be the $A_0$-submodule of $U_q^-$ generated by all $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}\mathbf 1$ ($r\ge0$), where $\mathbf 1$ is the unit of $U_q^-$. Here $\tilde f_i$ on $V(\lambda)$ are the module Kashiwara operators and $\tilde f_i$ on $U_q^-$ are the negative-half operators. Define
$$\mathcal B(\lambda):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda+q\mathcal L(\lambda):r\ge0\}\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)/q\mathcal L(\lambda),$$
$$\mathcal B(\infty):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}\mathbf 1+q\mathcal L(\infty):r\ge0\}\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)/q\mathcal L(\infty).$$

Then, with $\pi_\lambda:U_q^-\to V(\lambda)$, $\pi_\lambda(P)=Pv_\lambda$:

(a) $\mathcal L(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu$ with $\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu=\mathcal L(\lambda)\cap V(\lambda)_\mu$, and $\mathcal L(\infty)=\bigoplus_{\nu\in Q_+}\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}$ with $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}=\mathcal L(\infty)\cap U_q^-[-\nu]$; correspondingly $\mathcal B(\lambda)=\bigsqcup_\mu\mathcal B(\lambda)_\mu$ and $\mathcal B(\infty)=\bigsqcup_\nu\mathcal B(\infty)_{-\nu}$.

(b) $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)$ and $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\infty)\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)$.

(c) (Recursive spanning.) For $\alpha\in Q_+\setminus\{0\}$,
$$\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}=\sum_{i\in I}\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha+\alpha_i},\qquad \mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}=\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\tilde f_i\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha+\alpha_i}\Bigr)\setminus\{0\},$$
and the same formulas with $\mathcal L(\infty),\mathcal B(\infty)$. Each $\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$ and each $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha}$ is generated over $A_0$ by finitely many monomials of total length at most $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$, hence is a finitely generated $A_0$-module.

No basis property, scalar-extension spanning or crystal-lattice property of $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ or $\mathcal L(\infty)$ is asserted here; these are conclusions of the grand loop. The script letters avoid the collision with the simple module $L(\lambda)$. No choice principle is used. Each fixed component is torsionfree inside a field vector space and generated by finitely many words of its fixed height, so it is free over the DVR $A_0$; its full field-span is proved later. The field map $\pi_\lambda$ is surjective, but exact equality on Kashiwara monomial generators is not asserted.
Every finitely generated torsion-free module over a principal ideal domain is finite free.

Let $M$ be an integrable chosen $P$-graded type-1 module ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) and fix $i\in I$. By [[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]] every $u\in M_\lambda$ has a unique admissible decomposition
$$u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}=\ker(E_i)\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i},$$
with $u_n=0$ whenever $n>\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$. Define the **Kashiwara operators**
$$\tilde e_i u:=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_i u:=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n+1)}u_n .$$
Both are linear maps on $M$, shifting the label weight by $+\alpha_i$, respectively $-\alpha_i$. Along each string, $\tilde e_i$ moves $F_i^{(n)}u_n$ to $F_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ and kills the top position $n=0$, while $\tilde f_i$ moves it to $F_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ and kills a string exactly at its bottom, where $n=\langle\mathrm{wt}(u_n),h_i\rangle$.

Let $p_{\mathrm{top}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$ be the projections onto the top positions and the bottom positions of these strings:
$$p_{\mathrm{top}}u:=u_0,\qquad p_{\mathrm{bottom}}u:=\sum_{n:\,n=\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle}F_i^{(n)}u_n .$$
Then
$$\ker\tilde e_i=\ker E_i,\qquad \ker\tilde f_i=\ker F_i,\qquad \tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{top}},\qquad \tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{bottom}},$$
so $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ are inverse to each other on each existing string edge. Module homomorphisms commute with both operators, $p_{\mathrm{top}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$. On $\ker E_i$ one has $\tilde f_i=F_i$, and on $\ker F_i$ one has $\tilde e_i=E_i$. At interior positions the operators differ from the generators: in the rank-one module $L_i(2)$ with highest vector $v$ and $u=F_iv$, one has $F_iu=[2]_iF_i^{(2)}v$ while $\tilde f_iu=F_i^{(2)}v$, and $[2]_i\neq1$. No choice principle is used. The analogous Kashiwara operators on the negative half $U_q^-$ are the shifts of its unique $e_i'$-string decomposition ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]), constructed using the skew derivation of [[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]. Their strings have no bottom: $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}$ and $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-P_i$, where $P_i$ projects onto $\ker e_i'$; the second identity follows by subtracting the position-zero coefficient $u_0=P_iu$ from the string expansion. These string-shift operators are distinct from the skew derivations $e_i',e_i''$. No negative-half operator is used in the module verification below.

Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half of the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with its skew derivations $e_i',e_i'':U_q^-\to U_q^-$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]), fix $i\in I$, and write $f_i^{(n)}=F_i^n/[n]_i!$ for the divided powers ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]). Then:

(i) $e_i'$ is locally nilpotent on $U_q^-$, and the endomorphism
$$P_i:=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^mq_i^{-m(m-1)/2}F_i^{(m)}e_i'^{\,m}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q(q)}(U_q^-)$$
is well defined (each sum is finite on each element) and is the projection onto $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ along $f_iU_q^-$. In particular $e_i'P_i=0$, $P_iF_i=0$, $P_i^2=P_i$, $P_iu=u$ for $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$, and
$$U_q^-=\operatorname{Ker}e_i'\oplus f_iU_q^-.$$

(ii) Every $u\in U_q^-$ has a unique $i$-string decomposition
$$u=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i',\qquad u_n=0\ \text{for }n\gg0,$$
and the components are given by $u_n=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u$.

(iii) The **Kashiwara operators on the negative half**, defined on the string decomposition by
$$\tilde e_iu:=\sum_{n\ge1}f_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_iu:=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n+1)}u_n,$$
are $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear endomorphisms of $U_q^-$ with $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}_{U_q^-}$; $\tilde e_iu=0$ if and only if $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$; $\tilde f_i$ is injective and $\tilde f_i(1)=F_i$. Both operators preserve the root grading and shift its degree by $\mp\alpha_i$, that is $\tilde e_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu+\alpha_i]$ and $\tilde f_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu-\alpha_i]$.

No choice principle is used. Here $e_i'^{\,n}$ denotes the ordinary $n$-fold power of the derivation, not its divided power. The same projector and every string coefficient preserve the $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]), as proved by the integral skew-string supplier; this does not assert that lattice's freeness.

All $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps below preserve the chosen $P$-label gradings, as required of morphisms in [[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]. The $U_q^-$-linear map $S_{\lambda,\mu}$ instead shifts labels by $-\mu$.

Let $\lambda,\mu\in P^+$ and let $V(\lambda)=L(\lambda)$, $V(\mu)$, $V(\lambda+\mu)$ be the simple integrable highest weight modules with highest weight vectors $v_\lambda,v_\mu,v_{\lambda+\mu}$ ([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]). Equip $V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)$ with the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module structure given by the coproduct $\Delta$ of [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]] ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

(i) $v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$ is a highest weight vector of weight $\lambda+\mu$, and its cyclic submodule $U_q(\mathfrak g)(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)$ is isomorphic to $V(\lambda+\mu)$.

(ii) There are unique $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps
$$\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}:V(\lambda+\mu)\to V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu),\qquad \Psi_{\lambda,\mu}:V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)\to V(\lambda+\mu)$$
with $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}(v_{\lambda+\mu})=v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$ and $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=v_{\lambda+\mu}$; they satisfy $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}\circ\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}=\operatorname{id}_{V(\lambda+\mu)}$, $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is injective with image $U_q(\mathfrak g)(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)$, $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is surjective, and $V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)=\operatorname{Im}\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}\oplus\ker\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$.

(iii) Let $(\ ,\ )$ be the contravariant form on $V(\lambda)$ of [[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]] and similarly on $V(\mu)$; define the symmetric bilinear form on $V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)$ by $(u_1\otimes u_2,v_1\otimes v_2)=(u_1,v_1)(u_2,v_2)$. Then for all $u,v$ and all $i\in I$, $h\in P^\vee$,
$$(K_hu,v)=(u,K_hv),\qquad (E_iu,v)=(u,q_iF_iK_i^{-1}v),\qquad (F_iu,v)=(u,q_i^{-1}K_iE_iv),$$
and the maps of (ii) are adjoint: $(\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}u,v)=(u,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v)$ for all $u\in V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)$, $v\in V(\lambda+\mu)$. In particular $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is an isometry onto its image.

(iv) The linear map $S_{\lambda,\mu}:V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)\to V(\lambda)$ defined by
$$S_{\lambda,\mu}(u\otimes v_\mu)=u\quad(u\in V(\lambda)),\qquad S_{\lambda,\mu}\Bigl(V(\lambda)\otimes\sum_{i\in I}F_iV(\mu)\Bigr)=0$$
is well defined, because $V(\mu)=\mathbb Q(q)v_\mu\oplus\sum_{i\in I}F_iV(\mu)$; it is $U_q^-$-linear for the left multiplication action of $U_q^-$, and $S_{\lambda,\mu}\circ\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is the unique $U_q^-$-linear surjection $V(\lambda+\mu)\to V(\lambda)$ with $v_{\lambda+\mu}\mapsto v_\lambda$. No choice principle is used.

Let $i\in I$, write $z=q_i$, and let $V(a)$, $V(b)$ be the simple rank-one modules of nonnegative integral highest weights $a,b$ for the subalgebra generated by $E_i,F_i,K_i^{\pm1}$, with divided bases $v_j=F_i^{(j)}v_0$ $(0\le j\le a)$ and $w_k=F_i^{(k)}w_0$ $(0\le k\le b)$ ([[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]]). Consider the tensor product with the coproduct $\Delta E_i=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes E_i$, $\Delta F_i=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i$ ([[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]), its Kashiwara operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ ([[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]]) and the $\mathbb Z$-graded $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector space $V(a)\otimes V(b)$ with the tensor lattice
$$L:=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{a}\bigoplus_{k=0}^{b}A_0\,(v_j\otimes w_k)$$
over the local ring $A_0$ ([[def-the-local-ring-at-q-zero]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a crystal lattice: it is a free $A_0$-module generating $V(a)\otimes V(b)$ over $\mathbb Q(q)$, it respects the weight grading, and $\tilde e_iL\subseteq L$, $\tilde f_iL\subseteq L$.

(ii) Modulo $q$ one has, for all $0\le j\le a$, $0\le k\le b$,
$$\tilde f_i(v_j\otimes w_k)=\begin{cases}v_{j+1}\otimes w_k & \text{if } a-j>k,\\ v_j\otimes w_{k+1} & \text{if } a-j\le k,\end{cases}$$
and
$$\tilde e_i(v_j\otimes w_k)=\begin{cases}v_{j-1}\otimes w_k & \text{if } a-j\ge k,\\ v_j\otimes w_{k-1} & \text{if } a-j<k,\end{cases}$$
where terms leaving the divided-basis ranges are $0$. In particular $\tilde f_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde e_ib'$ for residues $b,b'$ of the product basis (the partial-inverse property).

(iii) The nonzero residue strings are the chains $(0,t),(1,t),\dots,(a-t,t),(a-t,t+1),\dots,(a-t,b)$, $0\le t\le\min(a,b)$, and they partition the rectangle $0\le j\le a$, $0\le k\le b$.

This is a finite, choice-free calculation, independent of the grand loop and of global integral freeness.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum with $a_{ii}=2$ for
all $i$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and let $M$ be a
$P$-graded type-one quantum weight module
([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) whose support is contained in
a finite union of cones,

$$\operatorname{supp}M\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^{s}(\lambda_j-Q_+)\qquad(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_s\in P),$$

where $Q_+=\bigoplus_i\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$. Choose a finite free direct
coordinate summand $X_f\subseteq P$ (with respect to a free basis of $P$,
[[def-free-abelian-group]]) containing all $\lambda_j$ and all $\alpha_i$, and
set

$$Y_{\mathrm{aux}}:=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb ZH_i\Bigr)\oplus\operatorname{Hom}(X_f,\mathbb Z),\qquad X_{\mathrm{aux}}:=\operatorname{Hom}(Y_{\mathrm{aux}},\mathbb Z),$$

with the evaluation pairing $X_{\mathrm{aux}}\times Y_{\mathrm{aux}}\to\mathbb Z$.
Define $j\colon X_f\to X_{\mathrm{aux}}$ by $j(x)(H_i):=\langle x,h_i\rangle$ and
$j(x)(f):=f(x)$ for $f\in\operatorname{Hom}(X_f,\mathbb Z)$, and put
$\alpha_i^{\mathrm{aux}}:=j(\alpha_i)$. Then:

(i) $(I,A,D,X_{\mathrm{aux}},Y_{\mathrm{aux}},q)$ with the simple roots
$\alpha_i^{\mathrm{aux}}$ and simple coroots $H_i$ is a symmetrizable Cartan
datum for a quantum group with the same generalized Cartan matrix $A$ and the
same symmetrizer $D$; its pairing is perfect, the $\alpha_i^{\mathrm{aux}}$ are
linearly independent, the $H_i$ are primitive and independent, and integral
fundamental weights $\Lambda_j$ ($\Lambda_j(H_i)=\delta_{ij}$) exist. Here
$\langle\alpha_j^{\mathrm{aux}},H_i\rangle=a_{ij}$ is the original convention
([[def-realization-of-a-generalized-cartan-matrix]],
[[prop-minimal-realizations-exist-and-are-unique-up-to-isomorphism]]).

(ii) $M$ carries a unique structure of $X_{\mathrm{aux}}$-graded type-one
quantum weight module for the auxiliary datum with
$\operatorname{supp}M^{\mathrm{aux}}\subseteq j(X_f)$, namely
$$M^{\mathrm{aux}}_{j(x)}:=M_x\quad(x\in X_f),\qquad M^{\mathrm{aux}}_{\xi}:=0\quad(\xi\notin j(X_f)),$$
$$K_{(n,f)}\ \text{acts on}\ M_x\ \text{by}\ q^{\sum_in_i\langle x,h_i\rangle+f(x)}\qquad\bigl((n,f)\in\textstyle\bigoplus_i\mathbb ZH_i\oplus\operatorname{Hom}(X_f,\mathbb Z)\bigr),$$
with the actions of $E_i$, $F_i$ and of the simple coroots
$K_{d_iH_i}$ unchanged. In particular the old $K_h$ action is recovered from
the label $x$ as $q^{\langle x,h\rangle}$, and the old and auxiliary $E_i,F_i$
actions agree.

(iii) The two recipes are inverse on objects and grading-preserving morphisms:
on $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-modules with labels in $X_f$ and support as above, the
identity on underlying vector spaces is an equivalence between the category of
$P$-graded type-one modules and the corresponding full subcategory of
$X_{\mathrm{aux}}$-graded type-one modules with labels in $j(X_f)$. This is not
an embedding of the old torus algebra into the new one and is asserted only
inside this finite-support category.

(iv) The construction applies simultaneously to Verma modules and highest weight
modules (supported in $\lambda-Q_+$) and to finite tensor products of such
modules (labels add), by choosing one $X_f$ containing all participating upper
weights and all simple roots; the tensor-product $E_i,F_i$ formulas of [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]] are unchanged because only the diagonal toral characters change.

(v) Rationally, $h_{\mathrm{aux}}:=Y_{\mathrm{aux}}\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$
decomposes as $h_{\mathrm{aux}}=H_{\min}\oplus Z$, where $H_{\min}$ is a
minimal realization of $A$ (of dimension $2n-r$, $n=|I|$, $r=\operatorname{rank}A$)
and $Z\subseteq\ker\alpha$ is a complement on which all $\alpha_i^{\mathrm{aux}}$
vanish, so the elements of $Z$ are central in the correspondingly extended
Kac–Moody algebra; hence the classical Cartan and multiplicity comparisons of
[[prop-minimal-realizations-exist-and-are-unique-up-to-isomorphism]] apply to
$H_{\min}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $U_q^-=\bigoplus_{\nu\in Q_+}U_q^-[-\nu]$ be the negative half of the
Drinfeld-Jimbo algebra of a finite symmetrizable Cartan datum with $a_{ii}=2$
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]],
[[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]), with skew derivations
$e_i',e_i''$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]),
and let $(\ ,\ )$ be a bilinear form on $U_q^-$.

(i) **Existence and symmetry.** A bilinear form with $(1,1)=1$ and
$(F_iP,Q)=(P,e_i'(Q))$ for all $i,P,Q$ exists on $U_q^-$; every normalized
homogeneous form satisfying these conditions is symmetric; and by the
uniqueness of [[def-the-lusztig-kashiwara-bilinear-form-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]
there is exactly one such form. No separate right-adjunction formula for
$(P,QF_i)$ is asserted: in the rank-one subalgebra a formula
$(P,QF_i)=c\,(e_i''P,Q)$ with constant $c$ is false, as the explicit values in
(iv) show.

(ii) **Orthogonality.** $(U_q^-[-\nu],U_q^-[-\mu])=0$ whenever $\nu\ne\mu$.

(iii) **Nondegeneracy.** For every $0\ne x\in U_q^-$ there is $y\in U_q^-$ with
$(x,y)\ne0$; equivalently, the restriction of the form to each
finite-dimensional graded piece $U_q^-[-\nu]$ is nondegenerate.

(iv) **Integrality on the word lattice.** Let $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) and let $W\subseteq U_A^-$ be the
$A$-span of the monomials $F_{i_1}\cdots F_{i_k}$ ($k\ge0$). Then
$W\subseteq U_A^-$ (because $F_i^k=[k]_i!F_i^{(k)}$ and $[k]_i!\in A$), and
$(W,W)\subseteq A$. On the larger divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ the form is
*not* $A$-valued: in the rank-one subalgebra generated by a single $F_i$ one
has, for all $a,b\ge0$,
$$(F_i^{(a)},F_i^{(b)})=\delta_{ab}\frac{q_i^{-a(a-1)/2}}{[a]_i!}=\delta_{ab}\frac{1}{[a]_{q_i^2}!},$$
in particular $(F_i^{(2)},F_i^{(2)})=1/(1+q_i^2)\notin A$; here
$[a]_{q_i^2}!=\prod_{m=1}^a(1+q_i^2+\cdots+q_i^{2(m-1)})$. Globally, with
$A_{\mathrm{loc}}=A[s^{-1}:s\in S]$, the localization of $A$ inverting the
multiplicative set $S$ generated by $\{[r]_i!:i\in I,r\ge1\}$ (equivalently inverting the
Gaussian factorials $[r]_{q_i^2}!$), one has
$(U_A^-,U_A^-)\subseteq A_{\mathrm{loc}}$: divided-power words are word
vectors divided by finite products of these factorials. This is an exact
denominator bound, not an $A$-integrality assertion on $U_A^-$ in this
normalization.

Let $U_q^-=\bigoplus_{\nu\in Q_+}U_q^-[-\nu]$ be the negative half of the
Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with its skew derivations $e_i'$
([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]],
[[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]), and let
$\varepsilon\colon U_q^-\to\mathbb Q(q)$ be the **augmentation**, the projection
onto the degree-zero component $U_q^-[0]=\mathbb Q(q)\cdot1$ (so
$\varepsilon(Q)=0$ on all positive-height components and $\varepsilon(1)=1$).

The **normalized Lusztig–Kashiwara form** on $U_q^-$ is a bilinear form
$B\colon U_q^-\times U_q^-\to\mathbb Q(q)$ such that

(H) $B$ is **homogeneous**: $B\bigl(U_q^-[-\nu],U_q^-[-\mu]\bigr)=0$ whenever
$\nu\ne\mu$;

(N) $B(1,1)=1$;

(R) $B(F_iP,Q)=B(P,e_i'Q)$ for all $i\in I$ and all $P,Q\in U_q^-$.

Equivalently, axioms (H) and (N) may be replaced by the single **counit
normalization**

(C) $B(1,Q)=\varepsilon(Q)$ for all $Q\in U_q^-$,

in the presence of (R) (Verification, step 1.1).

Axioms (H) and (N) (equivalently (C)) are essential and not redundant: the
recursion (R) together with $B(1,1)=1$ alone neither forces symmetry nor
uniqueness, as the rank-one witness of step 2.2 shows.

The axioms determine $B$ uniquely: peeling first letters in the first argument
writes every positive-height $P$ as a finite sum $P=\sum_iF_iP_i$ and evaluates
$B(P,Q)=\sum_iB(P_i,e_i'Q)$, reducing the height; the base of the induction is
(C) (Verification, step 2.1). The **existence, symmetry and nondegeneracy** of
$B$ on $U_q^-$ for the actual quotient by the Serre ideal are not proved here:
they are the content of the negative-half form theorem
`thm-the-negative-half-bilinear-form-is-symmetric-nondegenerate-and-integral`,
the declared justification of this definition, which also settles the exact
integrality normalization ($A$-valuedness on the word lattice and the
Gaussian-factorial denominators on the divided-power lattice). That theorem
is proved on this page, and its statement is the declared supplier of
existence, symmetry and nondegeneracy; this definition itself claims only that
(H), (N) and (R) determine $B$ and that the normalization cannot be relaxed.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $I \trianglelefteq R$ be an ideal, and let $M$ be a finitely generated left $R$-module. If $IM=M$, then there exists $a \in I$ such that
$$ (1-a)M=0. $$

Let $q$ be transcendental over $\mathbb Q$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and let
$$A_0:=\mathbb Q[q]_{(q)}=\Big\{\frac fg\ :\ f,g\in\mathbb Q[q],\ g(0)\neq0\Big\}\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$$
be the localisation of the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q[q]$ at the prime ideal $(q)$ ([[def-localisation-at-a-prime-ideal]]). By [[ex-the-local-ring-of-polynomials-at-x]] with $F=\mathbb Q$, the ring $A_0$ is exactly the ring of rational functions regular at $q=0$, it is a local ring ([[def-local-ring]]) with unique maximal ideal $qA_0$, and evaluation at $0$ induces an isomorphism $A_0/qA_0\cong\mathbb Q$. Since $\mathbb Q[q]$ is a principal ideal domain ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-field-is-a-pid]]) with nonzero prime ideal $(q)$, the ring $A_0$ is a local principal ideal domain with nonzero maximal ideal; by the discrete valuation ring characterisations it is a discrete valuation ring with uniformiser $q/1$ ([[thm-equivalent-characterisations-of-a-dvr]], [[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]), and in particular a principal ideal domain ([[cor-dvr-is-a-pid]], [[def-principal-ideal-domain]]), with field of fractions $\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[cor-rational-function-field-as-a-fraction-field]]).

By [[def-discrete-valuation-ring]] a discrete valuation ring is the valuation ring $V_v=\{x:v(x)\ge0\}$ of a discrete valuation $v$ on its fraction field. The discrete valuation of $\mathbb Q(q)$ with $V_v=A_0$ and $v(q)=1$ is the **$q$-adic valuation**; write it $\operatorname{ord}_q$, so that
$$\operatorname{ord}_q:\mathbb Q(q)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\cup\{\infty\},\qquad A_0=\{h\in\mathbb Q(q):\operatorname{ord}_q(h)\ge0\},\qquad \operatorname{ord}_q(q)=1 .$$
Equivalently, $\operatorname{ord}_q$ is the vanishing order at $q=0$. The units of $A_0$ are exactly the fractions $f/g$ with $f(0)\neq0$ and $g(0)\neq0$, and $qA_0$ is the maximal ideal, so $q$ is a uniformiser of $A_0$ ([[thm-localisation-at-a-prime-is-local]]).

This ring $A_0$ is the **crystal limiting ring** of the crystal development below, and it is different from the Laurent ring $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ of [[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]: $q^{-1}\in A\setminus A_0$, while $(1+q)^{-1}\in A_0\setminus A$; neither ring contains the other, and both are subrings of $\mathbb Q(q)$. For every free $A_0$-module $L$ the canonical map
$$\mathbb Q\otimes_{A_0}L\longrightarrow L/qL,\qquad c\otimes\ell\mapsto c\,\ell+qL,$$
is an isomorphism, and for every $\lambda\in\mathbb Q(q)^\times$ one has $\lambda L/q\lambda L\cong L/qL$; passing from $L$ to $L/qL$ is the **crystal limit**. No freeness of any further module, no lattice and no choice principle is asserted here.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Field spanning. On any fixed label space, $\operatorname{im}F_i=\operatorname{im}\tilde f_i$: in a string expansion $x=\sum_nF_i^{(n)}x_n$, one has $F_ix=\tilde f_i\sum_n[n+1]_iF_i^{(n)}x_n$, and conversely $\tilde f_ix=F_i\sum_n[n+1]_i^{-1}F_i^{(n)}x_n$. Both sums have the same label as $x$. The same identities hold on the negative half. Since every positive-height space is $\sum_iF_i$ of the preceding spaces, it is also $\sum_i\tilde f_i$ of those spaces. Induction from the highest line or the unit therefore proves that the lowering words span every field component. Together with [F2] this makes each $\mathcal L$ component a finite free full lattice.

The base. [base] At height zero the top and unit have norm one, raising kills them and $\Phi,\Psi$ identify the tensor top. At degree $\alpha_i$, put $m=\lambda(h_i)$ and $n=\mu(h_i)$. The module lattice is $A_0F_iv_\lambda$ if $m>0$ and zero otherwise; the half lattice is $A_0F_i$. All projection, raising, basis and inverse clauses follow from these one-dimensional strings. In the tensor degree, $\Phi(F_iv_{\lambda+\mu})=F_iv_\lambda\otimes v_\mu+q_i^mv_\lambda\otimes F_iv_\mu$. If $m+n>0$, adjunction gives $\Psi(F_iv_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=d(m,1)d(m+n,1)^{-1}F_iv_{\lambda+\mu}$ and $\Psi(v_\lambda\otimes F_iv_\mu)=q_i^md(n,1)d(m+n,1)^{-1}F_iv_{\lambda+\mu}$, where $d(k,1)=(1-q_i^{2k})/(1-q_i^2)$ and absent vectors contribute zero. These coefficients lie in $A_0$; their residues are respectively $1,0$ if $m>0$, and $0,1$ if $m=0<n$. If $m=n=0$ the degree vanishes. Thus E, F and G hold at height one as well, and all A-O base clauses hold.

Induction hypothesis. [ih] Fix $r\ge2$ and assume A-O at every height $<r$, simultaneously for all dominant weights in one auxiliary regular datum supplied by [F6]. All subsequent large weights and fundamental weights are taken in that datum. The transported original highest-weight and tensor modules have the same $E_i,F_i,K_i$, string operators, normalized forms and lowering words; consequently the final conclusions on them restrict to the original labels.

String components below $r$. For $u=\sum_{n=0}^NF_i^{(n)}u_n\in\mathcal L_{\lambda-\alpha}$ with $|\alpha|<r$, the shift identity gives $u_N=\tilde e_i^Nu\in\mathcal L$. Subtract $\tilde f_i^Nu_N=F_i^{(N)}u_N$ and descend on $N$; each coefficient is integral. The same argument, using H$(r-1)$, applies to the half, and also applies to $q^k\mathcal L$ for every integer $k$. If $u$ represents a basis word residue, induct on $N$: when $\tilde e_iu\in q\mathcal L$, extracting its coefficients gives $u_n\in q\mathcal L$ for all $n\ge1$; otherwise its residue is a lower-height basis word by B or I, and C or J gives $u\equiv\tilde f_i\tilde e_iu\pmod{q\mathcal L}$. Induction and component extraction then leave exactly one nonzero coefficient residue, which is a highest word residue. This proves the lower-height single-string assertion without assuming it at height $r$.

Lower-height tensor control. Extract the string coefficients of two lattice inputs of factor heights $<r$ by step 2.1. For each pair of nonzero highest coefficients $h,h'$, the full divided-string rectangle $\sum_{j,k}A_0F_i^{(j)}h\otimes F_i^{(k)}h'$ lies in the tensor lattice, since each divided position is an iterate of $\tilde f_i$. The rank-one lemma [F5] proves stability of this rectangle and its residue rule, and linearity gives stability for the original inputs. For basis residues, the single-string assertion of step 2.1 gives the strict/non-strict tensor comparisons and their partial inverses. A lower-height module basis residue killed by every raising must be its top: otherwise its recursive lowering predecessor and C$(r-1)$ supply a nonzero raising. Hence a tensor basis residue of lower factor heights killed by all raisings has first factor $v_\lambda$. Moreover, on a top-second tensor, lowering agrees modulo $q$ with lowering the first factor whenever that first lowering is nonzero; iterating this rule along a word that survives in the first factor gives the same word on the tensor top modulo $q$.

Large-weight estimates. Write $T_i=q_i^{-1}K_iE_i$. On $F_i^{(n)}u_n$ with top integer $a$, its coefficient to the preceding position is $q_i^{a-2n+1}[a-n+1]_i=q_i^{1-n}(1-q_i^{2(a-n+1)})/(1-q_i^2)$, whose inverse lies in $A_0$ for admissible $n\ge1$. If $T_iu\in q^N\mathcal L$ in the preceding degree, step 2.1 extracts each $u_n\in q^N\mathcal L$ for $n\ge1$. For fixed degree and fixed $m$, the differences between $\tilde f_i^mu$, $F_i^{(m)}u$ and between $\tilde e_iF_i^{(m)}u$, $F_i^{(m-1)}u$ involve only these positive components with Gaussian coefficients of bounded pole order; the second comparison requires $m\le\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(u)\rangle$, so the top term is not killed at its bottom. Taking $N$ larger than those finitely many pole orders makes both differences lie in $q\mathcal L$. Now for $e_i'Q=0$, the commutator gives $T_i(Qv_\lambda)=-(1-q_i^2)^{-1}q_i^{2\langle h_i,\lambda+\alpha_i+\mathrm{wt}Q\rangle}(e_i''Q)v_\lambda$. The last vector has degree below $r$; express it in a fixed finite set of half lowering words and apply L$(r-1)$ to obtain a pole bound independent of $\lambda$. The displayed power makes this arbitrarily small when $\lambda$ is large. Applying the two comparisons to each fixed half string $F_i^{(n)}Q$ proves the large-weight operator congruences needed at degrees $r-1$ and $r$, uniformly on any specified finite family of vectors. Finally $\pi_\lambda$ is a field isomorphism at degree $\alpha$ when $\lambda(h_j)\ge|\alpha|$: the highest-weight quotient ideal is generated by $F_j^{(\lambda(h_j)+1)}v_\lambda$, which are highest vectors by the rank-one formula and $[E_i,F_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$. Their generated submodules have degrees at least $\lambda(h_j)+1$, so they cannot meet that degree.

E(r). The height-$r$ module lattice is the sum of $\tilde f_i$ of height-$r-1$ components. By naturality, $\Phi\tilde f_i=\tilde f_i\Phi$. E$(r-1)$ puts each preceding image in the tensor lattice; every tensor summand there has both factor heights $<r$, so step 3.1 proves the required lowering stability on those inputs. Thus $\Phi\mathcal L(\lambda+\mu)_{\lambda+\mu-\alpha}\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)\otimes\mathcal L(\mu)$.

Splitting at the last color change. For a nonpure word $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}$ take $t<r$ with $i_t\ne i_{t+1}=\cdots=i_r$, put $\lambda_0=\Lambda_{i_t}$ and take $\mu$ large. The repeated tail acts only on the second factor of $v_{\lambda_0}\otimes v_\mu$, because $\lambda_0(h_{i_r})=0$. The resulting tensor is $E_{i_t}$-highest, since $E_{i_t}$ commutes with that different-color tail; its next lowering equals $F_{i_t}v_{\lambda_0}\otimes\text{tail}+q_{i_t}v_{\lambda_0}\otimes F_{i_t}\text{tail}$. The second term lies in $q$ times the tensor lattice, and the first has both factor heights positive. Applying the remaining prefix uses only the lower factor-height rules of step 3.1. Consequently the full tensor word is congruent to a product of basis word residues, or zero, with both factor heights strictly between $0$ and $r$. This decomposition is used for large total weight $\lambda_0+\mu$, not for an arbitrary $\lambda$ lacking such a dominant subtraction.

M(r), L(r) and large-weight lattice isomorphism. For $P\in\mathcal L(\infty)$ of degree at most $r-1$, take $\mu$ large and apply $\Phi$ to the large-weight lowering congruence of step 3.2. E(r), already proved, carries its error into $q$ times the tensor lattice; L$(r-1)$ and E$(r-1)$ put $P(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)$ in that lattice. The retraction $S$ sends the tensor lattice onto $\mathcal L(\lambda)$: it extracts the second top coefficient. It commutes with lowering modulo $q$ on these inputs by step 3.1: string tensors with a positive-degree second factor are killed both before and after lowering, while a second top gives the first-factor lowering or a zero first-factor endpoint. Applying $S$ therefore gives M(r). Iterating along a word gives integrality of its projection and equality with the module word modulo $q$. Hence $\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}=\pi_\lambda(\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha})+q\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$; Nakayama on the finitely generated quotient proves L(r). Nonzero projected word residues are precisely $\mathcal B(\lambda)$. For large $\lambda$, step 3.2 makes $\pi_\lambda$ a field isomorphism; L(r) then makes it a lattice isomorphism and hence a bijection on nonzero word residues, before any independence claim at height $r$.

Tensor-lattice decomposition. At total degree $\alpha$ of height $r$, put $T=(\mathcal L(\lambda)\otimes\mathcal L(\mu))_{\lambda+\mu-\alpha}$ and $T'=\sum_i\tilde f_iT_{\lambda+\mu-\alpha+\alpha_i}+v_\lambda\otimes\mathcal L(\mu)_{\mu-\alpha}$. Step 3.1 gives $T'\subseteq T$ on the preceding degrees. An interior product basis residue has both factor heights below $r$ and positive first height; the top detection and partial inverse in step 3.1 give a nonzero raising and write it as the lowering of its predecessor. Thus every interior tensor lies in $T'+qT$. The second-top boundary is generated by module lowering words tensored with $v_\mu$; each nonzero such residue is congruent to its word on $v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$ by step 3.1, and that tensor word belongs to the lowering-image part of $T'$. Zero word residues already lie in $qT$. The remaining boundary is exactly $v_\lambda\otimes\mathcal L(\mu)_{\mu-\alpha}$. Hence $T=T'+qT$.

Nakayama upgrade. The quotient $T/T'$ is finitely generated, and step 5.2 says $T/T'=q(T/T')$. Nakayama [F8] makes it zero. Thus the tensor decomposition is an exact lattice equality at height $r$, with the first-top boundary $v_\lambda\otimes\mathcal L(\mu)$; it does not require a basis of either factor at height $r$.

A(r) and H(r). Fix $i,\alpha$ and a finite set of dominant weights containing the desired $\tau$ and all $\Lambda_j$. Finite full lattices give a common pole bound $N$ for raising on these components and on the half. Steps 3.2 and 5.1 extend that bound to every sufficiently large weight. The same bound applies to raising on the total-degree tensor lattice: interior inputs are already integral by step 3.1; at a boundary, extracting the positive string coefficients of the raised factor in $q^{-N}\mathcal L$ uses only preceding degrees, and applying the rank-one rectangles bounds their tensor raising by $q^{-N}$. If $N>0$, a pure-color word raises integrally by rank one. For a nonpure word at large weight $\Lambda_j+\mu$, step 4.2 splits its tensor lift into an integral interior residue plus $qT$. Raising therefore lies in $T+q^{1-N}T=q^{1-N}T$, and applying $\Psi$ in raised degree uses F$(r-1)$ to improve its module bound to $q^{1-N}$. For any fixed $\tau$ and word $u$, if $u\in q\mathcal L(\tau)$ the old bound already improves by one; otherwise its tensor word is congruent to $u\otimes v_\mu$. The improved bound at large $\tau+\mu$, followed by E$(r-1)$, bounds the raising of that tensor word by $q^{1-N}T$. The $qT$ error also raises into $q^{1-N}T$. Extracting the positive string coefficients of $u$ into $q^{-N}\mathcal L(\tau)$ and using the rank-one top-second rule gives $\tilde e_i(u\otimes v_\mu)\equiv(\tilde e_iu)\otimes v_\mu\pmod{q^{1-N}T}$; extracting the second top then improves the bound for $u$. N(r) is the residue surjectivity of step 5.1 together with injectivity: if two surviving preimages have the same module image, raise by an index $i$ that does not kill that common image, use O(r) and the lower clause N$(r-1)$ to see that the raised negative-half residues agree, and apply J(r) to conclude that the two preimages were equal.

D(r) and K(r). Take a finite linear relation among the residue classes of the lowering words at height $r$ and apply each $\tilde e_i$: below $r$ the raised residues form an independent basis, and the partial-inverse statement makes the surviving preimages under each $\tilde e_i$ distinct, so every positive-degree word residue has a nonzero raising edge — in $V(\lambda)$ it is a $\tilde f_i$-predecessor and the string-component argument gives the inverse, in $U_q^-$ the identity $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}$ on the lattice does. If a field vector has all raisings in the lattice, take its minimal $q$-pole $N$; if $N>0$, its normalized nonzero residue is killed by all raisings, a contradiction, so the vector lies in the lattice. These least-index choices give a basis of the graded direct sum. Thus $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ is a free $A_0$-module by [F2] with $\mathbb Q(q)\otimes_{A_0}\mathcal L(\lambda)=V(\lambda)$ by step 1.1, stable under both operators by A(r); $\mathcal B(\lambda)$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $\mathcal L(\lambda)/q\mathcal L(\lambda)$ with the graded decomposition and operator stability by B, D and the definition, and the partial-inverse axiom is C(r); hence $(\mathcal L(\lambda),\mathcal B(\lambda))$ is a crystal basis in the sense of [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]. The transported labels are the original ones by [F6]. No global $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness, tensor-crystal theorem or $A_0$-perfectness premise is used; AC is inherited from the field-form supplier used in step 9.2, as declared in [F9].

boundaries.evidence: The induction is anchored at $r=0$, where $Q_+(0)=\{0\}$ and the only component is $\mathcal L(\lambda)_\lambda=A_0v_\lambda$, respectively $\mathcal L(\infty)_0=A_0\mathbf 1$; step 1.2 checks all clauses A-O there and at $r=1$, so the base of the loop is the empty-sum case.
The height-zero base in step 1.2 is the highest/unit line. Endpoint and killed-residue zeros are treated in steps 2.1, 7.1, 10.1 and 11.1, with raising projection restricted to surviving residues.

The base $r=1$ is step 1.2: strings of length $\lambda(h_i)+1$ at a highest vector, the unit $\mathbf 1$ in $U_q^-$, the one-dimensional residue sets, and the top tensors, all checked exactly before the induction begins.

No finite-dimensionality of whole modules or separating original torus is assumed. Finite component dimensions and the form suppliers are explicit prerequisites. Step 1.3 proves the auxiliary-weight loop and restricts it to the transported original modules; auxiliary probes need not lie in the transported label subgroup.

String endpoints are handled at $n=0$ and at the bottom: steps 2.1 and 6.2 treat top and bottom components with the endpoint terms zero, and step 9.2 decomposes the tensor lattice with the boundary term $v_\lambda\otimes\mathcal L(\mu)$ separated.

AC is declared conservatively through the field-form supplier. Step 7.2 constructs and separates the same form on finite components without AC; step 9.2 selects only one finite basis and its uniquely determined field dual, so it adds no simultaneous choice.

The partial-inverse clause C(r) is a biconditional of the loop; its forward direction for a surviving module edge is step 11.1, which extracts strings and applies the lower partial-inverse clauses to produce the inverse edge.

Step 10.1 lifts a module residue through the current-height word-image result L(r), uses O(r) and J(r), and projects its lowering predecessor by M(r). It does not invoke only lower-height L and O for a current-height residue.

risk_review.notes: Read the complete 23-step authored induction and complete JKK §7 pp.24–49, including 7.3–7.36, plus Kashiwara pp.499–500 and the full finite-support regularization supplier. Checked A–O dependency order: field spans/base 0–1; coefficient extraction and tensor rectangles; E before M/L; finite large-weight injection from singular-generator degree bounds; first-top tensor boundary and Nakayama; simultaneous improvement of finite/large/half pole bounds; I/O/B; unit string pairing; corrected module= C_nu times half constant term; finite-dual transfer before special F and J; both directions of C and then N/D/K; general F/G. N before D uses the already proved C to find a nonzero raising of the common word image, so no circular independence. The added finite polynomial form/separation alternative uses e-prime e-double-prime q-commutation and large-weight injectivity, not a global dual-basis choice. Empty pieces, zero coroot labels, pure words, killed bottom and surviving-only raising are covered. Inherited AC is declared; least rational-index finite bases give the direct-sum basis without extra simultaneous choice. Reader reconstruction preserves all A–O interfaces and is sound. Amended F4: only graded tensor maps have the stated uniqueness, and uniqueness of S Phi concerns its cyclic domain, not the entire tensor retraction S. No Statement change or same-height perfectness/global-basis assumption.

and let $(\ ,\ )$ be a bilinear form on $U_q^-$.

(i) **Existence and symmetry.** A bilinear form with $(1,1)=1$ and
$(F_iP,Q)=(P,e_i'(Q))$ for all $i,P,Q$ exists on $U_q^-$; every normalized
homogeneous form satisfying these conditions is symmetric; and by the
uniqueness of [[def-the-lusztig-kashiwara-bilinear-form-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]
there is exactly one such form. No separate right-adjunction formula for
$(P,QF_i)$ is asserted: in the rank-one subalgebra a formula
$(P,QF_i)=c\,(e_i''P,Q)$ with constant $c$ is false, as the explicit values in
(iv) show.

(ii) **Orthogonality.** $(U_q^-[-\nu],U_q^-[-\mu])=0$ whenever $\nu\ne\mu$.

(iii) **Nondegeneracy.** For every $0\ne x\in U_q^-$ there is $y\in U_q^-$ with
$(x,y)\ne0$; equivalently, the restriction of the form to each
finite-dimensional graded piece $U_q^-[-\nu]$ is nondegenerate.

(iv) **Integrality on the word lattice.** Let $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) and let $W\subseteq U_A^-$ be the
$A$-span of the monomials $F_{i_1}\cdots F_{i_k}$ ($k\ge0$). Then
$W\subseteq U_A^-$ (because $F_i^k=[k]_i!F_i^{(k)}$ and $[k]_i!\in A$), and
$(W,W)\subseteq A$. On the larger divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ the form is
*not* $A$-valued: in the rank-one subalgebra generated by a single $F_i$ one
has, for all $a,b\ge0$,
$$(F_i^{(a)},F_i^{(b)})=\delta_{ab}\frac{q_i^{-a(a-1)/2}}{[a]_i!}=\delta_{ab}\frac{1}{[a]_{q_i^2}!},$$
in particular $(F_i^{(2)},F_i^{(2)})=1/(1+q_i^2)\notin A$; here
$[a]_{q_i^2}!=\prod_{m=1}^a(1+q_i^2+\cdots+q_i^{2(m-1)})$. Globally, with
$A_{\mathrm{loc}}=A[s^{-1}:s\in S]$, the localization of $A$ inverting the
multiplicative set $S$ generated by $\{[r]_i!:i\in I,r\ge1\}$ (equivalently inverting the
Gaussian factorials $[r]_{q_i^2}!$), one has
$(U_A^-,U_A^-)\subseteq A_{\mathrm{loc}}$: divided-power words are word
vectors divided by finite products of these factorials. This is an exact
denominator bound, not an $A$-integrality assertion on $U_A^-$ in this
normalization.

Let $\lambda\in P$, let $M(\lambda)$ be the Verma module with its canonical
$P$-label grading and highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]]), and let
$\sigma$ be the linear contravariant anti-involution of
[[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]]
($\sigma(K_h)=K_h$, $\sigma(E_i)=q_iF_iK_i^{-1}$,
$\sigma(F_i)=q_i^{-1}K_iE_i$).

(i) **Existence and uniqueness.** Define the $\lambda$-weight functional
$\eta\colon U_q(\mathfrak g)\to\mathbb Q(q)$ by $\eta(y):=$ the coefficient of
$v_\lambda$ in $yv_\lambda$ (so $\eta(y)$ is unchanged by adding an element of
the Verma ideal $J(\lambda)$, and $\eta(1)=1$). Then
$$B\bigl(av_\lambda,bv_\lambda\bigr):=\eta\bigl(\sigma(a)b\bigr)\qquad(a,b\in U_q^-)$$
is a well-defined bilinear form on $M(\lambda)$; it is homogeneous, normalized
($B(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$) and $\sigma$-contravariant,
$B(xu,v)=B(u,\sigma(x)v)$. It is the unique such form on $M(\lambda)$, in the
sense of [[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]].

(ii) **Radical and descent.** The radical
$\operatorname{rad}B=\{u:B(u,M(\lambda))=0\}$ equals the sum $N(\lambda)$ of all
proper graded submodules of $M(\lambda)$; consequently $B$ descends to a
nondegenerate normalized $\sigma$-contravariant form on the simple highest
weight quotient $L(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$.

(iii) **Rank-one norms and dominant singular vectors.** If
$m_i=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$ (that is, $\lambda$ dominant), then for
every $r\ge0$
$$B\bigl(F_i^{(r)}v_\lambda,F_i^{(r)}v_\lambda\bigr)=q_i^{\,r(m_i-r)}\binom{m_i}{r}_i,$$
with the Gaussian binomial interpreted as $0$ for $r>m_i$; in particular each
$F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$ lies in the radical, so $B$ factors through the Serre
quotient $M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$. (The same
computation proves the norm formula for every $\lambda$ and all $r$ for which
the right-hand side is read with $m_i=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle$.)

(iv) **Ordinary simplicity.** Let $V$ be an integrable cyclic graded quotient of
$M(\lambda)$ with support in $\lambda-Q_+$ on which the descended form is
nondegenerate. Then $V$ is simple as an ordinary module (not only as a graded
module).

(v) **Integrality of the lattice values.** If $\lambda$ is integral and
$V_A:=U_Av_\lambda=U_A^-v_\lambda\subseteq L(\lambda)$ is the highest lattice of
the Lusztig form ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]), then
$B(V_A,V_A)\subseteq A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. No perfectness of $B$ over $A$ is
asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Residue orthonormality. Induct on $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$. For residues $b,b'\in\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$ choose $i$ with $\tilde e_ib\neq0$; then $b=\tilde f_i\tilde e_ib$ by clause C(r) and J(r), so the adjunction of [F1] gives $\langle b,b'\rangle_0=\langle\tilde e_ib,\tilde e_ib'\rangle_0$. If $\tilde e_ib'=0$ this is $0$; otherwise $\tilde e_ib'$ lies at lower height and, by the lower-height orthonormality and the injectivity of $\tilde e_i$ on the surviving string positions, the pairing is $\delta_{b,b'}$. The top vector has norm $1$, and since all $a_{ii}=2$ the operator $Q_i$ of [F2] is the identity, so no norm larger than $1$ occurs.

Perfection and self-duality. By step 1.1 the Gram matrix of the finite component in the residue basis is congruent to the identity modulo $q$; by [F3] its determinant is a unit of $A_0$ and the matrix is invertible, so the pairing on the finite component is perfect and the dual lattice with respect to the field form equals the lattice itself: $\mathcal L^\vee=\mathcal L$.

The negative half. For $U_q^-$ use the corrected degree/colour comparison of [F2] with a sufficiently large regularised dominant weight: $\pi_\lambda$ is a lattice isomorphism on the component and a bijection on its crystal residue sets, and $C_\nu\equiv1\bmod q$; hence the Gram residue of the half lattice is the identity as well, and the same finite-matrix argument gives $A_0$-valuedness, perfection and $\mathcal L(\infty)^\vee=\mathcal L(\infty)$ on each finite component.

The norm criterion. Suppose $\langle x,x\rangle\in A_0$ but $x$ has a pole in the lattice. Choose the minimal $N>0$ with $q^Nx\in\mathcal L$ and let $\bar x\neq0$ be its residue. In the orthonormal residue basis of step 1.1, $\langle\bar x,\bar x\rangle$ is a sum of squares of rational coordinates, hence a positive rational; on the other hand $q^{2N}\langle x,x\rangle\in qA_0$ has residue $0$, a contradiction. Therefore $\mathcal L=\{x:\langle x,x\rangle\in A_0\}$ inside the field scalar extension.
Choice. The only choice used is the inherited hypothesis of the negative-half field form, already declared in [F2]; the finite Gram computations and the norm criterion use no further choice.

boundaries.evidence: On a zero component the Gram matrix is empty with determinant $1$ and the orthonormality claim is vacuous; step 1.1's induction starts at height zero, where the component is the one-dimensional span of the top residue $v_\lambda$ (respectively $\mathbf 1$) and the claim reads $\langle b,b\rangle_0=1$.

A vanishing norm forces the zero vector: step 4.1's norm criterion takes a minimal pole $N>0$ and a nonzero residue $\bar x$, in the orthonormal residue basis of step 1.1 the value $\langle\bar x,\bar x\rangle$ is a sum of squares of rational coordinates, which is positive unless $\bar x=0$, contradicting the nonzero choice of $\bar x$.

The rank-one case is the base of the induction in step 1.1: $\langle b,b\rangle_0=1$ for the single residue of a top component, and step 2.1's Gram matrix is the one-by-one matrix $(1)$, whose determinant is a unit of $A_0$.

All determinants are formed on finite label or root components only, so no infinite Gram determinant appears; the negative half is reduced componentwise in step 3.1 through the large-weight isomorphism and the congruence $C_\nu\equiv1\bmod q$, and no largeness hypothesis remains in the final statement.

The height induction of step 1.1 terminates at the top of each component where the string has one vertex, and step 4.1's boundary is the minimal pole $N>0$ separating $\mathcal L$ from its proper superlattices; both ends of the component argument are thus disposed of explicitly.

Step 5.1 records that the only choice used is the inherited hypothesis of the negative-half field form, already declared in [F2]; the finite Gram computations of steps 1.1-2.1, the reduction of step 3.1 and the norm criterion of step 4.1 add no further choice.

The set equality $\mathcal L=\{x:\langle x,x\rangle\in A_0\}$ is proved as two inclusions with step 4.1 supplying the non-obvious one; read forward, every $x\in\mathcal L$ satisfies $\langle x,x\rangle\in A_0$ by the integrality of the normalised polarization and the $A_0$-valuedness proved in steps 1.1-2.1.

Read in reverse, $\langle x,x\rangle\in A_0$ forces $x\in\mathcal L$; this is exactly the minimal-pole contradiction of step 4.1, so the two inclusions together give the displayed set equality and both directions are established.

risk_review.notes: Checked all five steps against grand-loop 7.2/8.1 and both exact form suppliers; read JKK Corollary 7.37, Remark 7.38 and Lemma 7.39 pp.48–49. Module induction starts at top norm one; C gives a nonzero raising for each positive-height basis vertex and injectivity on surviving edges. Residue adjunction proves orthonormality with Q_i=id for real roots. Lifting the finite residue basis gives Gram matrix congruent to identity, hence unit determinant/perfection. Large-weight component isomorphism and C_nu=1 mod q transfer both A0-valuedness and residue identity to half; this does not assume equality of the two field forms. Finite-support norm sum of rational squares excludes a pole, including x=0. Self-duality is componentwise and extends to the finite-support direct sum. Inherited AC is declared, and no simultaneous basis selection is used. Reader distinction of forms and corrected comparison citation is sound.
